## Brown v. Summit Realty

599 S.W.3d 211 · Mo. App. W.D. · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that landlords must engage in an interactive process regarding reasonable accommodation requests and cannot summarily reject them as unreasonable. The judgment was remanded for a proper analysis of feasibility and undue burden. The tenant filed a lawsuit alleging that the landlord engaged in discriminatory practices by refusing to make reasonable accommodations for their disability, as requested under the Fair Housing Act. The landlord argued that the requested modifications were structurally impractical and imposed an undue financial burden on the property owner. The trial court entered judgment for the landlord, concluding that the requests for specific structural changes were unreasonable as a matter of law given the age and design of the residential apartment complex. The appellate court reviewed the standard for 'reasonable accommodation' and the burden-shifting framework applicable to discrimination claims in housing. The court determined that the trial court failed to adequately weigh the necessity of the accommodation against the actual costs and technical feasibility. The decision was reversed and remanded, with the appellate court directing the lower court to apply a more rigorous analysis of the interactive process between the landlord and the disabled tenant required by federal and state fair housing regulations.

## Brown v. Tri-State Bank

713 S.W.2d 861 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1986 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while the bank had a right to repossess, there was sufficient evidence that it did not act in good faith when accelerating the debt, thus making the repossession wrongful. The plaintiffs sued Tri-State Bank for wrongful repossession. The bank had repossessed collateral, claiming a default had occurred. The plaintiffs contended that the default was fabricated or that they were not in default, making the repossession unauthorized. The court examined the terms of the security agreement, which allowed for acceleration of the debt upon 'insecurity' or default. The legal standard for 'good faith' acceleration of debt was at the center of the dispute. The court discussed the requirements for a secured party to act in good faith when exercising a right to repossess without judicial process (self-help repossession). This case provides a clear look at the balance between a secured party's rights to repossess collateral and the debtor's right to be protected from arbitrary or bad-faith actions. It underscores the high standard of conduct required by lenders when using self-help measures to protect their security interests.

## Brown v. Tyson Foods

565 S.W.3d 255 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an injury occurring on the employer's premises during an unpaid lunch break is compensable. The 'on-premises' rule provides coverage for injuries sustained during reasonable breaks on site. The claimant, a worker at a poultry processing facility, suffered an injury when she slipped on a wet floor in a common area during her lunch break. The employer contested the claim, arguing that the injury did not arise 'out of and in the course of employment' because the break period was unpaid and the employee was not performing work duties at the time. The Commission determined that the injury was compensable because it occurred on the employer's premises during a time that was functionally necessary for the employee's workday. The employer appealed, arguing that the 'coming and going' rule and the 'lunch break' exclusion should prevent the claimant from recovering. The appellate court evaluated the scope of the 'on-premises' exception. The court held that injuries occurring on the employer's property during a break are generally considered work-related if the area is part of the work environment. The court rejected the employer's narrow interpretation and affirmed the award, finding that the break activity was incidental to the employment.

## Brown v. Tyson Foods, Inc.

641 S.W.3d 315 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the Commission's ruling, holding that the finding of causation was supported by competent and substantial evidence. It emphasized the deference given to the Commission's assessment of expert medical testimony. The employee claimed a work-related shoulder injury caused by repetitive lifting. Tyson Foods challenged the medical causation, claiming the condition was age-related arthritis. The Labor and Industrial Relations Commission found the injury compensable, determining that the work activity was the prevailing factor in the shoulder condition. The employer appealed, arguing that the Commission misread the medical evidence and failed to give proper weight to the physician who attributed the condition to natural degeneration. The court's role was to determine whether the Commission's findings were supported by competent and substantial evidence. The court examined the definition of 'prevailing factor' and whether the medical expert testimony supported the Commission's finding of causation. The opinion highlights the standard of review on appeal, specifically noting that the court does not re-weigh evidence but rather determines if the record as a whole supports the findings reached by the administrative body.

## Brown v. Tyson Foods, Inc.

563 S.W.3d 815 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the calculation of the average weekly wage must include all earnings, including overtime. The court rejected the employer's attempt to exclude overtime hours from the total weekly wage calculation. The employee suffered a hand injury while operating machinery at a meat processing plant. The dispute centered on the calculation of the 'average weekly wage' for the purpose of determining permanent partial disability benefits. The employer argued that the calculation should include only the base pay rate, excluding intermittent overtime hours that were not guaranteed by the contract. The employee contended that the average weekly wage should reflect his actual earnings over the preceding fifty-two weeks. The court reviewed the statutory formula for determining wages in cases of variable income. This case involved the interpretation of 'seasonal' or 'irregular' employment as defined by Missouri labor laws. The court analyzed the intent of the compensation system, which aims to replace a portion of the worker's lost earning capacity. The decision provides clarity on how employers should report and calculate wages for hourly workers who frequently fluctuate in their weekly hours, ensuring consistency across various industries and compensation models.

## Brown v. Van Noy

879 S.W.2d 667 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 1994 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an owner is strictly liable for damages caused by a dog if they have knowledge of its dangerous propensities. Because the plaintiff was an invitee and not a trespasser, the defendant owed a duty of reasonable care. The plaintiff sued the defendant for injuries sustained during a dog attack. The legal theory was grounded in strict liability for domestic animals with known dangerous propensities, as well as negligence in the failure to secure the animal. The defendant argued that the dog had no prior history of aggression and that the plaintiff was trespassing at the time of the incident, thereby limiting the owner's liability. The court conducted an extensive review of Missouri's 'dog bite' statutes and common law regarding animal control. The evidentiary phase centered on the defendant's prior knowledge of the dog's behavior and the measures taken to contain the animal. The court evaluated whether the plaintiff's status on the property barred a claim for negligence, leading to a discussion on the duties owed to trespassers versus invitees.

## Buchanan v. Mitchell

785 S.W.2d 317 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1990 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that while the implied warranty of habitability exists in Missouri, a tenant cannot unilaterally withhold rent without first providing proper notice and opportunity for the landlord to cure the defects. The breach must be substantial to justify the refusal to pay. The landlord brought an action for unlawful detainer against a residential tenant who failed to pay rent. The tenant claimed that the property was uninhabitable due to severe mold, plumbing issues, and lack of adequate heat, and argued that these conditions constituted a breach of the implied warranty of habitability. The trial court granted possession to the landlord, finding that the tenant's evidence of uninhabitable conditions was insufficient to excuse the non-payment of rent. The tenant appealed, challenging the trial court's application of the warranty of habitability doctrine. The appellate court reviewed the scope of the implied warranty of habitability in Missouri for residential properties. The court analyzed whether the tenant's withholding of rent was a permissible remedy for the landlord's failure to provide essential services. The discussion focused on the necessity of showing that the landlord had notice of the defects and a reasonable opportunity to repair them. The case highlights the standards that residential tenants must meet in order to successfully assert the breach of warranty of habitability as a defense against a summary eviction action brought by a landlord.

## Buchanan v. State

551 S.W.3d 672 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an inmate must show actual prejudice to a non-frivolous legal claim to prevail on a Section 1983 access-to-courts claim. Because the prisoner failed to show the outcome of his case was harmed, the claim was dismissed. This case involved a prisoner's Section 1983 claim regarding the denial of access to the courts, alleging that prison officials intentionally interfered with his ability to file legal documents. The right of access to the courts is a fundamental civil right protected under the Due Process Clause of the 14th Amendment. The court analyzed whether the inmate had suffered 'actual injury' to his litigation efforts, a necessary component for a constitutional access-to-court claim. The analysis scrutinized the prison's mail and legal assistance procedures to determine if they were reasonably related to legitimate penological interests as established by Turner v. Safley. The appellate court focused on whether the administrative delays and denial of supplies constituted a constitutional violation or were merely operational inconveniences within the prison system.

## Buchheit v. Missouri Department of Corrections

98 S.W.3d 568 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the evidence was sufficient to support the jury's verdict on both the harassment and retaliation claims. It upheld the award of compensatory damages, finding the jury instructions to be appropriate. A correctional officer brought an action against the Department of Corrections for sexual harassment and retaliation under the Missouri Human Rights Act. The plaintiff alleged that she was subjected to a hostile work environment by coworkers and supervisors, including offensive comments and physical intimidation. After reporting the behavior, she claimed that her shifts were changed and she was denied overtime, which she interpreted as retaliatory. The state argued that the actions were based on staffing needs. The trial court entered judgment on a jury verdict in favor of the plaintiff for both harassment and retaliation. On appeal, the defendant challenged the jury instructions and the sufficiency of the evidence. The appellate court reviewed the standards for employer liability for coworker

Second stored summary harassment, noting the requirement that an employer must take prompt and effective remedial action once it is aware of the offensive behavior. The court also addressed the calculation of damages for emotional distress.

## Buck v. Monsanto Co.

281 S.W.3d 375 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2009 · Missouri

Holding: Expert testimony in complex negligence cases must meet the gatekeeping requirements for scientific reliability. If key testimony is properly excluded as unreliable, the plaintiff cannot meet the burden of proving causation, leading to summary judgment. The plaintiffs brought a negligence and nuisance claim against a corporation for alleged chemical contamination of their property. The central legal question involved the admissibility of expert testimony under the Daubert standard and whether the plaintiffs' proof of causation was sufficient. The defendant argued that the plaintiffs' experts relied on speculative data and failed to scientifically link the chemical levels to any specific health damage. The trial court excluded the plaintiffs' key expert testimony, resulting in a summary judgment for the defendant. On appeal, the court reviewed the trial court's role as a gatekeeper of expert evidence. The appellate court found that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in excluding the testimony, as it lacked a reliable scientific foundation. The appellate court affirmed the dismissal, noting that without competent expert evidence on causation, the plaintiffs could not prove their case of negligence or harm resulting from the defendant's industrial operations.

## Bucklew v. Precythe

139 S. Ct. 1112 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2019 · Federal

Holding: The Eighth Amendment does not require that executions be painless. A prisoner challenging an execution method must demonstrate that the state's method causes avoidable, severe pain and must provide a readily available, feasible alternative that significantly reduces that risk. Bucklew, a death row inmate in Missouri, challenged his execution by lethal injection on the basis that his unique medical condition, cavernous hemangioma, would cause him to choke on his own blood, resulting in severe pain. He sought to use nitrogen hypoxia as an alternative method of execution. The Supreme Court held that the Eighth Amendment does not guarantee a painless death. Following the precedent of Baze and Glossip, the Court reaffirmed that a prisoner challenging an execution method must prove the state's chosen method causes 'superadded' pain that can be avoided by a 'readily available' alternative. The Court ruled that Bucklew failed to demonstrate that his proposed alternative, nitrogen hypoxia, was 'readily available' and 'feasible.' The decision underscored the high burden placed on death row inmates to substantiate Eighth Amendment claims and reaffirmed the judicial deference afforded to state-mandated execution protocols when the prisoner fails to meet the stringent criteria for establishing a constitutional violation.

## Buckley v. Fitzsimmons

509 U.S. 259 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1993 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that prosecutors are entitled only to qualified immunity, not absolute immunity, when they act in an investigatory capacity or make statements to the press. Absolute immunity only applies to actions taken in the role of an advocate. A man was arrested and later acquitted for a violent crime. He sued the prosecutors under 42 U.S.C. 1983, alleging that they had fabricated evidence during the preliminary investigation and made false statements at a press conference. The prosecutors moved to dismiss, claiming they were protected by absolute immunity, which shields prosecutors from liability for activities closely associated with the judicial phase of the criminal process. The Seventh Circuit held that the prosecutors were entitled to absolute immunity for all their actions. The Supreme Court reviewed this decision to determine the scope of prosecutorial immunity, distinguishing between a prosecutor's role as an advocate in the courtroom and their role as an investigator gathering evidence before an indictment.

## Buckner v. City of O'Fallon

484 S.W.3d 813 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that attorney-client privilege in a public body is limited to communications involving legal advice or pending litigation. Administrative emails are not protected simply because they are sent to or from legal counsel. The plaintiff filed a petition against the City of O'Fallon alleging violations of the Sunshine Law after the city denied a request for specific government emails. The city argued that the emails were between the city attorney and staff and thus protected by attorney-client privilege. The appellate court had to weigh the attorney-client privilege exemption against the Sunshine Law's mandate of openness. The court recognized that while the Sunshine Law allows closed meetings and records for legal matters, the privilege does not cover every communication involving a lawyer. The court performed an in-camera review of the contested records to determine which portions were truly related to pending litigation or legal advice and which were simply administrative communications. This case clarifies the standard for applying attorney-client privilege in the context of the Sunshine Law, ensuring that the privilege is not used as a blanket excuse to hide municipal communications from public view.

## Bugg v. City of St. Louis

Holding: The court held that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in limiting the scope of statistical evidence presented. It affirmed that individual disparate treatment claims require a specific, individualized showing of discriminatory intent, not just generalized statistical trends. A former police officer sued the city alleging that he was subjected to racial discrimination in his disciplinary proceedings. The plaintiff presented statistical evidence and anecdotal accounts of other officers' experiences to argue a systemic pattern of discrimination within the department. The city countered that the disciplinary actions were based on documented policy violations. The appellate court evaluated the relevance of evidence concerning 'other bad acts' and the admissibility of statistical data in individual disparate treatment cases. The court explored the limits of what a plaintiff must prove to shift the burden to the employer. The decision focused on the gatekeeping role of the trial court in determining whether such statistical evidence is probative enough to allow a jury to infer discriminatory intent. ## Building Erection Services Co. v. Plastic Sales, Inc.

163 S.W.3d 472 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2005 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the doctrine of substantial performance applied, preventing the general contractor from withholding all payment. The subcontractor was entitled to the contract price less the cost of remedying minor identified defects. This contract dispute arose from a construction project where a subcontractor sought payment from the general contractor for services rendered. The central issue was whether the subcontractor had satisfied all conditions precedent to receive final payment under the agreement. The general contractor alleged that the subcontractor's work was defective and that it had failed to provide the necessary lien waivers as required by the contract. The subcontractor argued that it had substantially performed its obligations under the contract and that any defects were minor and remediable. The dispute focused on the application of the doctrine of substantial performance and whether the general contractor could withhold the entire final payment despite the completion of the majority of the work. The court examined the construction contract's language concerning payment milestones, inspection rights, and the requirements for final release of retainage. This case provided clarity on the standards required for proving substantial performance in construction litigation and the limitations on withholding payment when a project is largely finished.

## Bullard v. Blue Hills Bank

575 U.S. 238 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2015 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Supreme Court held that an order denying confirmation of a Chapter 13 bankruptcy plan is not a final order for purposes of appellate review. Consequently, the debtor must wait until a plan is confirmed or the case is dismissed to seek an appeal. This case involved a debtor, Roy Bullard, who filed for Chapter 13 bankruptcy. The bankruptcy court denied his proposed repayment plan, ruling that it was not confirmable under the Bankruptcy Code. Bullard attempted to appeal this denial, arguing that it was a final, appealable order. The appellate court and eventually the Supreme Court addressed whether the denial of a plan confirmation constitutes a final order for appellate purposes. The Supreme Court examined the procedural structure of Chapter 13, noting that plan confirmation is the central event of the process. If a plan is denied, the debtor is permitted to propose a new one, meaning the litigation process is ongoing rather than concluded. The Court determined that allowing immediate appeals of every denial would lead to piecemeal litigation, consuming judicial resources and delaying the distribution of assets to creditors. The ruling emphasized the need for finality in the bankruptcy process, concluding that only the confirmation or denial of a confirmable plan that ends the bankruptcy case or resolves a discrete dispute qualifies as a final order.

## Bultemeyer v. Fort Wayne Community Schools

100 F.3d 1281 · 7th Cir. · 1996 · Federal

Holding: The court held that employers have a heightened duty to engage in the interactive process when an employee has a known mental disability that prevents them from adequately communicating their own needs. Bultemeyer, a school custodian, suffered from bipolar disorder and schizophrenia. After a leave of absence, he was returned to a job with different, more stressful responsibilities, which led to a nervous breakdown. He eventually resigned and sued under the ADA, claiming that the employer did not accommodate his mental disability. The district court dismissed the claim, but the Seventh Circuit reversed. The court explained that when a plaintiff has a mental disability that makes it difficult for them to express their needs, the employer has a heightened duty to engage in the interactive process. The school district failed to communicate effectively with the employee's doctors after receiving notice that he could not perform the assigned duties. The court held that the school's failure to follow up properly constituted a violation of the interactive process mandate, especially when the employer had reason to know of the severity of the employee's mental health issues.

## Burch v. City of St. Louis

615 S.W.3d 928 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: A dangerous condition of public property can include natural features, like trees, if they are situated such that they pose a risk to users of public property and the entity had notice of the defect. The duty to maintain public paths extends to ensuring the safety of the immediate surrounding area. The plaintiff was injured while riding a bicycle on a public path when a tree branch fell, striking the cyclist. The plaintiff sued the City, alleging that the city was negligent in its maintenance of the path and the surrounding landscaping. The City asserted immunity, claiming the tree was not part of the 'public property' that carries an exception to sovereign immunity. The court examined the definition of 'dangerous condition of public property.' The appellate court concluded that the city's duty to maintain public ways includes the duty to ensure that trees adjacent to the path do not present an unreasonable risk of harm to users. The court found that if the tree was diseased and the city had notice, the condition could be considered a 'dangerous condition' of the property. The court reversed the trial court's dismissal, holding that the plaintiff sufficiently pleaded that the tree condition was a dangerous condition of public property.

## Burch v. HCA Health Services

542 S.W.3d 395 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the Commission's determination of causation is a factual issue supported by substantial evidence. It affirmed the rejection of medical testimony that the Commission found to be speculative. The employee filed for workers' compensation regarding a repetitive stress injury involving her wrists. The case was contested based on the sufficiency of the medical evidence regarding the 'prevailing factor' of her condition. The Commission denied the claim, stating that the medical expert's testimony was too speculative to support a finding that the employment was the prevailing factor. The employee appealed, arguing that the Commission misread the medical evidence and the applicable standard of law. The Court of Appeals analyzed the Commission's reliance on the expert testimony, acknowledging that the Commission is the final arbiter of fact and that it is authorized to disregard evidence it deems unpersuasive. The court confirmed that there was substantial evidence in the record to support the Commission's conclusion that the claimant's condition was multifactorial and not primarily caused by her work duties. The decision was affirmed, with the court noting that it lacked the authority to re-examine the credibility of the medical professionals who testified during the original hearing.

## Burch v. Kansas City Board of Police Commissioners

505 S.W.3d 335 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the de minimis doctrine is not applicable when the work performed is regular, recurring, and results in a measurable accumulation of unpaid time. The employees were entitled to compensation for the mandatory pre-shift duties. Police dispatchers brought a suit against the Board of Police Commissioners for failure to pay overtime for the time they were required to spend logging into systems and reviewing status updates before their official shifts began. The Board argued that this time was de minimis and part of standard transition procedures that were not intended to be compensable. The litigation addressed the application of the 'de minimis' doctrine to pre-shift computer tasks in the public sector. The plaintiffs demonstrated that these tasks were recurring and consumed significant collective time, even if individual sessions were brief. The court examined the administrative structure of the Board and the extent to which they were bound by the MMWL compared to specific municipal or departmental regulations. The case analyzed whether the 'de minimis' rule could be used to excuse repeated, daily non-payment of small increments of time that accumulated into substantial wage losses over the course of the employees' tenures.

## Burch v. Missouri Department of Corrections

569 S.W.3d 513 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the denial of benefits for an infectious disease, holding that the claimant failed to prove the work environment presented a unique, elevated risk. General community exposure is not compensable. The claimant sought workers compensation benefits after contracting an infectious disease while working in a correctional facility. The employer argued that the injury was not an 'accident' because it was not a sudden event, but rather a result of gradual exposure. The Commission determined that the disease was an occupational disease, not an accident, and that the claimant failed to prove that the risk of contracting the disease was greater in the workplace than in general public life. On appeal, the claimant argued that the high-density environment of the prison made the exposure a unique work-related hazard. The appellate court reviewed the law regarding infectious diseases in workers compensation, noting that for such a condition to be compensable, the claimant must demonstrate that the disease is a direct result of the specific employment conditions. The court concluded that the claimant failed to provide sufficient medical or epidemiological evidence to distinguish his workplace exposure from general community risk, and therefore, the denial of benefits was affirmed.

## Burch v. Nextage Realty

399 S.W.3d 831 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the employer failed to prove the plaintiff fell within the administrative exemption, as her primary duties were clerical rather than administrative. The decision reaffirmed that exemptions are to be narrowly construed and the employer bears the burden of proof. The plaintiff, a real estate office assistant, alleged that her employer failed to pay her the minimum wage and overtime. The employer countered that the plaintiff was exempt from these requirements because she worked in a 'bona fide executive, administrative, or professional capacity.' The central dispute involved the classification of the assistant's duties and whether they met the high threshold required for exemption from the Missouri Minimum Wage Law. The trial court ruled in favor of the employer, based on the job description and the employer's characterization of the role. On appeal, the Missouri Court of Appeals scrutinized the actual duties performed by the

Second stored summary plaintiff rather than the employer's title or job description. The court found that the plaintiff's tasks were primarily clerical in nature, lacking the required degree of independent decision-making and management authority over business operations to qualify for the administrative exemption. Consequently, the appellate court reversed the trial court's judgment, emphasizing that courts must engage in a functional analysis of the employee's role. The court reaffirmed that the burden of proving an exemption rests with the employer and that these exemptions must be narrowly construed against the employer to protect the remedial purpose of the wage statutes.

## Burchett v. Target Corp.

340 F.3d 510 · 8th Cir. · 2003 · Federal

Holding: The court held that for a mental condition to constitute a disability under the ADA, it must substantially limit a major life activity, not merely cause workplace stress. The duty to engage in an interactive process is satisfied by good-faith communication. The plaintiff, a retail employee, suffered from depression and anxiety that she claimed impeded her ability to work in a high-stress environment. She sought accommodations, including a transfer to a quieter department. Target denied the request, leading to her resignation and subsequent lawsuit for failure to accommodate and constructive discharge. The Eighth Circuit reviewed the case and held that the plaintiff failed to show that her depression substantially limited a major life activity. Furthermore, even if she were considered disabled, the court found the company had participated in the interactive process by meeting with the employee to discuss her needs. The court noted that 'stress' is generally not considered a disability, and the workplace environment at a retail store is inherently fast-paced. The court affirmed summary judgment for Target, stating that the plaintiff did not produce enough evidence to suggest her firing or resignation was the result of discriminatory animus rather than a failure to meet performance standards.

## Burlington Industries, Inc. v. Ellerth

524 U.S. 742 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1998 · Federal

3 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: Similar to Faragher, the Court established that an employer can be vicariously liable for a supervisor's creation of a hostile work environment. However, if no tangible employment action occurred, the employer may assert an affirmative defense by demonstrating reasonable preventive measures and the employee's failure to use them. Decided the same day as Faragher, Ellerth addressed employer liability for supervisory sexual harassment when no tangible employment action resulted. Ellerth claimed she was subjected to constant sexual harassment by a supervisor but was never fired, demoted, or subjected to other economic harm. The Court held that an employer is subject to vicarious liability for an actionable hostile

Second stored summary environment created by a supervisor, but it can raise an affirmative defense if no tangible employment action is taken. This defense requires proof of reasonable care by the employer to prevent and correct harassment and unreasonable failure by the employee to report or avoid harm.

## Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Railway Co. v. United States

556 U.S. 599 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2009 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: Apportionment of liability under CERCLA is appropriate when there is a reasonable basis for determining the contribution of each tortfeasor to the harm. A party cannot be held liable as an arranger for disposal of hazardous substances simply because it knew that some leakage might occur during the transport or handling of a useful product. This CERCLA case arose from the contamination of a site by a chemical distributor, Brown & Bryant, which operated on land leased in part from the Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Railway Company. The EPA and the State of California spent millions to clean up the site and sought to recover costs from the railway as an 'owner' and from Shell Oil Company, which had supplied chemicals to the distributor. The district court found both companies liable but apportioned only 9% of the cleanup costs to the railway, citing the limited usage of the land. The Ninth Circuit reversed, holding the railway jointly and severally liable and rejecting the apportionment. The Supreme Court reversed the Ninth Circuit, ruling that the district court had a sufficient factual basis to apportion liability based on the proportion of the site used by the railway and the duration of usage. The Court also held that Shell was not liable as an 'arranger' because it lacked the requisite intent to dispose of hazardous substances, as its primary purpose was the sale of a useful product.

## Burlington Northern & Santa Fe Railway Co. v. White

548 U.S. 53 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2006 · Federal

3 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court held that a retaliation claim is not limited to employment-related acts, but covers any action that would dissuade a reasonable worker from making a discrimination claim. The plaintiff complained of sexual harassment and subsequently experienced a change in her job responsibilities and a suspension. She sued for retaliation. The Supreme Court addressed what constitutes an 'adverse employment action' sufficient to support a retaliation claim. The Court held that an adverse action is any action that a reasonable employee would find 'materially adverse,' meaning it might dissuade a reasonable worker from making a charge of discrimination. This standard is broader than the 'tangible employment action' standard for underlying discrimination claims. This case is crucial for ADEA litigants because it expands the types of actions that can support a retaliation claim beyond just firing or demotion. A transfer to a less desirable shift, a change in working conditions, or even disciplinary actions might qualify as retaliatory if they would discourage an older worker from complaining about age discrimination. The decision provides essential protection for employees against subtle forms of workplace retaliation that stop short of immediate termination.

## Burnett v. Environmental Utilities, Inc.

2016 WL 8745650 (Mo. App. W.D. Mar. 15, 2016) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's dismissal of the wrongful termination claim and remanded the case. The court held that the plaintiff presented sufficient evidence to establish a submissible case for wrongful discharge in violation of public policy. The court found that the plaintiff's refusal to falsify reports constituted protected activity and that there was a genuine issue of material fact regarding whether the employer's stated reasons for termination were a pretext for retaliation for this protected activity. The plaintiff, a former employee, alleged wrongful termination in violation of public policy after he was fired for refusing to falsify environmental reports. He argued that his discharge contravened public policy favoring truthful reporting of environmental data. The employer maintained that the plaintiff was terminated for insubordination and poor job performance, unrelated to the alleged falsification of reports. The court considered the plaintiff's refusal to falsify the reports, his subsequent termination, and the employer's justification for the discharge. The critical question was whether the employer's stated reasons were pretextual.

## Burns v. Smith

303 S.W.3d 505 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2010 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an insurer that refuses to defend a claim without obtaining a judicial determination of non-coverage is estopped from asserting policy exclusions during an equitable garnishment action. The duty to defend is broader than the duty to indemnify and is triggered by the potential for coverage. This case addressed the intersection of insurance law and the doctrine of 'equitable garnishment' under Section 379.200. Following a personal injury judgment against the insured, the judgment creditor sought to garnish the proceeds of the insured's liability policy. The insurer resisted, arguing that it had no duty to defend or indemnify the insured because the underlying claim involved intentional conduct, which was excluded under the 'expected or intended' injury provision of the policy. The trial court determined that the insurer had breached its duty to defend, thereby estopping the insurer from asserting coverage exclusions in the subsequent garnishment action. The Supreme Court of Missouri analyzed the duty to defend versus the duty to indemnify. The court held that if an insurer refuses to defend without seeking a declaratory judgment, it does so at its own peril. Because the insurer failed to provide a defense, it was precluded from relitigating the issue of intent, which was a central component of the liability claim, in the garnishment phase of the case.

## Burson v. Freeman

504 U.S. 191 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1992 · Federal

Holding: The Court upheld the statute as constitutional. It held that states may limit speech near polling places to protect the integrity and secrecy of the voting process. Tennessee law prohibited the solicitation of votes and the display of campaign materials within 100 feet of the entrance to a polling place on election day. Mary Rebecca Freeman challenged the law, arguing that it burdened her right to political speech in a public forum. The case required the Court to balance the First Amendment right to free speech with the state's interest in preventing voter intimidation and ensuring election integrity. The Supreme Court held that the law was constitutional, recognizing that states have a compelling interest in protecting the right of their citizens to vote freely and for candidates of their choice without undue influence. The Court applied strict scrutiny, acknowledging that while the restriction was content-based, it was narrowly tailored to achieve the state's compelling objective of protecting the sanctity of the electoral process.

## Burt v. City of Fulton

936 S.W.2d 169 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1996 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while environmental reporting is protected under public policy, the plaintiff must still prove causation. The employer's evidence of a valid, non-discriminatory reason for termination successfully rebutted the claim. The plaintiff was a municipal employee who was fired after he complained about the city's waste disposal practices, which he alleged violated environmental regulations. He claimed that his termination violated public policy because his reports were necessary to protect the local environment and public health. The city countered that as an at-will employee, his termination was lawful and that his complaints did not meet the criteria for whistleblowing protections. The court evaluated the public policy exception as it applies to reports of environmental violations. It held that environmental laws and regulations serve as a clear expression of public policy intended to safeguard the welfare of the community. Therefore, reporting activities that contravene these laws is protected conduct. However, the court found that the evidence provided by the plaintiff did not clearly show that his complaints were the reason for his termination. The city provided evidence of budgetary constraints and reorganization as the basis for the decision to lay off the plaintiff. The court determined that the plaintiff failed to bridge the gap between his protected report and the adverse employment action, leading to an affirmation of the judgment in favor of the employer.

## Burt v. Moore

860 S.W.2d 378 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1993 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the finding of a prescriptive easement. The evidence established open, continuous, and adverse use of the lane for more than the statutory ten-year period.

Second stored summary The plaintiffs brought a lawsuit seeking a judicial declaration that they held a prescriptive easement over a lane located on the defendant's property. The defendant sought to obstruct the lane, preventing the plaintiffs from accessing the rear of their lot. The plaintiffs claimed they had used the lane daily for over thirty years to reach a garage. The defendant argued that the usage was sporadic and only with his express permission, thereby preventing the formation of a prescriptive easement. The appellate court scrutinized the evidence of the 'continuous' and 'adverse' use requirements. The court noted that 'continuous' does not mean 'constant,' but rather use that is consistent with the nature of the property and the needs of the user. The court found that the testimony clearly showed the plaintiffs used the lane as a matter of right and without seeking the defendant's permission for many years. The court rejected the defendant's claim of permissive use, stating that his failure to object to the long-standing, open use by the neighbors essentially made the use 'adverse' in the eyes of the law.

## Butters v. City of Independence

513 S.W.2d 418 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1974 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the insurance policy's language regarding 'damages because of bodily injury or property damage' did not extend to cover intangible civil rights violations. Therefore, the insurer was not obligated to defend the city in the underlying constitutional suit. This insurance coverage dispute arose from a municipal liability policy. The City of Independence sought coverage for damages resulting from a police action. The primary issue was whether the city's insurance policy provided coverage for civil rights violations and constitutional torts, or if it was strictly limited to traditional bodily injury and property damage. The insurer argued that the policy language did not contemplate coverage for legal liability arising from governmental acts of this nature. The trial court initially ruled against the city. On appeal, the Supreme Court of Missouri examined the policy definitions of 'occurrence' and 'damages.' The case highlighted the tension between the broadening scope of municipal liability under federal law and the limited, specific coverage provided by traditional liability policies held by cities. The court scrutinized the insurance contract to see if the language was broad enough to encompass non-physical harm. This case established important precedent regarding the interpretation of government entity insurance policies and the duty of insurers to defend against civil rights claims, emphasizing that the language of the policy remains the primary guide for the extent of the insurer's liability.

## C & J Delivery, Inc. v. Vinyard & Lee & Partners, Inc.

647 S.W.2d 564 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1983 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a professional service contract implies a duty to perform services according to professional standards. Failure to perform with due care constitutes a breach of contract, even in the absence of a guarantee of success. A corporate plaintiff sued a consulting firm for breach of a service contract, alleging that the firm's negligent tax advice led to penalties and interest owed to the IRS. The defendant argued that the contract did not include a guarantee of specific tax outcomes and that the plaintiff was responsible for its own business decisions. The trial court ruled in favor of the plaintiff, awarding damages for the professional services failure. On appeal, the defendant argued that the trial court erroneously interpreted the scope of the services contract and that the damages were too speculative. The appellate court focused on the language of the engagement letter. The court held that while a professional consultant does not guarantee the outcome of an IRS audit, the consultant is obligated to perform the contracted work with the degree of skill, care, and diligence expected of a reasonably competent professional in that field. The court found that the defendant's failure to provide accurate tax planning advice constituted a material breach of the professional services agreement, thereby affirming the trial court's finding of liability for the resulting financial loss.

## C & J Fertilizer, Inc. v. Allied Mutual Insurance Co.

227 N.W.2d 169 (Applied in MO) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1975 · Missouri

Holding: Commercial agreements, including security arrangements and associated insurance, should be interpreted to protect the reasonable expectations of the contracting parties. Ambiguous provisions should be construed against the party who drafted the language. While often cited in insurance and contract law, this case frequently appears in discussions regarding the 'reasonable expectations' of parties in commercial transactions, which is a foundational concept in the UCC. The court examined whether an insurance policy covering collateral was sufficient to protect the secured party's interest. The dispute arose when the insurer denied a claim for lost inventory, arguing that the policy language excluded the type of loss sustained. The court emphasized that the insured, a business entity, had a reasonable expectation that its inventory collateral was fully covered. The court's analysis touched upon the duties of good faith and the importance of ensuring that security interests are adequately protected by insurance, which is a common requirement in security agreements. This case illustrates the broader judicial philosophy that commercial documents should be interpreted in a way that aligns with the legitimate expectations of the parties involved in the secured transaction, rather than strictly focusing on obscure contract language.

## C & R Exploration, Inc. v. GAB Robins N. Am., Inc.

297 S.W.3d 114 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2009 · Missouri

Holding: The Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District, affirmed the trial court's judgment. The court found that C & R failed to present sufficient evidence to establish that GAB Robins breached the contract or failed to meet the applicable standard of care. The court also affirmed the award of unpaid fees to GAB Robins. This case involved a dispute over an insurance adjusting services contract. C & R Exploration, Inc. (C & R) hired GAB Robins North America, Inc. (GAB Robins) to provide adjusting services for insurance claims related to property damage. C & R alleged that GAB Robins breached its contract by failing to perform services diligently and competently, resulting in inadequate claim settlements. GAB Robins counterclaimed for unpaid fees. The trial court entered judgment in favor of GAB Robins on its counterclaim and against C & R on its breach of contract claim. C & R appealed, arguing that the trial court erred in its findings of fact and conclusions of law, particularly regarding the standard of care for insurance adjusters and the evidence of damages. The appellate court examined the terms of the contract and the evidence presented regarding the performance of the adjusting services.

## C.A.W. v. R.M.W.

388 S.W.3d 522 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's award of joint legal custody and primary physical custody to the father, along with the mother's visitation schedule. The court found these decisions to be in the children's best interests and supported by substantial evidence. This appeal concerned a divorce decree that allocated parental responsibilities, including child custody and visitation. The mother appealed the trial court's award of joint legal custody and primary physical custody to the father, as well as the established visitation schedule for herself. She argued that the custody and visitation orders were not in the children's best interests. The appellate court reviewed the evidence presented, including testimony concerning the parents' fitness and the children's relationships with each parent. The court applied the "best interests of the child" factors and examined the trial court's discretion. The court found that the trial court's findings were supported by substantial evidence and that the custody and visitation awards were in the children's best interests, despite the mother's arguments to the contrary.

## C.B. v. Mercy Hospital St. Louis

597 S.W.3d 256 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the hospital was not vicariously liable because the evidence failed to establish a clear case of apparent agency. The judgment in favor of the hospital was affirmed, emphasizing that the patient must rely on the hospital's representation of agency. This case involved a claim against a hospital and medical staff regarding the care provided during the birth of a child, which allegedly resulted in permanent injury. The central issue was whether the hospital could be held vicariously liable for the actions of a physician who was an independent contractor rather than an employee. The hospital argued that under Missouri law, it could not be held responsible for the independent contractor's alleged malpractice. The plaintiffs argued that the 'apparent agency' doctrine should apply, asserting that the hospital held the physician out to the public as their agent, thereby inducing the patient to rely on the hospital's reputation. The appellate court analyzed the scope of the apparent agency doctrine in Missouri and the specific facts demonstrating whether the patient reasonably believed the physician was an employee of the hospital. The decision provides critical guidance on how hospitals can defend against vicarious liability claims by clearly defining the nature of the relationships with medical personnel working within their facilities.

## C.B. v. S.B.

640 S.W.3d 315 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's judgment on debt allocation and child custody. The court held that the trial court's discretion was properly exercised in both financial and custodial determinations. The parties appealed the trial court's judgment concerning the division of debt and child custody. The wife sought to modify the debt allocation, arguing that the husband's gambling debt should not be classified as marital. The husband contested the custody ruling, claiming it did not provide him with enough residential time. The trial court classified the gambling debt as marital because it was incurred during the marriage and for family expenses, and it maintained the custody schedule to ensure consistency for the child. The appellate court reviewed the trial court's decision under the Murphy v. Carron standard, looking for substantial evidence and legal error. The court held that debt incurred during the marriage is typically presumed marital regardless of its origin unless shown otherwise. On custody, the appellate court found that the trial court's schedule was reasonable given the distance between the parents' homes. The court reaffirmed that trial court judges are in the best position to assess the logistics of custodial schedules and the characterization of marital liabilities, refusing to disturb the ruling where it did not reflect an abuse of judicial discretion.

## C.B. v. Shelter Mutual Insurance Co.

620 S.W.3d 315 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that there was sufficient evidence for the jury to find by a preponderance of the evidence that the fire was intentionally set by the insured. The court affirmed the judgment denying coverage. This dispute arose from a denial of a claim for property damage following a fire. The insurer denied coverage, alleging that the insured committed arson. The policy contained a condition that rendered the contract void in the event of intentional misrepresentation or fraud regarding the claim. The insurer provided evidence of an investigation by the fire marshal pointing toward an incendiary origin. The

Second stored summary insured claimed that the fire was accidental and that the insurer's investigation was biased. The case revolved around the burden of proof in arson-based coverage denials and the standard for 'clear and convincing evidence' required to void a policy. The court reviewed the evidence submitted by the insurer to determine if it satisfied the threshold for a finding of arson. The court also examined the insured's arguments regarding the adequacy of the investigation and the interpretation of the policy's fraud and concealment clause. The appeal centered on whether the jury verdict, which favored the insurer, was supported by sufficient evidence, and if any instructional errors occurred during the trial.

## C.B. v. St. Louis Public Schools

642 S.W.3d 378 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The sovereign immunity waiver for dangerous conditions on public property does not extend to claims of negligent supervision. Absent a physical defect in the property, a public entity remains immune from negligence claims related to the conduct of third parties. A student was injured by another student on school property and sued the school district for negligence, alleging failure to supervise. The district asserted sovereign immunity, claiming it was not liable for the intentional torts of students against one another. The trial court granted summary judgment to the district. The appellate court analyzed the scope of the sovereign immunity waiver for dangerous conditions. The court held that the failure to supervise does not constitute a 'dangerous condition' of the physical premises itself. Thus, the school district's immunity remained intact regarding the alleged negligent supervision. The court distinguished between physical hazards on school grounds, for which the district might be liable under the dangerous condition exception, and the administrative failure to supervise, which does not trigger the statutory waiver of sovereign immunity. The judgment for the district was affirmed.

## C.H. v. Mid-America Baptist Theological Seminary

576 S.W.3d 299 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The open and obvious doctrine precludes recovery in premises liability when a hazard is clearly visible. The distraction exception requires proof that the plaintiff was forced to divert their attention due to a circumstance beyond their control. In this premises liability case, the plaintiff sued for injuries sustained after slipping on ice on the defendant's parking lot. The key issue was the 'open and obvious' doctrine, which shields landowners from liability for conditions that are visible and apparent to a reasonable person. The defendant argued the ice was clearly visible and therefore they had no duty to warn or remove it. The trial court granted summary judgment, finding that the hazard was open and obvious as a matter of law. On appeal, the court reviewed whether the conditions necessitated a departure from the general rule. The plaintiff argued that the 'distraction exception' applied, suggesting the area was a busy thoroughfare. The appellate court noted that the distraction exception requires evidence of a specific, compelling distraction that would divert a reasonable person's attention from an obvious hazard. Finding no such evidence, the court affirmed the summary judgment, concluding that the defendant was not required to eliminate the hazard under the circumstances.

## C.H.C. Ltd. v. K.L.P.

936 S.W.2d 866 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1997 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the ruling that a tenant must strictly comply with notice requirements set forth in the lease agreement to claim constructive eviction. Without providing the landlord the opportunity to cure the defect as specified, the tenant is liable for remaining rent. The dispute involved a commercial landlord-tenant relationship where the landlord filed suit for rent due after the tenant vacated the premises before the end of the lease term. The tenant asserted that the premises were rendered uninhabitable due to a series of failures in the climate control system, which the landlord failed to remedy after repeated requests. The landlord argued that the tenant's departure constituted an anticipatory breach of the lease. The trial court ruled that the tenant's failure to provide written notice as required by the lease precluded the claim of constructive eviction. On appeal, the tenant argued that the landlord's failure to maintain essential systems excused the performance of the lease obligations, regardless of the notice formalities. The appellate court examined

Second stored summary the doctrine of constructive eviction in Missouri and the specific requirements for notice and opportunity to cure defects. The court also considered whether the landlord's refusal to address the climate control issue manifested an intent to waive the notice requirement. The review focused on the balance between contractual obligations and the tenant's right to operate in a habitable business environment, specifically looking at whether the condition was severe enough to justify termination of the lease agreement under the circumstances.

## C.J. v. Missouri Dept. of Mental Health

395 S.W.3d 609 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the plaintiff failed to show a violation of constitutional magnitude, as the acts did not meet the standard of professional indifference required for Section 1983. This case involved a Section 1983 suit brought by a patient against the Department of Mental Health, alleging that staff negligence led to constitutional violations of his rights to safety while under state care. The primary issue was whether the state, in holding an individual in a mental health facility, had a special relationship creating a duty to protect him from foreseeable harm. The court analyzed the 'Youngberg v. Romeo' standard, which dictates the rights of individuals in involuntary state custody. The appellate court held that while the facility has a duty to provide a safe environment, not every injury constitutes a constitutional violation under Section 1983. The court required the plaintiff to demonstrate that the state officials exhibited a level of professional negligence that amounted to a departure from accepted standards. The decision clarifies the threshold for liability for state agencies when individuals are under their mandatory supervision and the specific constitutional obligations they hold.

## C.J.L. v. Missouri Department of Social Services

443 S.W.3d 699 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while the state's interest is compelling, the procedures utilized must sufficiently protect the fundamental rights of the parents. It remanded for further proceedings to ensure compliance with due process. This case dealt with allegations of violations of familial rights and due process by a state administrative agency. The plaintiff argued that the Department of Social Services failed to provide sufficient procedural safeguards during a child custody investigation, thereby violating the parents' fundamental rights to family integrity. The state agency defended its actions by citing statutory authority and the primary goal of child safety. The court assessed the administrative proceedings against the backdrop of constitutional requirements for

Second stored summary parental rights, noting that while the state has a compelling interest in child protection, its actions must remain within constitutional bounds. The appellate court evaluated whether the agency's internal processes adequately protected the parents from arbitrary state intrusion. This decision is frequently cited regarding the limits of administrative discretion when that discretion impacts deeply rooted liberty interests, such as those involving the family unit, and it underscores the necessity of clear, fair, and transparent agency procedures.

## C.J.S. v. R.S.D.

319 S.W.3d 479 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2010 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the prenuptial agreement was valid, finding that there was full and fair disclosure and that the agreement was not unconscionable. The court rejected the claims of duress and failure to disclose. This case involved a dispute over a prenuptial agreement. One party attempted to set aside the agreement during divorce proceedings, arguing that it was unconscionable and was signed under duress. The party further claimed that there had been a failure of full and fair disclosure of financial assets at the time the agreement was signed. The court examined the standard for reviewing prenuptial agreements, which are treated as contracts under Missouri law. The focus was on whether the agreement was procedurally and substantively fair. The court looked at the financial situation of the parties, the amount of time they had to review the document with legal counsel, and whether the disclosures were complete. The case explored the high threshold required to invalidate such contracts, emphasizing the strong public policy in favor of enforcing voluntary, informed agreements between prospective spouses, provided that the terms are not so egregious as to be unconscionable at the time of enforcement.

## C.J.V. v. K.S.

632 S.W.2d 284 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1982 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the landlord's allocation method was inconsistent with the explicit 'pro rata' language of the lease. The court ordered an accounting to determine the correct amounts owed. The dispute in this matter concerned the calculation of property tax escalations passed through to a commercial tenant under the terms of a 'net lease.' The tenant challenged the landlord's method of allocating tax increases among multiple tenants within the same building. The core issue was whether the allocation methodology complied with the 'pro rata' share language in the lease agreement. The court evaluated the contract's definition of the tenant's share and whether the landlord had properly credited the tenant for tax abatements or reductions received. This case highlights the complexity of common area maintenance (CAM) and tax escalation clauses in multi-tenant commercial leases. The decision provides insights into how courts interpret fiscal responsibility in net leases and the fiduciary-like duties, if any, that a landlord has when calculating shared operating expenses to ensure transparency and accuracy as demanded by the contract language.

## C.J.V., Inc. v. Washington County

456 S.W.3d 897 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the contract was unenforceable because it failed to comply with statutory competitive bidding requirements. The court ruled that the public policy interest in transparent government procurement overrides the contractor's claim for breach of contract. This case involved a dispute over a governmental contract for the construction and operation of a jail facility. The private contractor, C.J.V., alleged that the county breached the agreement by failing to fulfill payment obligations and by unilaterally altering the scope of operations. The county argued that the contract was void ab initio due to lack of competitive bidding and other statutory requirements governing public contracts. The court examined the principles of public policy as they relate to government contracts, specifically focusing on the requirement that public entities strictly adhere to statutory procurement procedures. The case underscores the significant risk contractors face when dealing with municipal entities, as contracts that fail to comply with statutory requirements may be deemed unenforceable, regardless of the work performed. The decision emphasizes that parties contracting with the government are charged with the knowledge of relevant statutes, and the doctrine of estoppel generally does not apply to validate unauthorized or illegal government contracts.

## C.L. v. Hafer

562 S.W.2d 391 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Kansas City District · 1978 · Missouri

Holding: A tenant's knowledge of a defect does not automatically waive a landlord's duty to provide safe premises. The doctrine of assumption of risk does not bar recovery where the landlord fails to remediate known dangerous conditions. The plaintiffs were tenants who sued their landlord for damages resulting from a fire caused by faulty wiring in the rental property. The tenants alleged that the landlord was aware of the faulty wiring because of prior 'tripped' breakers and intermittent power issues, but did nothing to rectify the problem. The trial court found the landlord liable for negligence. The landlord appealed, asserting that the tenants had equal knowledge of the electrical problems and therefore assumed the risk. The appellate court examined the doctrine of 'assumed risk' and its application in landlord-tenant cases. The court clarified that a tenant does not assume the risk of the landlord's negligence simply by remaining on the premises, especially when the defect involves a hidden danger like improper wiring. The court highlighted that the landlord has a duty to maintain the premises in a safe condition and that this duty is not mitigated by the tenant's knowledge of a defect unless the tenant voluntarily and knowingly exposes themselves to an unreasonable risk. Finding sufficient evidence that the landlord was aware of the electrical system's dangerous condition and failed to remediate it, the court affirmed the judgment, confirming that the landlord's negligence was the proximate cause of the fire.

## C.M. v. L.M.

566 S.W.3d 608 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the trial court's imputation of income was supported by substantial evidence regarding the father's previous financial history and his voluntary reduction of work hours. The court also held that the conditions for physical custody were reasonably related to the children's best interests. The parties involved in this dissolution action disputed the allocation of physical custody and the calculation of child support based on the income of the respective parties. The father, a self-employed business owner, argued that the trial court improperly imputed income to him based on his past earnings rather than his current, reduced income. Furthermore, the mother sought sole legal custody, citing a history of domestic disturbances and the father's failure to participate in school-related activities. The trial court heard extensive testimony from both parties and a court-appointed guardian ad litem. The court ultimately concluded that the father's testimony regarding his financial decline lacked credibility and that the statutory factors for child support warranted the imputation of income at a level consistent with his historical earning capacity. Regarding custody, the trial court awarded joint legal and physical custody but established a specific schedule that restricted the father's time until he completed a court-ordered parenting class and anger management counseling. The father appealed, contending that the conditions placed on his physical custody amounted to an abuse of discretion and that the imputation of income was unsupported by the financial records produced during the discovery process.

## C.P.O. v. Missouri Dept. of Social Services

539 S.W.3d 810 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the Department breached the contract by failing to follow the mandatory notice-to-cure provisions. The doctrine of sovereign immunity did not protect the agency from a suit based on a validly executed contract. The Department of Social Services terminated a contract with a service provider, alleging failure to comply with regulatory standards. The provider sued for breach of contract, contending that the Department failed to provide the notice and opportunity to cure as required by the terms of their written agreement. The court evaluated the administrative procedures embedded within the contract and whether the Department's deviation from these procedures constituted a material breach. The case raised significant questions regarding sovereign immunity and whether a state agency can be held liable for breach of contract when acting in its regulatory capacity. The court analyzed whether the contract contained a waiver of sovereign immunity and the limitations of such waivers under state law. The dispute also touched upon whether the provider's performance was satisfactory or whether the Department had legitimate grounds to

Second stored summary terminate for convenience. The resolution hinged on the interpretation of specific termination clauses and whether the state adhered to the procedural due process outlined in the parties' mutual agreement.

## C.R. v. Kansas City University of Medicine and Biosciences

531 S.W.3d 589 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the disclosures provided by the surgeon satisfied the legal requirements for informed consent. The judgment in favor of the defendants was affirmed. This case dealt with an informed consent claim, where the plaintiff alleged that a medical procedure was performed without adequately disclosing the risks involved. The core of the argument was whether the surgeon provided sufficient information regarding potential complications for the patient to make an informed decision. Missouri's informed consent law requires that a physician disclose risks that a reasonable patient would consider significant in deciding whether to undergo a procedure. The trial court found that the disclosures made were sufficient as a matter of law. On appeal, the court reviewed the patient's specific medical history and the nature of the risks involved. The decision clarifies the requirements for informed consent and explains that physicians are not required to disclose every remote possibility, but rather those that are material to the decision-making process of a reasonable person in the patient's position. It also addresses the burden of proof in informed consent cases, shifting from general negligence to a focus on the adequacy of the communication between doctor and patient.

## C.R. v. St. Luke's Hospital

644 S.W.3d 589 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a physician's duty to disclose includes risks that a reasonable patient would consider significant in deciding whether to undergo a procedure. It remanded for trial to determine if the disclosure was adequate. This case involved a claim of professional negligence against a surgeon following a botched procedure that led to chronic pain. The plaintiff argued that the surgeon failed to inform the patient of all potential material risks associated with the surgery, thereby invalidating the informed consent provided. The hospital maintained that the procedure was performed correctly and that the patient was fully aware of the general risks associated with the operation. The litigation focused on the doctrine of informed consent in Missouri, specifically whether a physician's duty to inform extends to all possible adverse outcomes or only those that are statistically significant. The court analyzed whether the surgeon's failure to disclose a specific, albeit rare, risk could serve as the basis for a medical malpractice claim when the outcome was not the result of a surgical error per se, but rather a known risk that the patient was not explicitly warned about.

## C.R. v. T.R.

468 S.W.3d 432 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The trial court's decision was affirmed. The court held that the trial court was justified in refusing to lower the support obligation after finding the father's decrease in income was not as significant as claimed. The parents in this case appealed the modification of a child support order. The father, who was the non-custodial parent, sought a reduction in his support obligations due to a significant decrease in his annual income. The mother argued that the reduction was not warranted as the father had voluntarily reduced his income. The trial court examined the father's employment history and the reasons for his job change. The appellate court reviewed the application of Form 14 and whether the trial court correctly exercised its authority to impute income. The opinion discusses the burden of proof required when a parent claims a involuntary reduction in earnings and the steps the court must take to ensure the child support award remains adequate. It underscores the duty of parents to remain employed to provide for their children and the criteria for evaluating whether a change in income constitutes a 'substantial and continuing change' under Missouri law.
