## Farrow v. Saint Francis Med. Ctr.

407 S.W.3d 579 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that if a meal break is frequently and substantially interrupted by work duties, it is not a bona fide meal period and must be compensated. It remanded the case for a determination of whether the interruptions were frequent enough to meet this threshold. The ruling reinforced the standard that employees must be truly free from duty to have a non-compensable break. This case involved a dispute over whether hospital employees were required to be paid for time spent during mandatory unpaid meal breaks, during which they were still subject to being paged for urgent medical matters. The hospital argued that the time was not compensable because the interruptions were infrequent and the time was largely for the employees' own benefit. The plaintiffs, representing a class of medical staff, argued that the interruptions were significant enough to interfere with the break, thereby making

Second stored summary the entire period compensable work time. The appellate court reviewed Missouri's standards for compensability of meal periods, specifically focusing on whether the employees were 'completely relieved of duty' during the breaks. The analysis necessitated a deep dive into the frequency and nature of the pages received during the breaks and whether the hospital's policies regarding pager use created a de facto work environment. The court examined the tension between operational medical necessity and the legal requirement to pay for hours actually worked.

## Farrow v. Saint Francis Medical Center

407 S.W.3d 579 · Missouri Supreme Court · 2013 · Missouri

4 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the public policy exception to at-will employment is limited to clear mandates in statutes or regulations. Because the plaintiff failed to identify a clear public policy mandate that specifically prohibited her termination, the claim was dismissed. The plaintiff, a nurse, alleged that she was terminated in retaliation for reporting regulatory violations regarding patient safety and hospital procedures. She asserted a claim for wrongful discharge in violation of public policy. The lower courts examined the public policy exception to the at-will employment doctrine. The Missouri Supreme Court reviewed the scope of the public policy exception, specifically whether a plaintiff must rely on a clear mandate found in a statute or regulation to support such a claim. The court analyzed whether the nursing regulations cited by the plaintiff sufficiently articulated a clear mandate protecting the public interest rather than merely private or internal administrative interests. The court considered the historical development of Missouri employment law, which strictly adheres to at-will employment unless a contract specifies otherwise or a statutory exception applies. The case required a detailed analysis of whether the whistleblower protections claimed by the nurse were sufficient to overcome the employer's right to discharge. The court ultimately determined that the plaintiff failed to identify a specific constitutional or statutory provision that was violated by her termination, as the regulations cited did not provide a clear mandate that created a public policy exception for her specific role.

## Farrow v. Saint Francis Medical Center

307 S.W.3d 179 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2010 · Missouri

3 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court affirmed the summary judgment, holding that the plaintiff's internal reports did not trigger the public policy exception. An employee must show their actions were required by a clear mandate of public policy to overcome the presumption of at-will employment. The plaintiff, a nurse, alleged that she was wrongfully terminated in retaliation for reporting perceived violations of medical standards and unsafe patient care practices. She claimed her discharge violated the public policy exception to the at-will employment doctrine, specifically citing regulations governing nursing practice and hospital operations. The trial court granted summary judgment in favor of the hospital, ruling that the plaintiff failed to establish that her internal complaints were protected by a clear mandate of public policy. The plaintiff appealed, arguing that she was discharged for actions that served the public interest and that the trial court misinterpreted the scope of the public policy exception. The appellate court reviewed the evidence, focusing on whether the reporting was mandated by a constitutional provision, statute, regulation, or rule promulgated by a governmental body. The court analyzed whether the specific regulations identified by the plaintiff constituted a clear public policy mandate sufficient to override the employer's right to terminate at-will employees for any reason or no reason. The court ultimately concluded that the plaintiff failed to demonstrate that her complaints fell within the narrow exceptions to the at-will doctrine, as she could not link her specific actions to a clear and unambiguous mandate of public policy requiring such reporting for the public good.

## Farrow v. West

320 F.3d 1235 · United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit · 2003 · Federal

Holding: Severe dental pain and the inability to eat are serious medical needs protected under the Eighth Amendment. Failure to provide necessary dental appliances or treatment, after being made aware of the prisoner's condition, constitutes deliberate indifference. Farrow, a prisoner, experienced severe problems with his dentures, which caused mouth pain, bleeding, and the inability to eat properly for over a year. He repeatedly requested dental treatment and the replacement of his ill-fitting dentures. Prison officials delayed treatment and provided inadequate assistance, leading Farrow to file a complaint under the Eighth Amendment. The district court dismissed the action, but the Eleventh Circuit reversed, holding that the prisoner had provided sufficient evidence to suggest that the dental care he received was so inadequate that it amounted to deliberate indifference. The court highlighted that a serious medical need includes conditions that, if left untreated, cause the prisoner to experience significant pain and discomfort, even if the condition is not life-threatening. The case serves as an important precedent in the Eleventh Circuit for protecting prisoners' access to dental care under the Eighth Amendment, rejecting the notion that dental suffering is not 'serious enough' to trigger constitutional protection.

## Fashion Originators' Guild of America, Inc. v. FTC

312 U.S. 457 · U.S. Supreme Court · 1941 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the Guild's boycott of retailers was an illegal restraint of trade under the Sherman Act. The Court emphasized that private groups may not engage in boycotts to enforce their own standards. The Fashion Originators' Guild was an association of fashion designers and manufacturers who sought to prevent 'style piracy'--the copying of their designs by other, cheaper retailers. Members of the Guild agreed not to sell to retailers who carried these knock-off designs. The FTC challenged this policy as an illegal boycott in violation of the Sherman Act. The Guild argued that their actions were self-help measures to protect their intellectual property rights. The Supreme Court, however, held that the agreement constituted an unlawful conspiracy and a restraint of trade. The Court reasoned that even if the goal of the boycotters was to stop illegal or immoral conduct (such as design theft), they did not have the right to organize a boycott to enforce those moral standards. The ruling affirmed

Second stored summary that private groups cannot use anticompetitive tactics to enforce their own private regulatory schemes, underscoring the dominance of federal antitrust policy over industry-led, restrictive trade agreements.

## Faulkner v. Enos

533 S.W.3d 256 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: Landowners may be liable for damage caused by natural conditions on their land if they have actual or constructive notice of a hazard. Mere presence of a natural condition does not automatically impose liability without proof of notice. This matter involved a negligence suit between neighbors regarding the maintenance of a large tree that fell and caused damage to the plaintiff's property. The plaintiff alleged that the defendant was aware that the tree was decayed and failed to act, constituting a breach of duty. The trial court entered judgment for the defendant, finding no evidence of actual notice of the tree's dangerous condition. On appeal, the court reviewed the duties of landowners regarding natural conditions on their land that threaten neighboring property. The court determined that a landowner has a duty to prevent harm to neighbors if they know or should know of a hazardous condition on their land. The court held that while there was evidence the tree was in poor condition, the plaintiff failed to provide sufficient evidence that the defendant had constructive or actual notice of the specific risk. The judgment was affirmed, establishing that the duty arises only when the owner has reason to know of the specific danger.

## Faulkner v. Homeowner's Association of Fox Hill

226 S.W.3d 184 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2007 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an easement holder's rights are limited by the specific purpose granted. Actions taken under a maintenance easement that go beyond what is reasonably necessary constitute an improper expansion and violation of the property owner's rights. This litigation involved the interpretation of a recorded restrictive covenant and easement granted to a neighborhood association for drainage and maintenance purposes. The homeowner claimed that the association exceeded its authority by removing trees and altering the grade of the land beyond what was reasonably necessary for drainage. The association argued that its broad easement rights included the power to manage vegetation and landscape to prevent erosion and ensure proper water flow. The trial court focused on the language of the easement agreement, which granted 'maintenance access' but did not explicitly define the scope of removal permitted. The appellate court reviewed whether the association's actions constituted an 'unreasonable use' of the easement. By weighing the association's obligation to maintain infrastructure against the homeowner's property interest in their landscaping, the court sought to define the limits of maintenance easements in residential settings. The decision clarified that easement holders must exercise their rights in a manner that is strictly necessary for the purpose of the easement, avoiding unnecessary destruction of the grantor's improvements.

## Faulkner v. State

136 S.W.3d 592 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a temporary hazardous condition caused by a leak can constitute a dangerous condition of public property if the government entity has actual or constructive notice. The case was remanded for a trial on the issue of notice. The plaintiff sought damages against the state following a slip and fall on a wet floor in a government office building. The state claimed sovereign immunity, arguing that the building's maintenance did not constitute a dangerous condition of public property. The plaintiff argued that the building staff knew of the leak and failed to mop or warn visitors. The appeal involved an analysis of the statutory waiver of immunity for injuries arising from the 'dangerous condition of public property.' The court looked at whether a temporary spill qualifies as a 'condition' of the property or merely a temporary event. The appellate court evaluated the trial court's application of the state law concerning notice requirements for government entities and whether the duty of the state extends to monitoring for transient hazards in high-traffic public offices.

## Faust v. Hillshire Brands Co.

517 S.W.3d 609 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The Court held that an employer's neutral medical leave policy can be considered a pretext for retaliation if it is applied selectively against employees who have filed workers' compensation claims. The Court reversed the summary judgment in favor of the employer. The plaintiff, a long-term employee at a manufacturing facility, brought a wrongful termination suit claiming he was fired for exercising his rights under the Missouri Workers' Compensation Law. He alleged that his employer terminated him shortly after he reported a work-related back injury. The employer asserted that the plaintiff was terminated due to a neutral policy regarding medical leaves of absence that exceeded a certain duration. The trial court granted summary judgment to the employer, finding no evidence of retaliatory intent. The plaintiff appealed, contending that the policy was applied in a discriminatory manner against injured workers. The appellate court examined the Missouri Workers' Compensation Act's protection against retaliation. The court found that there was significant evidence that the policy, while neutral on its face, was used to target employees who had filed compensation claims. The appellate court held that the trial court erred in granting summary judgment because a reasonable jury could find that the policy was a pretext for unlawful retaliation. The case was remanded for a full trial to evaluate the motive of the employer.

## Faust v. Mitchell

574 S.W.3d 261 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: An express easement that is silent regarding the specific type of use is not strictly limited to the usage at the time of creation. The dominant estate holder is entitled to reasonable usage that does not impose an undue burden on the servient estate.

Second stored summary The dispute centered on the scope and usage of an express easement granted by deed. The plaintiffs, owners of a dominant estate, sought to improve an existing gravel driveway easement to accommodate heavier vehicle traffic for a commercial operation. The defendants, owners of the servient estate, objected, arguing that the easement was intended only for residential access and that the increased traffic caused a nuisance and exceeded the original scope of the grant. The trial court entered a judgment limiting the plaintiffs' ability to pave the driveway and restricting the type of vehicles allowed. The appellate court reviewed the deed language, which was silent as to the specific type of usage permitted. The court applied the principle that an easement created by grant is not limited by the specific use at the time of creation, but by what is reasonable and necessary for the full enjoyment of the dominant estate. The court remanded the case, holding that the trial court's restrictions were overly burdensome given the lack of limiting language in the original deed.

## Faust v. Ryder Commercial Leasing & Services

954 S.W.2d 383 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1997 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while transportation safety constitutes a clear public policy, a plaintiff must establish that their report was the actual cause of their termination. The jury properly weighed the evidence regarding the employer's stated reasons for discharge. The plaintiff, a former employee, claimed wrongful discharge after reporting his employer for failing to maintain vehicles according to Department of Transportation safety standards. He argued that his reports were required by law and that his subsequent termination violated the public policy aimed at ensuring highway safety. The employer maintained that the employee was discharged for performance issues unrelated to his reporting. The appellate court examined the causal connection between the safety reports and the termination. The court acknowledged that transportation safety is a matter of clear public policy, but it also emphasized that the plaintiff must prove that the report was the 'but-for' cause of the termination. Upon review, the court found that the evidence suggested a close proximity in time between the reports and the firing, which created a factual issue for the jury. However, the court ultimately concluded that the jury's verdict in favor of the employer was supported by substantial evidence regarding legitimate business reasons for the discharge. The court clarified that the jury acts as the trier of fact regarding whether the motivation for the termination was the report or a separate, valid business decision, upholding the verdict in favor of the defendant.

## Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. v. Coltharp

766 S.W.2d 437 (Mo. App. W.D. 1989) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1989 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the FDIC had a valid and perfected security interest in the debtor's accounts receivable due to its timely UCC-1 filing. This perfection gave the FDIC priority over the subsequent assignee of the accounts. The FDIC's claim was superior. This appeal concerns the priority of a bank's security interest in accounts receivable against a subsequent assignee of those accounts. The FDIC, as receiver for a bank, claimed a perfected security interest in the accounts receivable of a debtor. Another party, who subsequently purchased or was assigned the accounts receivable, challenged the FDIC's priority. The central issue was whether the FDIC's security interest was properly perfected under UCC Article 9 and whether its perfection predated or had priority over the subsequent assignment. The court examined the requirements for perfection of a security interest in accounts receivable, which typically involves filing a UCC-1 financing statement. The dispute also touched upon the definition of "accounts receivable" under the UCC and the potential for competing claims. The court reviewed the evidence presented regarding the timing of the FDIC's filing and the details of the subsequent assignment to determine which party had superior rights to the accounts. The case highlighted the critical role of UCC filings in establishing priority in secured transactions involving intangible assets.

## Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. v. W. G. Baskin

756 S.W.2d 201 (Mo. App. W.D. 1988) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1988 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the financing statement filed by the FDIC was sufficient to perfect its security interest in the debtor's inventory and accounts receivable. The description of collateral, while general, provided adequate notice to third parties as required by the UCC. The filing was also deemed proper, establishing the FDIC's priority. This case involves a dispute over the priority of a security interest in inventory and accounts receivable. The FDIC, as successor to a bank, claimed a perfected security interest through a financing statement. A third-party creditor, who also claimed a security interest, challenged the FDIC's priority, arguing the financing statement was insufficient and improperly filed. The court examined the requirements for perfection under Missouri's Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), focusing on the adequacy of the description of collateral and the proper filing location. The dispute also touched upon whether the collateral was sufficiently identified to put subsequent creditors on notice of the FDIC's security interest, considering the nature of inventory and accounts receivable which are constantly changing. The appellate court reviewed the trial court's findings regarding the sufficiency of the financing statement and the perfection of the security interest. The case highlighted the importance of precise language in security agreements and financing statements to ensure enforceability and priority against other secured parties and the debtor. It also explored the concept of "notice filing" under the UCC and what constitutes adequate notice to third parties regarding the extent of a secured party's claim.

## Fender v. City of St. Louis

881 S.W.2d 267 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1994 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the regular rate of pay for overtime calculation must include all non-exempt forms of remuneration provided by the employer. Payments labeled as 'in-lieu' which are essentially regular salary components must be factored into the overtime pay base. Fender concerned the calculation of overtime for municipal firefighters. The central dispute was whether certain 'in-lieu' payments provided by the city should be factored into the 'regular rate of pay' for overtime calculation purposes. Under both federal and Missouri standards, overtime must be calculated based on the employee's regular hourly rate. The firefighters argued that these additional payments were essentially compensation for services rendered and therefore should be included. The city argued they were ancillary benefits, not 'wages' for the purpose of overtime calculation. The appellate court scrutinized the definition of the regular rate, examining the nature of the payments and whether they were predictable and tied to the employee's performance or status. This case addresses the complexities of 'base pay' in municipal employment, where compensation structures are often governed by complex collective bargaining agreements and city ordinances. The court's analysis provides a roadmap for determining which specific components of a paycheck must be included when determining the compensation base for statutory overtime calculations in the public sector.

## Fender v. Daniel

737 S.W.2d 255 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1987 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the summary judgment, holding that the plaintiff's claim was time-barred. It concluded that the statute of limitations began to run when the injury was discovered. The plaintiff sued a doctor for medical malpractice, alleging that the failure to diagnose a tumor resulted in a worsened prognosis for recovery. The defendant moved for summary judgment, arguing that the statute of limitations had expired. The core of the legal debate involved the 'discovery rule' and when the plaintiff knew, or should have known, that their injury was caused by the defendant's negligence. The trial court granted the summary judgment, finding that the plaintiff's knowledge of the diagnosis and the possibility of medical error triggered the start of the statute of limitations period. The appellate court reviewed the evidence to determine whether there were genuine issues of material fact regarding the timeline of the plaintiff's discovery of the injury. The decision highlights the strict adherence of Missouri courts to statute of limitations in medical cases and the burden on plaintiffs to exercise diligence in identifying potential malpractice.

## Fender v. Schiltz

568 S.W.3d 479 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a valid partnership contract existed and that the defendant breached the fiduciary duties and financial obligations contained therein. The court affirmed the trial court's award of damages based on the evidence presented at trial. This dispute arose from a partnership agreement between two business owners. After the business dissolved, one partner sued the other for breach of contract, alleging that the defendant failed to account for partnership assets and improperly diverted funds for personal use. The defense argued that the partnership was not clearly defined and that the parties had modified the terms of their agreement orally through their business practices. The court examined the sufficiency of the partnership agreement's terms and whether the parties' course of performance indicated a waiver of the strict financial reporting requirements stipulated in the initial written contract.

Second stored summary The case addressed the duties of partners to one another and the evidentiary requirements for proving the terms of an agreement in the absence of complete records. The appellate decision emphasizes the necessity of documenting changes to partnership agreements and the risks associated with informal business operations where financial accountings are not strictly maintained according to contract.

## Fender v. ServiceMaster

651 S.W.3d 810 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the Commission's decision, holding that an employer is liable for the full extent of a disability caused by a work-related aggravation of a pre-existing condition. The court ruled that apportioning disability is not required if the work injury is a substantial factor in the current impairment. The claimant, an employee for a cleaning service, suffered a lower back injury while lifting heavy equipment. The employer contested the extent of the permanent partial disability (PPD) awarded by the administrative law judge, arguing that the medical impairment rating was inflated and ignored prior existing back conditions. The Labor and Industrial Relations Commission affirmed the award, determining that the work injury exacerbated a pre-existing condition, thereby making the employer liable for the entire disability under the doctrine of the primary injury combined with subsequent aggravation. The employer appealed, asserting that the Commission failed to apportion the disability as required by statute when a pre-existing condition is clearly documented. The appellate court reviewed the administrative record to determine if the Commission's decision was based on competent and substantial evidence. The court addressed the standard for assessing PPD when multiple factors contribute to an impairment, noting that the employer is liable for the aggravation caused by the workplace accident. The court found that the medical evidence supported the conclusion that the specific work incident caused a measurable increase in functional impairment.

## Fendler v. Hudson Services

520 S.W.3d 502 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the denial of benefits. It held that the commission properly determined the fall was idiopathic and did not arise out of a hazard peculiar to the workplace. The claimant sought compensation for a fall at the workplace, but the commission denied the claim, finding that the claimant had not suffered an 'accident' arising out of and in the course of employment. The claimant had a history of dizziness and the employer argued that the fall was idiopathic, meaning it resulted from a personal medical condition rather than a work-related hazard. The appellate court reviewed the 'positional risk' doctrine in Missouri. The court analyzed whether the employment placed the claimant in a position that increased the risk of injury from a fall, regardless of whether the fall was caused by an internal medical event. The court discussed the threshold for compensability when a claimant falls on a level floor while performing duties. The appellate court examined the medical testimony concerning the cause of the fall and whether the evidence sufficiently established that the employment contributed to the injury. The decision emphasized that simply being at work is not enough; there must be a causative connection between the workplace environment and the occurrence of the accident.

## Fenney v. Dakota, Minnesota & Eastern Railroad Co.

327 F.3d 707 · 8th Cir. · 2003 · Federal

Holding: The court held that 'major life activities' include working and manual tasks. Denying minor accommodations to a worker with a significant physical injury that limits these activities constitutes a violation of the ADA. Fenney was a railroad employee who lost parts of his fingers in a work-related accident. Upon returning to work, he was provided with certain tasks but was denied the necessary accommodations to fully perform his job efficiently, such as extra time to perform documentation. The employer argued that the plaintiff's limitations were not 'substantial' enough to qualify as a disability under the ADA. The appellate court reversed the summary judgment in favor of the employer, noting that the 'substantially limited' analysis must focus on how the condition affects the ability to perform 'major life activities' like manual tasks in the workplace. The court held that the employer's conduct of failing to provide basic tools for him to complete his duties was a failure to accommodate. The court reminded the parties that the ADA intended to protect employees who have significant, though perhaps not total, loss of function, and the railroad's rigid adherence to standard operating times was discriminatory.

## Fielder v. HSBC Secs. (USA) Inc.

699 F. Supp. 2d 1105 · U.S. Dist. Ct. W.D. Mo. · 2010 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a genuine issue of material fact existed regarding whether the brokers' statements constituted deceptive practices under the MPA. It denied summary judgment for the defendant on the MPA claim, allowing the issue of reliance to proceed to trial. In a case involving federal and state law claims, investors sued a brokerage firm for violations of the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (MPA) and common law fraud. The investors claimed that the firm misled them by selling high-risk mortgage-backed securities as 'safe' and 'conservative' investments. The firm argued that the investment agreements included detailed risk disclosures and that the plaintiffs were sophisticated investors who understood the inherent risks of the market. The case explored the 'ascertainable loss' requirement of the MPA and whether a plaintiff must demonstrate specific reliance on the marketing representations when the written contract contains contradictory disclaimers. The litigation involved extensive analysis of the 'reasonable person' standard in the context of financial investment products. The court examined whether the firm's oral assurances could form the basis of an MPA claim if they directly contradicted the written prospectus provided to the investors, and to what extent the firm had a duty to ensure that the descriptions provided by its brokers matched the technical nature of the products sold to individual consumers.

## Fields v. City of Independence

557 S.W.3d 315 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2018 · Missouri

Also captioned Rinehart v. City of Independence

Holding: The court held that the city's practice of averaging hours over a two-week period violated the statutory requirement for overtime calculation. The court ordered the city to conform its pay periods to the weekly standard defined by state law. In this matter, municipal employees challenged the city's policy of calculating overtime based on a work period that exceeded the standard forty-hour work week, arguing that the city improperly calculated their pay by aggregating hours over a two-week period instead of a weekly one. The city defended its practice by citing its legislative authority to establish work schedules for public employees. The court examined whether the city's ordinances conflicted with the Missouri Minimum Wage Law and whether the law allowed for such

Second stored summary averaging of hours for municipal employees. The ruling clarified the scope of municipal power in setting compensation schedules and addressed the question of whether local ordinances can override the default weekly overtime threshold set by state statutes for non-exempt workers. The court emphasized that unless specific statutory exemptions apply, municipal employees are subject to the same overtime calculations as private sector workers, particularly regarding the standard weekly work period.

Second stored summary Holding: The court held that gap time is not compensable under Missouri state law unless an express contract or ordinance requires it. The court concluded that the city's pay structure did not violate the MMWL because the effective hourly rate remained above the legal minimum. This case addressed whether city firefighters were entitled to 'gap time' pay for time spent during their shifts that exceeded the standard work week but did not reach the threshold for overtime under the Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA) or state law. The firefighters argued that their salary agreement effectively reduced their hourly rate below the minimum wage when all hours on duty were accounted for. The city argued that as long as the total compensation divided by total hours worked stayed above the minimum wage, there was no violation. The court examined the standard for calculating 'regular rate' and whether the municipal ordinance incorporated state law definitions of work time. The litigation required a detailed analysis of how 'work time' is defined in the context of fire service, where shifts often include periods of rest or inactivity that might be compensable under specific contractual provisions but not necessarily under the baseline requirements of the Missouri Minimum Wage Law.

## Fields v. City of Kansas City

963 S.W.2d 386 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1998 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the officers had sufficient reasonable suspicion to conduct the stop. Furthermore, the court determined that the plaintiff failed to provide evidence of an unconstitutional municipal policy or custom, barring recovery under Section 1983. The plaintiff brought a Section 1983 action against the City of Kansas City and police officers, alleging that he was subjected to unlawful detention and civil rights violations during an investigation. The core of the complaint involved a Fourth Amendment challenge regarding the legality of the initial stop and the subsequent search of the plaintiff's person. The court examined whether the officers had reasonable suspicion to initiate the encounter and whether the detention exceeded the scope of a standard Terry stop. The litigation highlighted the tension between law enforcement needs in high-crime areas and the constitutional protections against unreasonable search and seizure. The court reviewed the evidence under a de novo standard as it related to the constitutional question of probable cause. The decision serves as a significant precedent for how Missouri courts should evaluate municipal liability for police conduct when the plaintiff asserts that the city failed to adequately train officers regarding stop-and-frisk procedures. The court emphasized that municipal liability under Monell requires proof of a specific policy or custom that caused the constitutional injury.

## Fierstein v. Missouri Power & Light Co.

341 S.W.2d 783 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1960 · Missouri

Holding: Commercial lease agreements cannot be used to delegate away non-delegable statutory duties concerning hazardous building infrastructure. Landlords remain responsible for the maintenance of essential building-wide utility systems. This case involved a dispute where a commercial tenant sued the landlord and an utility company for damages after an explosion caused by a gas leak in the rented facility. The tenant alleged that the landlord was liable for failing to maintain the gas lines, which were integral to the building's infrastructure. The trial court ruled in favor of the landlord, finding that the lease agreement shifted all liability for utility systems to the tenant. The tenant appealed, arguing that certain statutory provisions and the nature of the utility systems created a non-delegable duty for the landlord to maintain the main lines. The Supreme Court of Missouri reviewed the lease terms and the statutory duties of property owners. The court held that while commercial parties can contractually allocate repair duties, they cannot override statutory safety requirements regarding hazardous infrastructure. The court determined that the lease was not sufficiently clear to shift the duty of maintaining main gas lines, which remained a central part of the building's structural safety. The court reversed the judgment, finding that the landlord's failure to maintain the main gas infrastructure created a breach of duty, allowing the tenant to recover damages for the explosion.

## Fifth Third Bancorp v. Dudenhoeffer

573 U.S. 409 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2014 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court ruled that there is no presumption of prudence for ERISA fiduciaries managing ESOPs. Plaintiffs must demonstrate that a prudent fiduciary would have concluded that the investment was imprudent based on non-public information or other circumstances. This case involved Employee Stock Ownership Plan (ESOP) participants who sued Fifth Third Bancorp, alleging that fiduciaries breached their duties by continuing to invest in company stock despite knowing that the stock was overvalued due to public and non-public information. The lower courts applied a 'presumption of prudence' that made it difficult for plaintiffs to state a claim for breach of fiduciary duty regarding stock investments. The participants argued that the fiduciaries had inside information that the market price of the stock was inflated and that they should have stopped purchasing or sold the stock. The Supreme Court addressed whether ERISA fiduciaries, who are directed to invest in company stock, are entitled to a presumption of prudence in light of the market's efficiency. The Court rejected the existence of a presumption of prudence for ESOP fiduciaries, noting that ERISA does not grant such a privilege to fiduciaries when managing company stock. Instead, plaintiffs must plausibly allege that a prudent fiduciary in the same situation would not have made the investment decisions at issue.

## Firestone Tire & Rubber Co. v. Bruch

489 U.S. 101 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1989 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that judicial review of a denial of benefits under ERISA should be de novo unless the benefit plan provides the administrator with discretionary authority, in which case the standard is abuse of discretion. The plaintiffs were employees whose division was sold to another company. They sought severance pay under their original company's plan. The administrator denied the claims, interpreting the plan to exclude the employees because they had been hired by the purchasing company. The employees sued, and the central issue was the standard of review to be applied to the administrator's decision. The Supreme Court rejected the then-common 'arbitrary and capricious' standard for all ERISA cases. The Court held that a denial of benefits should be reviewed under a 'de novo' standard unless the plan clearly and explicitly grants the administrator the discretionary authority to interpret the plan or determine eligibility. If such authority is granted, the 'abuse of discretion' standard applies. This decision established the foundational rule for judicial review in ERISA cases, requiring courts to look to the language of the plan to determine the appropriate level of deference to accord to an administrator's decision-making process.

## First Bank of Sullivan v. Spivey

887 S.W.2d 753 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1994 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a perfected security interest under the UCC takes priority over a statutory landlord's lien. The UCC framework serves as the controlling priority mechanism for competing interests in personal property. This dispute concerned the priority between a bank's security interest in a debtor's inventory and the rights of a landlord asserting a landlord's lien. The bank had a perfected interest in all inventory. When the debtor defaulted, the landlord seized the inventory, claiming a superior lien for unpaid rent under Missouri state landlord-tenant laws. The bank argued that its UCC-perfected interest took priority over the landlord's lien because the UCC governs the perfection of security interests in inventory. The court examined the interaction between state landlord lien statutes and Article 9 of the UCC. The court determined that while a landlord may have a statutory lien, it is subordinate to a prior-perfected UCC security interest. The UCC's system of notice filing provides the priority mechanism that governs this conflict. The court concluded that the bank's security interest was superior because it was perfected before the landlord's lien attached. This decision clarifies that secured lenders under the UCC have a clear priority over landlords in inventory, provided the lender maintains their perfection status, and that specific state liens do not automatically trump UCC-based priority rules.

## First Missouri Bank & Trust Co. of Clayton v. Newman

653 S.W.2d 707 (Mo. App. E.D. 1983) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1983 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that perfection of a security interest in a mobile home requires notation on the certificate of title. The bank's lien was properly noted, providing constructive notice to subsequent purchasers. Therefore, Newman, as a subsequent purchaser, took the mobile home subject to the bank's perfected security interest. The bank's priority was affirmed. This case involves a dispute over a bank's security interest in a mobile home and its priority against a subsequent purchaser. First Missouri Bank & Trust Co. held a security interest in a mobile home, which was noted on its certificate of title. The debtor subsequently sold the mobile home to Newman, who claimed to be a good-faith purchaser without notice of the bank's lien. The bank argued that its security interest remained perfected and enforceable against Newman. The appellate court had to determine whether the certificate of title statute or UCC Article 9 governed the perfection and priority of security interests in mobile homes. The court analyzed the specific requirements for perfection, focusing on whether notation on the certificate of title was sufficient to provide notice to subsequent purchasers. The case addressed the interaction between UCC Article 9 and Missouri's certificate of title laws for mobile homes. The court considered the effectiveness of the lien notation on the title as notice to third parties.

## First Nat'l Bank of St. Charles v. Chemical Bank

637 S.W.2d 381 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1982 · Missouri

Holding: Under the 'first to file' rule of the UCC, the party that files a financing statement first generally holds priority, even if the description of the collateral is broad. Broad descriptions are sufficient to provide constructive notice to subsequent creditors to make further inquiries. The dispute was between two banks, both of which claimed a superior security interest in the same equipment. Both banks had filed financing statements, but there was a discrepancy regarding the perfection timing. The first bank had filed its financing statement, but the description of the collateral was arguably too broad. The second bank argued that their specific security agreement and filing were superior because the first bank's filing failed to properly describe the collateral. The court reviewed the UCC's 'first to file' rule. The core issue was whether the first bank's broad description of 'all equipment' was sufficient to cover the specific industrial machinery in question. The court held that the UCC favors notice filing, which does not require a granular list of every piece of equipment, but rather enough information to alert interested parties to inquire further. Because the first bank's financing statement provided notice of its interest in equipment, the second bank was on notice and should have investigated. The first bank's priority was upheld based on the first-to-file rule, confirming that broad descriptions in a financing statement are generally effective to perfect interests against later claimants.

The court's opinion clarified the procedural hurdles that must be met to secure a PMSI priority position in a competitive commercial environment, underscoring the strict statutory criteria for achieving such status.

The "all assets" description was deemed sufficient to put other creditors on notice. The judgment favoring FNBP was affirmed. This case involves a dispute over the priority of security interests in concrete mixing trucks. First National Bank of Prakash (FNBP) held a perfected security interest in the trucks. A.G. Concrete, Inc. (AGC), a subsequent creditor, claimed its interest had priority, alleging FNBP's financing statement was deficient and improperly filed. FNBP argued that its financing statement substantially complied with UCC requirements and that its security interest was properly perfected. The court examined the adequacy of the description of collateral in FNBP's financing statement and whether it provided sufficient notice to other creditors. The case also touched upon the "all assets" clause often used in financing statements and its validity under Missouri law. The appellate court reviewed the trial court's determination regarding the validity and priority of the security interests, considering the UCC's provisions on perfection and priority. The dispute highlighted the critical importance of accurate and sufficiently descriptive financing statements in maintaining priority in secured transactions.

## First National Bank of St. Charles v. Chemical Products, Inc.

637 S.W.2d 373 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1982 · Missouri

Also captioned First Nat'l Bank of St. Charles v. Chemical Prods., Inc.

Holding: The court held that the bank had a valid security interest in the proceeds of the accounts. The defendant's unauthorized use of the funds constituted conversion, and the bank was entitled to damages. This matter involved a claim of conversion involving accounts receivable. The bank had a security interest in the accounts receivable of Chemical Products, Inc. When the debtor collected payments from accounts and used them for general business operations instead of remitting them to the bank, the bank sued for conversion. The court examined whether the security interest in the accounts carried over to the cash payments made by the account debtors. The key issue was whether the bank could trace the funds and whether the defendant had improperly interfered with the bank's rights by using the proceeds. The case required an examination of the UCC's rules on 'proceeds' and the extent to which a secured creditor can assert claims against those who receive funds generated from collateral. The decision underscores the risks associated with revolving credit facilities and the necessity of monitoring accounts receivable to ensure that proceeds are properly managed under the security agreement.

Second stored summary Holding: The court held that the bank's prior-filed financing statement gave it priority over subsequent assignments and tax liens. The security interest in accounts receivable was properly perfected under the UCC. This litigation involved a complex priority dispute between a bank, a supplier, and a tax authority, all claiming interests in a company's accounts receivable. The bank had a perfected security interest in all existing and future accounts. The supplier argued that it had a superior interest based on a prior contract assignment, and the tax authority claimed priority for unpaid payroll taxes. The court evaluated the perfection requirements for security interests in accounts receivable under the UCC. It addressed the 'first to file' rule for accounts and whether the assignment of an account constitutes a security interest subject to the UCC's filing requirements. The decision analyzed the priority of a bank's floating lien on receivables versus statutory tax liens and assignments. The case serves as an example of the challenges involved in securing interest in intangible assets like receivables and the priority rules for conflicting claims on the same stream of payments.

## First National Bank v. Chemicals Unlimited, Inc.

656 S.W.2d 783 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1983 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that because the financier failed to perfect its PMSI within the statutory timeframe, it lost its super-priority status. Consequently, the bank's prior-filed financing statement remained superior. This litigation involved an interpleader action to determine the priority of competing security interests in the debtor's equipment. A bank and an equipment financier both claimed priority. The bank had filed a financing statement covering 'all present and after-acquired equipment.' The financier argued it held a PMSI in the equipment it sold to the debtor, but it failed to file its financing statement within the statutory grace period provided by the UCC. The court analyzed the priority rules between a general security interest holder and a late-filing PMSI claimant. The dispute underscored the strict adherence required to the time limitations for PMSI perfection. The court addressed whether the financier's failure to timely file allowed the bank's prior-filed, all-encompassing security interest to retain priority. The opinion details the mechanics of 'first to file' rules and the specific narrow exceptions provided for purchase money security interests under the Missouri UCC.

## First National Bank v. Craggs

656 S.W.2d 767 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1983 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the general description 'all machinery and equipment' was sufficient to reasonably identify the collateral. The security interest was therefore enforceable. A bank attempted to foreclose on collateral consisting of farm equipment, but the debtor claimed the bank's security interest was void because the security agreement did not adequately describe the collateral. The security agreement used a general description: 'all machinery and equipment now or hereafter owned.' The debtor argued that for a security interest to be valid, the collateral must be described with specific serial numbers or distinct identification. The bank argued that such a description was sufficient under the UCC, which requires only that the collateral be described in a way that reasonably identifies it. The court examined the standard of 'reasonable identification' in the context of farm equipment. The case involved whether a 'blanket' description in a security agreement is enforceable against a debtor, especially when the debtor later contends that they did not intend to pledge all of their tools and machinery. The appellate court looked at the precedent set by other UCC cases regarding the sufficiency of collateral descriptions in financing statements versus security agreements.

## First State Bank of Joplin v. Maxfield

485 S.W.2d 676 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Springfield District · 1972 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the first bank failed to perfect its interest because it filed in the wrong county. Consequently, the second bank's interest, even if later in time, was superior due to the first bank's defective perfection. This case involved a conflict between two banks over a security interest in a herd of cattle. The first bank had filed a financing statement in the county where the debtor resided, but failed to file in the county where the cattle were located, as required by the prevailing UCC provisions at the time. The second bank argued that the first bank's interest was unperfected due to the improper filing. The court analyzed the 'place of filing' requirements for farm-related collateral under Missouri law. The discussion centered on whether the failure to file in the correct location rendered the interest subordinate to subsequent creditors. The case provided a necessary interpretation of the UCC filing geography rules and emphasized that strict compliance with the statutory filing location is a condition precedent to maintaining a perfected security interest, even when the debtor's residency is known to the creditor.

## First State Bank of Purdy v. Coastal Express, Inc.

119 S.W.3d 583 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the bank's security interest continued in the equipment regardless of the lease agreement. The bank was entitled to enforce its lien against the lessee because the security agreement prohibited such unauthorized transfers. In this case, the court addressed the conflict between a bank's perfected security interest in a trucking company's assets and the company's subsequent efforts to lease or sell those assets. The bank had a blanket lien on the debtor's equipment and proceeds. The debtor entered into a lease agreement with Coastal Express, Inc., which the bank claimed violated the terms of the security agreement. The key issues involved the enforceability of a 'non-assignment' clause in the security agreement and whether a third-party lessee took the equipment subject to the bank's interest. The court analyzed whether the bank's security interest persisted despite the lease and whether the lessee had acted in good faith. The case required a detailed application of UCC Article 9 provisions concerning the transfer of collateral and the rights of secured creditors when the collateral is leased. The decision provides clarity on the interplay between security interests and contractual rights of third parties in commercial equipment.

## First State Bank v. American Grain & Cattle, Inc.

680 S.W.2d 381 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1984 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the bank's security interest did not prevail against the buyer because the bank failed to provide the required statutory notice. Therefore, the buyer took the cattle free of the security interest. This case addressed the 'farm products' rule and the 'buyer in the ordinary course' exception. A bank had a perfected security interest in cattle belonging to the debtor. The debtor sold the cattle to a third party, who then sold them to a packing plant. The bank sued the packing plant for conversion, arguing that its security interest in the cattle was not extinguished because the farm products rule allowed the creditor to follow the collateral. The defendant argued that it took free of the security interest as a buyer in the ordinary course. The court examined the historical farm products exception, which allowed secured creditors to recover from third-party buyers even if the buyer did not know of the lien. The court held that because the bank had not properly complied with the notification requirements under the Food Security Act and Missouri state law at the time of the sale, the buyer did not take subject to the lien. The case highlights the evolution of the farm products rule and the importance of creditors providing proper notice to potential buyers of farm collateral. It explains the interplay between state UCC law and federal agricultural legislation intended to protect good-faith purchasers of farm goods.

## First State Bank v. Columbia Nat'l Bank

563 S.W.2d 84 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1978 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the first bank to file in the correct location under the UCC's multi-location rules had priority. Because the debtor maintained a place of business in the county of the first filing, that bank's interest was perfected first. The court addressed a dispute between two banks, both claiming a perfected security interest in the same inventory. The debtor had pledged its inventory to both banks under two different security agreements. The case focused on which bank had priority based on the timing of their respective filings. The challenge arose because one bank filed in a different county than the other, and there was

Second stored summary confusion about whether the debtor was 'doing business' in both locations. The court examined the UCC rules for filing a financing statement when a debtor has multiple places of business. The decision turned on whether the 'central filing' rule was satisfied and whether the bank's filing in one location provided adequate notice to other potential creditors. This required an investigation into the debtor's operational structure at the time of the loan origination and the registration of the business entity in Missouri.

## First State Bank v. M-G-M Enterprises

713 S.W.2d 37 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1986 · Missouri

Holding: A security interest in accounts receivable is perfected by filing a financing statement that covers 'accounts.' This interest automatically attaches to future accounts as they are generated by the debtor, provided the financing statement is properly filed. This case involved a dispute over a security interest in accounts receivable. The bank had a perfected security interest in the debtor's present and future accounts. The debtor entered into a contract to provide services, and the right to payment was generated as an account receivable. A third party claimed a right to the same funds by assignment. The court examined the UCC's provisions regarding the perfection of security interests in accounts receivable. It was determined that the bank's financing statement, which explicitly listed 'accounts' as collateral, was sufficient to perfect an interest in accounts created after the filing. The court held that the bank's interest attached the moment the rights to payment arose under the service contract. The competing assignment was found to be inferior because the bank had completed its perfection well before the assignment occurred. The court clarified that 'accounts' in the UCC are broadly defined to include rights to payment for services rendered, and that perfection against accounts covers future proceeds from business activities as long as the financing statement is broad enough. The bank's claim to the funds was affirmed, reinforcing the reach of security interests in intangible property.

## First State Bank v. Stein

729 S.W.2d 626 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1987 · Missouri

Holding: Perfection of a security interest in a promissory note is validly achieved through possession. No financing statement is required to perfect an interest in an instrument held by the secured party. This case centered on the requirement of 'possession' for the perfection of a security interest in instruments and money. A lender claimed a security interest in a promissory note that the debtor had pledged as collateral. The creditor did not file a financing statement, instead claiming that their physical possession of the note constituted perfection. The debtor argued that a financing statement was required to perfect an interest in such an asset. The court analyzed the UCC rules regarding perfection by possession, confirming that security interests in instruments can be perfected by the secured party's possession. The court held that the bank's continuous possession of the note was sufficient to perfect their security interest, even without a financing statement. This decision underscores the alternative methods of perfection provided by Article 9 and confirms that for certain types of collateral, physical control and possession serve as a robust and legally sufficient substitute for public filing.

## Fischer v. City of St. Louis

961 F.3d 1007 · United States Court of Appeals, Eighth Circuit · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the employee did not have a federal cause of action under Section 1983 because the procedural violations of the city ordinance did not rise to the level of a constitutional due process violation under federal standards. A city employee brought a Section 1983 action alleging that the city violated his Fourteenth Amendment rights by failing to adhere to the procedures mandated by a city ordinance during a disciplinary investigation. The employee argued that the ordinance created a property interest in continued employment and that the failure to follow the ordinance's investigation steps constituted a violation of procedural due process. The city contended that the ordinance was directory rather than mandatory and that the employee received the minimum constitutional protections required by the Supreme Court in Loudermill. The court analyzed whether a state or local ordinance can create a constitutionally protected property interest that is enforceable under federal law. The court looked at the distinction between procedural rules that govern how a discharge is handled and substantive protections that determine whether a person can be discharged. The decision clarifies that a violation of a local procedural ordinance does not automatically constitute a violation of the federal Due Process Clause.

## Fischer v. First American Title Insurance Co.

388 S.W.3d 181 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2012 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that the plaintiffs' claims were barred by the filed rate doctrine, as the rates charged were those authorized by the regulatory body. The court affirmed that a breach of contract claim cannot be used as a vehicle to challenge rates that were properly filed and approved by the state. Fischer involved a class-action lawsuit against a title insurance company, alleging that the company violated the 'filed rate' doctrine by overcharging customers for title insurance premiums. The plaintiffs argued that the insurer's conduct constituted a breach of contract

Second stored summary and an unlawful trade practice. The insurer argued that its rates were approved by the Department of Insurance and that the filed rate doctrine precluded the court from adjudicating the claims. The court analyzed the statutory framework governing title insurance and whether the contractual relationship between the insurer and the insured allowed for such a claim. This case explores the boundary between administrative regulation and private contract enforcement. It is significant for its analysis of whether contract claims can be used to challenge regulated insurance rates and the extent to which the judiciary must defer to administrative agencies in the interpretation of insurance filings. The decision clarifies that courts will not entertain breach of contract claims that essentially seek to collaterally attack administrative decisions regarding insurance premium structures.

## Fischer v. Knauf

180 S.W.3d 529 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2005 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while the sellers had a duty to disclose known defects, the buyers failed to conduct adequate inspections. The 'as is' clause protected the sellers as the damage was discoverable through reasonable due diligence. The plaintiffs brought an action for breach of contract and fraud against the sellers of a residential property after discovering extensive water damage and mold in the basement following the purchase. The sellers argued that they had disclosed all known material defects in the real estate disclosure form and that the buyers had been given ample opportunity to perform inspections. The central legal issue was the duty of disclosure in residential real estate transactions and whether the sellers' silence regarding past repairs constituted fraud or concealment. The court reviewed the 'as is' clause in the contract and determined whether it protected the sellers from liability for latent defects that were actively concealed. The case involved a thorough analysis of the 'caveat emptor' doctrine as it pertains to residential sales in Missouri and the requirement for buyers to exercise due diligence in investigating property conditions before closing. The ruling provides insight into the limitations of 'as is' contracts when material facts are hidden.

## Fischer v. Knickmeyer

569 S.W.3d 465 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: Tenants in common have an absolute right to partition real property. If a physical division is inequitable, the court will order a public sale to distribute the proceeds. This dispute involved a claim for partition of real property. Following the death of a parent, siblings held the inherited family farm as tenants in common. One sibling sought to partition the land by sale, while the others wanted to retain the property or divide it in kind. The court analyzed the legal standards for partition actions under Missouri law, which state that any tenant in common has the absolute right to seek partition. The trial court determined that partition in kind was impractical due to the layout of the land and the disparity in value of different portions of the property, thus ordering a public sale. The appellate court affirmed, noting that the trial court correctly evaluated the feasibility of dividing the property and correctly determined that a sale was the only way to ensure each sibling received their fair share of the equity. The ruling emphasizes the statutory right to partition and the court's preference for public sale when physical division is not equitable or practical.

## Fischhoff v. Mitsubishi International Corp.

2017 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 10986 · U.S. District Court (Applying Missouri Law) · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that contractual waivers do not automatically bar an MPA claim. It ruled that claims involving fraud in the inducement of a contract remain actionable under the MPA despite standard disclaimers. This case involved a dispute over the sale of high-end equipment where the buyer claimed the seller engaged in deceptive practices by misrepresenting the capabilities and the history of the equipment. The defendant argued that the contract contained a disclaimer of warranties that precluded any claims under the MPA. The court examined the effectiveness of 'as is' clauses and merger clauses in shielding a party from liability for statutory consumer fraud. The buyer argued that such contractual waivers cannot waive the protections provided by the state's consumer protection act, as that would violate public policy. The analysis focused on whether the MPA creates non-waivable rights for consumers, especially in transactions where there is a disparity of information between the buyer and the seller, and whether the defendant's alleged misrepresentations regarding the machine's maintenance history rose to the level of a deceptive practice.

## Fisher v. Wheeler

89 S.W.3d 528 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2002 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a landlord who fails to provide an itemized list of damages within the statutory time frame forfeits the right to retain the security deposit. Furthermore, the burden of proving that damages exceed normal wear and tear rests strictly on the landlord. This case involved a dispute over a security deposit between a residential landlord and former tenants. After the tenants moved out, the landlord withheld a portion of the deposit, citing damages beyond normal wear and tear, including carpet stains and wall damage. The tenants sued in small claims court, arguing that the damages were either pre-existing or constituted normal use of the property. The small claims court found for the tenants, and the landlord appealed to the circuit court, which upheld the decision. The landlord subsequently appealed to the appellate court. The primary issue was whether the landlord had complied with the statutory requirements for providing an itemized list of damages within the timeframe mandated by Missouri law. Additionally, the court addressed the evidentiary requirements for establishing the condition of the premises at the start versus the end of the lease. The court examined the landlord's burden of proof regarding deductions from the security deposit and whether the trial court misapplied the law regarding statutory damages for the failure to return a deposit in a timely manner. The analysis focused on the protections afforded to residential tenants under Missouri's security deposit statute and the procedural obligations of landlords.

## Fite v. Bed Bath & Beyond, Inc.

503 S.W.3d 287 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while retail marketing allows for certain puffery, advertisements that create an illusory offer of a discount through obscured exclusions can constitute a deceptive practice under the Merchandising Practices Act. The court remanded for further findings of fact. The plaintiff brought a suit against Bed Bath & Beyond, alleging that the company violated the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (MPA) through its coupon and promotion policies. The plaintiff contended that the company advertised sales and coupons that were effectively unusable due to extensive exclusions, which were not clearly stated in the promotional materials. The company argued that the coupons contained explicit terms that the plaintiff failed to notice and that standard marketing puffery does not constitute a legal violation. The Missouri Court of Appeals addressed the intersection of retail marketing practices and consumer expectations. The court examined whether the 'average consumer' would be misled by the advertising campaign. The analysis focused on the clarity of the exclusions and whether they were presented in a manner that would lead a reasonable person to believe they could use the coupon. The court ruled that if the constraints on a coupon are so severe or obscured that they render the offer illusory, the practice may be considered deceptive. The opinion provided guidance on the burden of proof for plaintiffs in retail coupon litigation, noting that there must be proof that a reasonable person would have been misled to their detriment by the company's marketing strategy.

## Fite v. Missouri Department of Labor and Industrial Relations

490 S.W.3d 733 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an employer fulfills its duty under the MHRA by engaging in an interactive process to explore reasonable accommodations, and a claim of discrimination fails if the requested accommodation fundamentally alters the nature of the job. The agency met its burden of showing undue hardship. The Fite case concerned a claim of disability discrimination against a state agency. The employee, who had a physical impairment, alleged that the agency failed to provide a reasonable accommodation, thereby violating the MHRA. The primary legal issue was whether the requested accommodation was reasonable or whether it posed an undue hardship on the state agency's operations. The court reviewed the process by which employers must engage in an 'interactive process' with the employee to determine if a modification to work duties is feasible. The court emphasized that while employers are obligated to provide reasonable accommodations, they are not required to eliminate essential job functions or create new positions. The appellate analysis focused on the documentation of the interactive process and whether the agency acted in good faith when denying the specific request made by the employee during the vocational rehabilitation process.

## Fjellestad v. Pizza Hut of America, Inc.

188 F.3d 944 · 8th Cir. · 1999 · Federal

Holding: The court held that an employer's failure to engage in the interactive process is sufficient to defeat summary judgment. Employers have an affirmative obligation to assist in identifying a reasonable accommodation. Fjellestad, a restaurant manager, was injured in a car accident, resulting in permanent physical impairments. When she attempted to return to work, the company informed her that she could no longer perform the duties of a restaurant manager. She requested various accommodations, which were denied. The district court granted summary judgment to Pizza Hut. The appellate court reversed, finding that the company failed to engage in the required interactive process to find a reasonable accommodation. The court noted that there was evidence suggesting a modified schedule or a job share arrangement could have been reasonable. The court stressed that an employer's failure to participate in the interactive process is a 'prima facie' violation of the ADA in many circumstances because it prevents the discovery of effective, non-burdensome accommodations. The court remanded the case for a jury trial to determine whether the employer made a good-faith attempt to accommodate the plaintiff's needs.

## Flanders v. Pendergrass

Holding: The court held that the plaintiff established an easement by necessity, as the land was clearly landlocked after its severance from the larger parcel. The court granted the easement across the defendant's property. This case involved a dispute over an implied easement by necessity. The plaintiff purchased a landlocked parcel that had no direct access to a public road, and the defendant, a neighboring landowner, blocked the only path previously used to access the property. The plaintiff argued that because the property was severed from a larger tract and had no other access, an easement was implied by law to allow for ingress and egress. The defendant argued that alternative access was available through a nearby stream or by obtaining a different easement, which would be less burdensome on their land. The court analyzed the strict requirements for an easement by necessity, including the necessity for a common grantor at the time the land was divided. The opinion discusses how courts determine if a parcel is truly landlocked and whether the law should favor the utilization of land by providing an essential means of access. The case sets forth the evidentiary burden for showing that such an easement is not merely convenient but absolutely essential.
