## Gille v. Boone

208 S.W.3d 287 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2006 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's decision, holding that in a boundary dispute involving conflicting surveys, the trial court is entitled to weigh the credibility of the surveyors and choose the methodology that is most supported by the record. The parties in this dispute were neighbors who disagreed over the location of their shared property line. The dispute originated when the defendants began construction of a shed that the plaintiffs claimed encroached upon their property. Both parties produced surveys that conflicted regarding the true boundary line. The trial court conducted an evidentiary hearing and weighed the testimony of the surveyors. Ultimately, the court found the plaintiffs' surveyor more credible and ruled in their favor, ordering the removal of the shed. The defendants appealed, arguing that the court failed to account for a prior boundary line adjustment agreement. The appellate court reviewed the record and determined that the trial court had appropriately considered all evidence, including the history of the property and the methodology used by the respective surveyors. The appellate court concluded that the trial court's determination of the boundary was based on sound evidence and that no reversible error occurred in the proceedings or the final judgment regarding the encroachment.

## Gille v. Diekemper

936 S.W.2d 860 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1997 · Missouri

Holding: An easement by estoppel may be created when an owner allows another to use their land and that party makes substantial improvements in reliance on that permission. The owner is then barred from revoking the access if such action would result in an unfair burden on the party who reasonably relied on the promise. This case dealt with an easement by estoppel. The plaintiffs claimed that the defendants, after promising to allow access through their property for the construction of the plaintiffs' driveway, had reneged and blocked the route. The plaintiffs had already spent significant funds building their driveway in reliance on this oral promise. The trial court found that the plaintiffs' investment was made with the express permission of the defendants. The defendants argued that the permission was revocable, as it was never memorialized in a writing. The appellate court held that while easements are typically required to be in writing under the statute of frauds, the doctrine of equitable estoppel can create an 'easement by estoppel' when a party has made a promise and the other party has reasonably relied on that promise to their detriment. Because the defendants knew of and encouraged the plaintiffs' construction efforts, they were estopped

Second stored summary from denying the access. The court ordered the defendants to honor the agreement, demonstrating that equity can intervene in property disputes to prevent manifest injustice despite the lack of a formal deed.

## Gille v. Diekemper

100 S.W.3d 114 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the doctrine of acquiescence serves to stabilize boundary lines that have been long recognized by neighbors. When evidence demonstrates a mutual, long-term acceptance of a physical marker, that marker becomes the binding legal boundary regardless of conflicting survey data. This appeal concerned a boundary line dispute where one party sought to establish title by adverse possession and, alternatively, by acquiescence. The parties agreed that a hedge had long been considered the boundary, but the defendants installed a fence based on a recent survey. The plaintiffs sued to enjoin the fence installation and have the hedge recognized as the boundary. The appellate court examined the 'acquiescence' doctrine, emphasizing that it is a separate theory from adverse possession, relying on a long-standing mutual recognition of a line. The court found that the evidence showed both parties had treated the hedge as the boundary line for over twenty years, with neither side questioning the location until the survey was performed. The court held that the trial court erred in failing to apply the doctrine of acquiescence, noting that once a boundary is settled by agreement or long-term conduct, a new survey cannot disturb that established title. The court reversed and remanded for the entry of a judgment establishing the hedge as the legal boundary line.

## Gille v. Kimmons

787 S.W.2d 317 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1990 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the judgment, holding that the plaintiffs established a prescriptive easement. The long-term, unexplained use shifted the burden to the defendants to prove permissive use. The plaintiffs brought a quiet title action to establish their right to an easement by prescription over the defendants' land to access a lake. The defendants argued that the plaintiffs' use was sporadic and only occurred when the defendants were not in residence, making the use permissive and not adverse. The court reviewed the elements of a prescriptive easement: open, notorious, continuous, and adverse use for ten years. The court found that the plaintiffs had used the path regularly for over twenty years to reach the lake for recreational purposes. The defendants failed to provide evidence that they had ever granted permission to the plaintiffs, nor did they show that they ever prohibited the usage until the dispute began. The court applied the rule that if the use of an easement is open and continuous for the statutory period, the burden shifts to the servient owner to prove that the use was permissive. As the defendants could not carry this burden, the prescriptive easement was upheld.

## Gille v. Lutes

397 S.W.3d 528 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a long-standing fence line serves as the boundary between properties under the doctrine of acquiescence, overriding contrary survey evidence. Long-term mutual recognition of a boundary creates a legal presumption that it is the correct division. This boundary dispute concerned a strip of land between two farms. The plaintiff claimed ownership through a survey, while the defendants claimed the land through long-term maintenance and the existence of an old wire fence. The trial court awarded the land to the defendants under the doctrine of boundary by acquiescence. The appellate court reviewed whether the evidence established that the fence had been treated as the boundary for the statutory period. The record contained testimony from previous owners confirming that the fence line was accepted as the division between the properties for over thirty years. The plaintiff argued that the survey was the definitive source of the boundary, but the court ruled that equity favors the stabilization of long-recognized boundaries over the technical results of a modern survey if the elements of acquiescence are met. The trial court's decision to quiet title in the defendants' favor was upheld as being based on consistent and credible evidence.

## Gille v. Lutes

48 S.W.3d 676 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2001 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that long-standing acquiescence to a boundary line, evidenced by fences or physical markers, can supersede the original deed descriptions. Adverse possession can be established even when parties mistakenly believe the fence is the legal boundary. This boundary dispute concerned a disputed strip of land between two residential properties defined by a long-standing hedge and fence line rather than the recorded legal description. The plaintiff, who had recently purchased the property, sued to force the defendant to move the fence to match the survey description. The defendant countered that they had acquired the land via adverse possession because the fence line had been treated as the boundary for over thirty years. The trial court determined that the fence line acted as an agreed-upon boundary, and even if it didn't, the defendant had satisfied the elements of adverse possession. The appellate court looked at the doctrine of 'acquiescence,' which holds that where owners treat a specific line as their boundary for a period of time, they are bound by that line even if a subsequent survey shows it to be incorrect. The court affirmed that the law favors the certainty of established physical boundaries over the precision of old survey records, provided the elements of visible possession are demonstrated by the occupant.

## Gilleard v. Missouri State Board of Chiropractic Examiners

178 S.W.3d 596 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2005 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the Board could not contract away its statutory authority. Even if a settlement agreement existed, an agency cannot limit its regulatory duties through private contract.

Second stored summary This administrative law case touched upon contractual relationships in the context of professional licensing. A chiropractor challenged a disciplinary action taken by the Board, arguing that the Board's requirements violated a prior settlement agreement between the parties regarding the regulation of his practice. The dispute centered on whether the Board had the legal authority to enter into a contract that would limit its future regulatory duties. The court examined the separation of powers and the nature of administrative agency authority. It held that while a state agency can enter into certain agreements, it cannot contract away its fundamental statutory authority to protect the public. The court found that even if the Board had entered into an agreement as the chiropractor suggested, such a contract would be unenforceable because it would infringe upon the agency's mandatory police powers. This decision serves as a significant precedent regarding the limits of administrative agencies in signing contracts that restrict their statutory mandates, distinguishing public regulatory obligations from private contract law.

## Gilleland v. Gilleland

603 S.W.3d 725 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the lower court's finding of breach. It held that specific performance was a proper remedy given the unique nature of the real estate and the specific provisions of the settlement agreement. The parties in this case were involved in a dispute over the enforcement of a settlement agreement concerning real estate following the dissolution of their partnership. The partnership owned several commercial and residential properties, and the dissolution agreement mandated the sale of these assets and the distribution of proceeds. One party alleged that the other party failed to cooperate in the sale, intentionally undervalued the properties, and breached the terms of the agreement. The trial court found that the defendant's actions constituted a breach of contract and that specific performance or damages were warranted. The appellate court addressed the principles of contract interpretation in the context of real estate assets and the remedies available when a party obstructs the agreed-upon disposition of shared property. The court analyzed whether the trial court correctly calculated damages and whether the remedy of specific performance was appropriate given the nature of the partnership assets involved. This case serves as a reminder of the litigation risks associated with poorly drafted property dissolution agreements and the importance of clear, enforceable terms for disposing of real estate assets.

## Gilleland v. Gilleland

403 S.W.3d 674 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the evidence was insufficient to support an easement by necessity. It ruled that necessity does not arise simply because an existing route is more convenient or less expensive than creating a new access point. This case involved a dispute over an implied easement arising from the severance of a larger farm into smaller parcels for different family members. One parcel became landlocked, and the owner claimed an easement by necessity over the road that crossed the other parcel. The defendants argued that no such easement existed because at the time of severance, there was another way to reach the property, even if that way was significantly less convenient. The trial court examined the 'strict necessity' standard required for an implied easement in Missouri. The court analyzed the historical plats and the physical state of the land at the time of the initial division. The case highlighted the difference between 'convenience' and 'necessity' when establishing property rights that restrict the use of a neighbor's land. The court had to determine if the burden of proving necessity was met by demonstrating the financial and physical impossibility of building a road through the owner's own property, rather than just the high cost of doing so.

## Gilleland v. Ramey

75 S.W.3d 315 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2002 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the lower court's judgment, holding that the defendant failed to prove a valid oral agreement regarding the boundary. The surveyor's report was found to be the most credible evidence. The property owners sued their neighbor regarding a dispute over a boundary fence. The plaintiff's survey indicated the fence was built on their property, while the defendant argued that the fence was the historical boundary line. The trial court determined the location of the boundary based on the survey and ordered the fence to be removed. The appellate court reviewed the application of the 'agreed boundary' doctrine, which can settle disputes when parties have orally agreed to a boundary and acted in reliance on that agreement. The defendant claimed there was such an agreement, but the court found that the evidence did not support a meeting of the minds between the parties or their predecessors. The case highlights the strict burden of proof required to establish an agreed boundary line that deviates from the official deed description. The court upheld the trial court's reliance on the surveyor's testimony, noting that surveyor opinions are fact-based and entitled to substantial weight in boundary disputes where deed descriptions might be ambiguous.

## Gillen v. State

481 S.W.3d 609 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a violation of safety standards on public property can support a claim under the dangerous condition exception to sovereign immunity. Design immunity does not apply when property fails to meet mandatory safety requirements. Gillen suffered injuries on a public facility stairway that lacked a handrail, which he claimed violated safety codes. He sued the state for negligence under the dangerous condition exception to sovereign immunity. The trial court dismissed the suit, stating that the lack of a handrail was a design choice protected by official immunity. The appellate court reviewed whether a violation of building codes could constitute a 'dangerous condition.' The court held that while design choices are often protected, the failure to maintain a facility in compliance with mandatory safety standards that prevent common injuries can expose the state to liability. The case was remanded to determine if the lack of a handrail was a physical defect that rendered the property unreasonably dangerous. This decision is significant for establishing that government bodies are not entirely immune to liability when their property fails to meet basic, objectively established safety standards for public use.

## Gillenwaters v. Knight

553 S.W.3d 347 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the jury's verdict, holding that the trial court did not abuse its discretion in admitting the evidence and that the record contained sufficient expert testimony to establish a breach of the standard of care. The judgment was upheld. The plaintiffs brought a wrongful death and medical malpractice suit against a physician after the patient died following a surgical procedure. The main allegation was that the surgeon failed to manage the patient's anticoagulation medication before and after the surgery, which contributed to a fatal blood clot. The case centered on the standard of care regarding preoperative assessment and postoperative monitoring of patients on anticoagulant therapy. During the trial, disputes arose over the admissibility of evidence regarding the surgeon's prior adherence to clinical guidelines. The trial court admitted certain records over the defendant's objection. Upon appeal, the court examined whether the trial court erred in its evidentiary rulings and whether the evidence was sufficient to support the jury's verdict in favor of the plaintiff. The opinion highlights the importance of internal clinical guidelines and whether they are admissible as evidence of the standard of care in medical malpractice cases, alongside the requirement for expert testimony to interpret those guidelines.

## Gilleylen v. City of Bridgeton

505 F.3d 785 · United States Court of Appeals, Eighth Circuit · 2007 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that summary judgment was inappropriate because there were disputed questions of fact regarding whether the city's stated reasons for termination were pretextual. The case was remanded for a trial on the retaliation claim. This case involved a Section 1983 claim where a former police officer alleged that his constitutional rights were violated when he was terminated. The officer claimed that his firing was in retaliation for his involvement in a labor union and for supporting a political candidate for police chief. The city argued that the officer was terminated for valid disciplinary reasons, specifically for insubordination and neglect of duty. The court analyzed the First Amendment's protection of public employees regarding their speech and associational activities. The analysis focused on the Pickering balancing test, which weighs the employee's interest in speech against the government's interest in the efficiency of the public services it provides. The court further looked at the evidence of causation--whether the employer would have made the same decision even in the absence of the protected activity. The decision provides a detailed look at how federal courts analyze the 'mixed-motive' defense in public employment cases where there is evidence of both protected activity and legitimate, non-protected reasons for termination.

## Gilleylen v. City of St. Louis

596 S.W.3d 627 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court reversed the summary judgment in favor of the officers, holding that they were not entitled to qualified immunity because the legality of the warrantless search was not clearly established. It allowed the case to proceed to discovery. In this Section 1983 action, the plaintiff alleged that municipal police officers violated his Fourth Amendment rights through an illegal search and seizure. The plaintiff claimed that officers lacked probable cause or a valid warrant, leading to a detention that infringed upon his constitutional liberties. The City of St. Louis asserted qualified immunity, arguing that the officers acted based on a good-faith belief that their actions were lawful. The appellate court examined the standard for qualified immunity in the context of warrantless searches, emphasizing that the burden is on the plaintiff to show that the constitutional right was 'clearly established' at the time of the incident. The analysis delved into the specifics of the 'exigent circumstances' exception to the warrant requirement, with the court finding that the city failed to meet the threshold for such an exception in the current record. This case serves as a reminder of the narrow scope of qualified immunity and the stringent requirements officers must meet to avoid liability for constitutional violations during investigatory stops and property searches.

## Gilleylen v. St. Luke's Hospital

616 S.W.3d 378 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that res ipsa loquitur is applicable to cases involving a foreign object left in a patient during surgery. Therefore, the plaintiff did not need initial expert testimony to establish a prima facie case of negligence. Plaintiff sued for damages arising from a surgical error that left a foreign object inside the patient's body following an operation. The litigation focused on the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur, which allows a jury to infer negligence when an event occurs that normally would not happen without a breach of the standard of care. The hospital argued that the doctrine was inapplicable because the plaintiff failed to produce expert testimony establishing a breach of the standard of care by a specific individual. The trial court denied the hospital's motion for summary judgment, leading to an appeal regarding the sufficiency of evidence required in foreign-body cases. The appellate court examined whether the presence of a foreign object constitutes sufficient evidence of negligence to shift the burden of production to the defendant. The decision provides a clear analysis of how Missouri law treats cases of obvious medical error in the absence of explicit expert testimony regarding surgical procedures.

## Gingery v. City of Glendale

573 S.W.2d 712 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1978 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that municipal ordinances requiring occupancy permits are a valid exercise of police power. It ruled that such regulations are reasonably related to ensuring residential health and safety. This case involved the constitutionality of a municipal ordinance requiring a landlord to obtain an occupancy permit for every change in tenants. The landlord argued that the ordinance was an unconstitutional invasion of privacy and an excessive exercise of police power by the municipality. The court examined the balance between the city's interest in maintaining health and safety standards through property inspections and the landlord's right to conduct business without undue interference. The opinion acknowledges that while municipalities have the authority to regulate property maintenance, such regulations must be reasonably related to legitimate

Second stored summary governmental objectives. The court concluded that the permit requirement was a valid exercise of local government power intended to ensure that rental housing meets basic safety standards before new tenants move in. The decision highlights the broad deference courts provide to municipal zoning and housing code enforcement, provided the regulations are not arbitrary or discriminatory against landlords or tenants.

## Gingrich v. Smith

501 S.W.3d 520 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a long-standing fence can constitute a legal boundary by acquiescence regardless of survey results. Evidence of historical usage and intent must be considered in determining property boundaries. The plaintiff initiated a lawsuit to challenge a boundary line established by a recent survey. The plaintiff argued that a historical boundary fence, which differed from the survey results, should be legally recognized under the doctrine of boundary by acquiescence. The defendant, who had commissioned the new survey, contended that the survey was the definitive proof of the property line and that the fence was merely a barrier for livestock, not a boundary. The trial court ruled in favor of the defendant, holding that the survey was controlling. The plaintiff appealed, arguing that the court failed to properly weigh the history of the fence's location. The appellate court reversed, noting that Missouri law recognizes that a long-standing fence can serve as the legal boundary if neighbors have treated it as such for the statutory period. The court held that the trial court erred in failing to give sufficient weight to evidence of the parties' conduct and usage of the land. It remanded the case for a new trial with instructions to consider the elements of acquiescence in the context of the fence's placement. This case demonstrates that survey markers are not always the final word in property disputes if established usage and historical conduct show a different mutual understanding of the boundary.

## Gipson v. General Motors Corp.

430 S.W.3d 285 · Mo. Ct. App. W.D. · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the employees were not exempt professionals because their duties, although highly technical, were primarily manual and mechanical. The employer was ordered to pay back-overtime wages. The dispute in this case centered on the classification of skilled maintenance workers as exempt employees under the professional exemption of the MMWL. The workers argued that their roles, while highly skilled, were essentially technical and did not meet the requirement of 'intellectual' work that requires an advanced degree. General Motors argued that the complexity of the systems maintained by these workers necessitated an exemption from overtime pay. The appellate court looked at the Department of Labor regulations defining professional exemptions and compared those with the duties performed by the plaintiffs. The case clarifies the high threshold required for employers to successfully invoke the professional exemption for skilled tradespeople, emphasizing that advanced skill sets alone are insufficient without the corresponding level of discretion and theoretical knowledge required by the statutory definitions.

## Gipson v. Kansas City Transit, Inc.

451 S.W.2d 101 (Mo. 1970) · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1970 · Missouri

Holding: The Supreme Court of Missouri reversed the trial court's judgment. The court held that the bus driver's actions in stopping suddenly to avoid striking a child constituted a reasonable response to an emergency situation created by the child's actions, and therefore, the driver was not negligent. The court found that the evidence did not support a finding that the driver's actions were negligent or failed to meet the standard of care expected of a reasonable driver under similar emergency circumstances. This case involved a passenger who was injured when a bus operated by Kansas City Transit, Inc. suddenly stopped. The passenger alleged that the bus driver was negligent in operating the bus, causing a violent stop that threw her from her seat and resulted in injuries. The transit company argued that the stop was necessary to avoid hitting a child who ran into the street, and therefore, the stop was reasonable and not negligent. The trial court entered judgment for the passenger, and the transit company appealed. The central issue was whether the driver's actions constituted negligence or were a reasonable response to an emergency situation.

## Glastris v. Nelson

542 S.W.3d 388 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The Supreme Court of Missouri affirmed the trial court's judgment. The Court held that Nelson's dissatisfaction was based on objective financial performance metrics outlined in the contract and that he acted in good faith in withholding the final payment. The Court found that the satisfaction clause was properly applied, and therefore, Nelson did not breach the contract. This case concerned a dispute over a contract for the sale of a business. Glastris sold his business to Nelson pursuant to a written agreement. A dispute arose regarding the final payment, which was contingent upon Nelson's satisfaction with the business's financial performance post-sale. Nelson refused to make the final payment, alleging that the business's performance did not meet the contractual standards and that he was dissatisfied. Glastris sued for breach of contract. The trial court entered judgment in favor of Nelson, finding that his dissatisfaction was genuine and in good faith. Glastris appealed, arguing that Nelson's dissatisfaction was not in good faith and that the contract's satisfaction clause was being improperly applied. The Supreme Court examined the "satisfaction clause" in contracts and the standard for determining good faith.

## Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A.

563 U.S. 754 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2011 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that induced patent infringement requires knowledge that the induced acts constitute infringement. Willful blindness toward the existence of a patent satisfies the knowledge requirement. SEB sued Global-Tech for inducing patent infringement. The central issue was the standard for the defendant's state of mind required to establish 'induced infringement' under 35 U.S.C. Section 271(b). Global-Tech argued that they should have had 'actual knowledge' of the patent to be liable for inducement. The Supreme Court clarified that induced infringement requires knowledge that the induced acts constitute patent infringement. The Court adopted the 'willful blindness' doctrine for this purpose, holding that it is sufficient to prove that a defendant deliberately shielded themselves from clear evidence of infringement while knowing a high probability of infringement existed. Because Global-Tech had copied the patented product from a competitor and conducted no patent search before marketing their version, the Court found they were willfully blind to the existence of the patent. This decision clarified that defendants cannot intentionally remain ignorant of existing patents and subsequently escape liability for inducing others to infringe on that protected intellectual property.

## Gobeille v. Liberty Mutual Insurance Co.

Holding: The Supreme Court held that ERISA preempts state laws that impose reporting requirements on self-funded ERISA plans. Liberty Mutual, which maintained a self-funded plan, challenged the requirement, arguing that ERISA preempts state laws that interfere with the uniform administration of benefits. Vermont contended that the law was a valid exercise of its police power to regulate healthcare data. The case focused on the 'conflict preemption' doctrine, specifically whether state reporting requirements impose significant administrative burdens that undermine the goal of uniform federal regulation under ERISA. The Court considered whether the administrative reporting requirements were an impermissible intrusion into the core function of plan administration. The Court determined that the reporting requirements were 'of central concern' to ERISA's administrative structure, as they required plans to modify their administrative practices to accommodate different state-by-state data standards. The ruling emphasized the importance of federal uniformity for multi-state employers, holding that ERISA prevents states from imposing such burdens on self-funded benefit plans.

Holding: The Court held that due process requires an evidentiary hearing prior to the termination of welfare benefits. Recipients must have the opportunity to present evidence, confront witnesses, and be represented by counsel. New York City terminated welfare benefits to several recipients without affording them a prior evidentiary hearing, citing administrative efficiency. The recipients challenged this action, asserting it violated their right to due process under the Fourteenth Amendment. The Supreme Court addressed whether a state may terminate public assistance payments to a particular recipient without affording him the opportunity for an evidentiary hearing prior to termination. The Court emphasized that welfare benefits are a matter of statutory entitlement for persons qualified to receive them and are essential for survival. Therefore, the termination of benefits without an opportunity for the recipient to personally appear and present evidence, confront witnesses, and argue their case against the government's evidence constitutes a denial of procedural due process. While a full judicial-style trial is not required, the state must provide adequate notice, the opportunity to be heard, and the right to counsel or representation at the pre-termination stage. This landmark decision underscored the necessity of robust due process protections when the state seeks to deprive individuals of essential lifelines, fundamentally shifting the administration of social welfare programs.

Holding: The Court held that courts must consider the generic nature of alleged misrepresentations when evaluating price impact for the purpose of class certification. Broad, vague statements are less likely to support the fraud-on-the-market presumption of reliance. This case clarified how courts should evaluate 'generic' misstatements when applying the price impact defense at class certification. Goldman Sachs was sued over statements it made about managing conflicts of interest, which the plaintiffs claimed were misleading and inflated the stock price. Goldman argued that these statements were too broad and vague to have actually influenced the stock price. The Supreme Court held that in assessing price impact for class certification, a court must consider the nature of the statement. If a statement is generic (e.g., 'we care about our clients'), it is less likely to have had a price impact than a specific, concrete misstatement. The Court emphasized that a court should not ignore the generic nature of a statement simply because it was made at the class certification stage. By requiring courts to evaluate whether such vague statements could actually impact a stock price, the ruling limits the use of 'puffery' as a basis for massive class-action securities claims.

## Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. v. Arkansas Teacher Retirement System

594 U.S. 113 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2021 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that courts must consider the generic nature of an alleged misrepresentation when determining whether it had a price impact at the class certification stage. This case revisited the fraud-on-the-market theory and the role of 'price impact' at the class certification stage. The plaintiffs alleged that Goldman Sachs made generic, vague statements about its conflicts of interest that inflated its stock price. When the truth about the conflicts emerged, the price dropped. The question for the Court was whether the 'genericity' of the statements should be considered by the judge when determining if there was price impact. Goldman Sachs argued that generic statements do not affect the market price because investors are smart enough to disregard them. The Supreme Court remanded the case, instructing the lower courts that they must consider all evidence of price impact, including the nature of the statements themselves. The Court clarified that the 'generic' nature of a statement is highly relevant to whether it actually moved the stock price, and that courts should engage in a robust analysis of this factor.

## Gomez v. Bi-State Development Agency

The Commission denied the claim, finding that while the work environment likely aggravated the back condition, the evidence did not show that it was the primary, prevailing factor. The Court of Appeals reviewed the legislative intent behind the prevailing factor requirement, which was designed to limit workers' compensation to conditions primarily caused by work. The court affirmed the Commission, emphasizing that in cases of chronic, degenerative conditions, the claimant must produce clear, expert medical evidence that distinguishes the workplace impact from non-occupational factors, and failing that, the claim must be denied to adhere to the strict statutory interpretation.

The court reviewed whether the employee had a reasonable belief that the law was being violated and whether that report was the cause of his termination. The court discussed the necessity for the plaintiff to show that the employer's stated reason for termination was pretextual, specifically analyzing the timing of the budget cuts in relation to the reports. The case provides insight into the challenges of suing a municipal entity for wrongful discharge and the evidentiary hurdles for proving pretext in the face of fiscal defense claims.

## Google LLC v. Oracle America, Inc.

593 U.S. 1 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2021 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court held that Google's copying of the Java API declaring code constituted fair use as a matter of law. The use was transformative, serving a new purpose in a different technological context, and fostered competition and innovation. The dispute involved Google's use of portions of the Java SE Application Programming Interface (API) in the development of its Android mobile operating system. Oracle, which held the copyrights to the Java platform, sued Google for copyright infringement. Google argued that its copying of the declaring code in the Java APIs was a fair use. The district court found that the API code was not copyrightable, but the Federal Circuit reversed, holding that the code was copyrightable and that the copying was not fair use. The Supreme Court assumed for the sake of the argument that the code was copyrightable and focused on the fair use defense. The Court concluded that Google's copying was a 'transformative' use because it allowed programmers to use their skills to create new programs for a different platform (mobile phones) rather than merely replicating the functionality of the Java platform for desktop computers. The Court emphasized that the nature of the API code, which is bound up with uncopyrightable ideas and methods, and the public benefit of enabling innovation in the software industry, weighed in favor of fair use. This decision provides significant protection for developers using APIs in creating interoperable software.

## Gorman v. Freely

271 S.W.3d 608 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2008 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an easement by necessity is unavailable if any reasonable legal access to the property exists, regardless of the difficulty, cost, or convenience of that access. This matter involved a claim for an easement by necessity that was denied due to the availability of an alternative access point. The plaintiff owned a landlocked parcel and sought to establish an easement across the defendant's field. The defendant argued that the plaintiff had access to a public road via a rugged, overgrown path that went through a different part of the property. The plaintiff argued that this path was 'commercially unfeasible' and 'too difficult' to use for residential construction. The court of appeals reaffirmed that 'necessity' means the lack of a legal right to access one's land, not a lack of a convenient or inexpensive route. The court noted that if any path exists that can legally be used to access the parcel, the requirement for an easement by necessity is not met. The case set a high bar for property owners seeking to force access across a neighbor's land when alternative legal routes, however difficult, are available.

## Gorman v. Shop-N-Save Warehouse Foods, Inc.

999 S.W.2d 284 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1999 · Missouri

Holding: A jury may infer constructive notice in slip and fall cases when the business's method of operation creates a foreseeable risk of hazard. Retailers are expected to maintain vigilance in areas where debris is common due to store displays. The plaintiff, an elderly shopper, slipped on a grape in a grocery store aisle. The issue was whether the store had constructive notice of the grape on the floor. Shop-N-Save argued that the plaintiff offered no evidence regarding how long the grape had been there, making a negligence finding speculative. The trial court granted summary judgment. On appeal, the court looked at the 'mode of operation' theory. While Missouri courts have been cautious about fully adopting the mode of operation rule, the court determined that the presence of loose produce in a self-service area increases the risk of debris. The court held that the jury could infer that the store's business practices made the spill foreseeable, effectively satisfying the notice requirement. This case refined the application of notice rules in grocery store settings, highlighting the balance between demanding evidence of actual knowledge versus holding retailers accountable for operational hazards inherent in their business model.

## Goss v. Lopez

419 U.S. 565 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1975 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court held that students facing suspension have property and liberty interests that trigger due process protection. Consequently, schools must provide notice and an informal hearing before imposing a short-term suspension. Several students in Ohio public schools were suspended for up to ten days without a hearing, following allegations of misconduct. The students argued that their suspension without a chance to be heard violated their Fourteenth Amendment due process rights. The Supreme Court addressed whether a public school student has a property or liberty interest that warrants due process protection. The Court affirmed that because the state provided a public education, students had a legitimate property interest in their education and a liberty interest in their reputation. Therefore, the school could not suspend students without providing at least minimal due process protections. The Court established that for suspensions of ten days or less, the student must be given oral or written notice of the charges against them and, if they deny them, an explanation of the evidence the authorities have and an opportunity to present their side of the story. This ruling established that schools must balance the need for swift discipline with the student's fundamental right to be informed and heard before suffering a loss of educational opportunity.

## Graham v. Connor

490 U.S. 386 · U.S. Supreme Court · 1989 · Federal

5 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Supreme Court held that all claims of excessive force by law enforcement during an arrest must be analyzed under the Fourth Amendment's 'objective reasonableness' standard. This standard focuses on whether the officer's actions were objectively reasonable in light of the facts and circumstances, without regard to the officer's underlying intent. Dethorne Graham, a diabetic, asked a friend to drive him to a store to get sugar for an insulin reaction. Upon seeing a long line, he ran out. A police officer became suspicious and stopped the car. During the encounter, officers used force to restrain Graham, injuring him. Graham filed a § 1983 lawsuit alleging that the officers used excessive force, violating his constitutional rights. The lower courts applied a 'substantive due process' test, asking whether the officers acted in good faith or maliciously. The Supreme Court took the case to clarify the standard to be applied in excessive force claims against law enforcement officers. The question presented was whether the 'malicious and sadistic' standard applied to prison conditions should also apply to arrests, or if a different constitutional analysis was required for police interactions during a stop.

## Graham v. Florida

560 U.S. 48 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2010 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the Eighth Amendment prohibits sentencing a juvenile offender to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole for a non-homicide offense. The state must provide some meaningful opportunity for release for such offenders. Terrence Graham was convicted of armed burglary and attempted robbery at age 16. As a repeat offender, he was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. Graham challenged this sentence under the Eighth Amendment, arguing that it was unconstitutional to impose life without parole on a juvenile who had not committed homicide. The Supreme Court reviewed the national consensus and the culpability of juveniles. The Court concluded that the Eighth Amendment prohibits the imposition of a life without parole sentence on a juvenile offender who did not commit homicide. The Court emphasized that juveniles have diminished culpability and greater prospects for reform compared to adults. Because a sentence of life without parole denies the offender any chance of demonstrating maturation and rehabilitation, it is disproportionately severe for non-homicide offenses. The decision required that states provide some meaningful opportunity for release based on demonstrated maturity and rehabilitation for juveniles convicted of non-homicide crimes.

## Grame v. Missouri Department of Health

967 S.W.2d 692 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1998 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that public employees must strictly comply with administrative grievance procedures. Absent evidence of bad faith or clear retaliatory intent, employment termination decisions related to legitimate reductions in force are within the discretion of the state agency. The appellant, a former state employee, alleged wrongful discharge from the Department of Health, claiming he was terminated in retaliation for his opposition to certain departmental practices. The Department claimed the firing was due to the elimination of the appellant's position for budgetary reasons. The case involved complex procedural requirements regarding the exhaustion of administrative remedies before pursuing judicial review. The court examined whether the appellant followed the necessary grievance procedures provided under Missouri civil service law. The appellant argued that his termination was a violation of his constitutional rights to free speech and due process. The court found that the appellant did not provide evidence sufficient to establish that his speech was a substantial or motivating factor in the decision-making process for his termination. Additionally, the court highlighted that the administrative law judge had conducted a thorough review of the record and found no evidence of discriminatory or retaliatory intent. The appellate court affirmed the decision, noting that when an agency follows established personnel procedures and provides a legitimate, non-discriminatory reason for a reduction in force, the courts will not interfere in the decision-making process absent clear evidence of bad faith.

## Gramex Corp. v. Feinstein

900 S.W.2d 257 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1995 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a retailer may be held strictly liable in tort for a defective product even if they did not manufacture it. However, the plaintiff must establish that the product was in a defective condition unreasonably dangerous to the user at the time of sale. The plaintiffs brought a strict liability action against a retailer for injuries sustained by a minor who ingested a corrosive substance sold by the store. The case centers on whether a retailer can be held strictly liable for the sale of a defective product when the manufacturer is known and the retailer did not alter the product. The Missouri Court of Appeals examined the application of the Restatement (Second) of Torts regarding the liability of sellers of products in a defective condition unreasonably dangerous to the user or consumer. The court looked at whether the product's packaging failed to provide adequate warnings regarding its hazardous nature, thereby rendering it defective. The analysis weighed the retailer's duty against the consumer's responsibility and the inherent nature of the product. The lower court's judgment was reviewed to determine if the trial court erred in its application of the 'unreasonably dangerous' standard. The appellate court ultimately focused on the specific requirements to establish a cause of action against a non-manufacturing seller, emphasizing the necessity of proving the product was defective at the time of sale and that the defect caused the injury.

## Gramex Corp. v. Green Supply, Inc.

89 S.W.3d 432 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2002 · Missouri

3 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that a seller is subject to strict liability even if the seller was not the manufacturer. However, the plaintiff failed to meet the burden of proving that the specific product was defective at the time it left the distributor's control, thus affirming the summary judgment. This case involved a fire originating in a warehouse that destroyed property and merchandise. The plaintiff, Gramex Corp., brought a products liability action against the distributor of a fluorescent light ballast, alleging that the ballast was defectively designed and manufactured. The central issue was whether the strict liability standard applied to the distributor under Missouri law for a defect that was latent and undiscoverable by reasonable inspection. The court had to determine the liability of a middleman when a product fails to meet safety standards. The trial court had granted summary judgment in favor of the distributor, reasoning that there was insufficient evidence to prove the product was defective at the time it left the distributor's control. The plaintiff appealed, arguing that the res ipsa loquitur doctrine should apply and that there was circumstantial evidence of a defect. The appellate court examined the requirements for a prima facie case in strict liability, emphasizing that the plaintiff must demonstrate that the product was in a defective condition unreasonably dangerous when it left the defendant's possession.

## Gramex Corp. v. Snyder

936 S.W.2d 586 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1996 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a retailer cannot be held liable under strict products liability for a product that has not yet been purchased. The court found that the doctrine of strict liability applies only to those who place a product into the stream of commerce through a sale, which had not occurred in this case. This case involved a plaintiff who sustained injuries after slipping on a liquid spill at a retail store. The core issue was whether the premises liability principles or strict products liability applied, and specifically whether the store could be held liable under strict liability for a product that had not yet been purchased or used. The court examined the standard for strict liability for defective products under Section 402A of the Restatement (Second) of Torts. The plaintiff argued the product was defective because it was in a container that leaked. The court had to determine if the store acted as a 'seller' of the product at the time of the incident before the checkout process occurred. The analysis focused on the definition of a sale and the transfer of possession. The court also considered whether the store had constructive notice of the dangerous condition created by the leaking product. The decision refined the boundaries of when strict

Second stored summary liability applies to retailers in Missouri and clarified the distinction between strict liability and traditional negligence theories.

## Gramex Corp. v. Snyder

890 S.W.2d 381 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1994 · Missouri

Holding: A retailer can be held strictly liable for failure to warn of a product's danger if the product is found to be unreasonably dangerous in the absence of such warnings. The court held that the duty to warn applies to retailers who are part of the stream of commerce when the danger is inherent in the product's nature. The plaintiff, a minor, suffered severe burns when a bottle of denatured alcohol ignited near him. He brought a product liability suit against the retailer, Gramex Corp., alleging that the product was sold without adequate warnings regarding its flammability and potential for ignition. The retailer argued that it was merely a passive seller and did not know or have reason to know of the specific danger. The evidence at trial established that the product was inherently dangerous and that the label lacked sufficient warnings to warn an ordinary consumer of the high volatility of the substance in close proximity to heat sources. The jury found in favor of the plaintiff. On appeal, the court reviewed whether the retailer could be held strictly liable for the failure to warn even if it did not manufacture the product. The court examined the standard of care expected of sellers in the chain of distribution and the necessity of adequate instructions for safe use. The appellate court analyzed whether the retailer had a duty to inspect and warn users about the product's risks, ultimately focusing on the 'learned intermediary' doctrine and the seller's duty to provide the warnings provided by the manufacturer.

## Graves v. Finch Pruyn & Co.

353 F. App'x 558 · 2d Cir. · 2009 · Federal

Holding: The court held that an employer is not required to convert a temporary light-duty position into a permanent role under the ADA. The duty to accommodate does not require the creation of new positions. Graves, a mill worker, was diagnosed with a permanent disability that limited his ability to perform heavy lifting. After returning from medical leave, the employer attempted to place him in a light-duty position. The plaintiff alleged that the employer did not provide a reasonable accommodation and that his subsequent termination was motivated by discrimination. The employer argued that the light-duty position was temporary and that no permanent position existed that the plaintiff could perform within his medical restrictions. The appellate court held that the employer fulfilled its obligation under the ADA by attempting to place the plaintiff in available roles. It noted that the ADA does not mandate the creation of new permanent positions for individuals who cannot perform the essential functions of their original jobs. The court affirmed the lower court's dismissal, ruling that the plaintiff failed to show he was a 'qualified individual' for the permanent roles available at the time of his termination.

## Graves v. Hartford Accident & Indem. Co.

713 S.W.2d 589 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1986 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the business property exclusion was applicable. It affirmed the lower court's finding that the items were primarily for business use. The insureds sought recovery under their homeowners policy for loss of personal property due to theft. The insurer, Hartford, denied the claim on the basis of a 'business property' exclusion, arguing that the stolen items were used for business purposes and thus excluded from coverage for personal property. The trial court granted judgment to the insurer. The insureds appealed, contending that the items were dual-purpose and that the exclusion should not apply to items used at least partially for personal reasons. The appellate court analyzed the policy language, which excluded 'property pertaining to business.' The court reasoned that if property is used primarily for business, it falls under the exclusion, regardless of incidental personal use. After reviewing the evidence presented at trial regarding the nature and primary use of the items in question, the court determined that the trial court's finding was supported by substantial evidence. The decision reinforced that insurers may rely on specific property exclusions to narrow the scope of their liability for personal property coverage in homeowners policies.

## Grayson v. Chicago Title Insurance Co.

592 S.W.3d 371 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an employee performing internal compliance duties does not automatically trigger the public policy exception to at-will employment. A plaintiff must demonstrate a clear violation of a specific statute or public mandate. Grayson brought a suit for wrongful discharge after his employment with Chicago Title was terminated. He alleged that his termination was a result of his refusal to participate in practices that violated state insurance regulations, which he argued constituted a violation of public policy. The employer argued that Grayson's job responsibilities included compliance and that his termination was due to disagreements regarding his interpretation of those regulations. The central issue was whether the public policy exception applies to an employee whose job description includes oversight of the very laws he allegedly reported. The court distinguished between reporting an illegality and merely doing one's job in a way that creates friction with superiors. The appellate court found that the plaintiff failed to identify a specific, clear mandate of public policy that was violated by his termination. The decision clarified that simply performing job duties that require adherence to laws does not automatically give an employee whistleblower status or protection against termination under the public policy exception. This case provides a clear limit on the expansion of whistleblower protections.

## Great-West Life & Annuity Insurance Co. v. Knudson

534 U.S. 204 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2002 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that Section 502(a)(3) only allows for 'equitable' relief. An action for money damages to enforce a reimbursement provision is a legal remedy, not an equitable one, and is therefore not permitted under the statute. Knudson was injured in a car accident, and her ERISA-governed health plan paid for her medical care. The plan included a reimbursement provision. Knudson sued the party responsible for the accident and recovered a settlement, a portion of which was allocated to medical expenses. The plan sought to recover the medical expenses from the settlement proceeds. When Knudson placed the funds in a special needs trust, the plan sued under ERISA Section 502(a)(3) to compel reimbursement. The Supreme Court addressed whether the plan could obtain 'appropriate equitable relief' to recover the money. The Court ruled that the relief sought was essentially legal, not equitable. Because the plan was seeking to impose personal liability on the defendant to pay a debt, rather than seeking to recover a specific, identifiable fund that was currently in the defendant's possession, the action did not qualify as equitable relief under the statute. The Court's decision strictly limited the forms of relief available to ERISA plans under the 'equitable' rubric to those recognized by courts of equity in the 19th century.

## Green v. B & D Properties

588 S.W.3d 115 · Mo. App. S.D. · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a written lease with an integration clause supersedes any alleged oral modifications. It affirmed the eviction, ruling that the tenant was bound by the written lease terms regarding pets. The landlord initiated an eviction action based on a breach of the lease's 'pet policy' clause. The tenant argued that the landlord had informally permitted the pet, which the landlord denied. The trial court ruled for the landlord, finding that the written lease agreement contained an integration clause that barred the consideration of any oral modifications. The appellate court examined the role of integration clauses in residential leases. The court affirmed the decision, holding that when a lease explicitly states it is the entire agreement and requires any modifications to be in writing, the parol evidence rule prevents the tenant from relying on alleged oral statements that conflict with the written terms. This case reinforces the importance of written documentation in landlord-tenant relationships and demonstrates the courts' adherence to the 'four corners' rule in contract disputes, discouraging tenants from relying on verbal assurances that contradict formal, signed lease documents regarding pet policies or other restrictions.

## Green v. BNSF Railway

390 S.W.3d 875 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the claimant was an employee under the control test. The award of workers' compensation was affirmed. The claimant was injured while working on a train maintenance task. The dispute was whether the claimant was an employee entitled to workers' compensation or an independent contractor. The Commission found the claimant was an employee based on the level of control exercised by the company. The employer appealed, challenging the classification. The appellate court reviewed the common law 'control test' used to distinguish between employees and independent contractors. The court noted that the employer dictated the claimant's hours, provided the tools, required specific training, and controlled the methods of work performance. Despite a contract labeling the claimant as an independent contractor, the court looked at the 'substance over form' of the relationship. The court held that the Commission's finding of an employment relationship was well-supported by the evidence of the employer's total control over the claimant's work. The decision awarding workers' compensation benefits was upheld, confirming that the statutory definition of an employee in Missouri is broad and designed to include workers who function as employees in all practical respects.

## Greer v. Sysco Food Services

475 S.W.3d 655 · Missouri Supreme Court · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The Court held that the prevailing factor standard requires that the employment-related injury be the primary cause of the disability. The denial of benefits was affirmed because the claimant failed to prove that the work incident was the prevailing factor. The claimant sought workers' compensation benefits after suffering a back injury. The employer contested the claim, arguing the injury was not the prevailing factor in the disability. The case proceeded through the Labor and Industrial Relations Commission, which denied benefits based on the statutory requirement that the work-related injury be the prevailing factor in causing the medical condition and the disability. The claimant appealed, arguing that the Commission misapplied the law regarding the causation standard under Section 287.020.3(1). The Missouri Supreme Court reviewed the definition of 'prevailing factor,' clarifying that it requires the injury to be the primary cause of the condition, not merely a contributing factor among many. This case significantly tightened the standard for medical causation in Missouri workers' compensation claims, necessitating that medical experts specifically testify that the workplace incident was the primary reason for the resulting disability to satisfy the heightened evidentiary burden imposed by the legislative reforms of 2005.

Under Missouri law, the court noted that temporary departures for minor personal tasks do not necessarily remove an employee from the scope of employment if the primary purpose of the activity remains work-related. The court found that the Commission failed to properly apply the 'deviation' doctrine and reversed the denial, remanding the matter for further findings on whether the act occurred within the professional scope.

## Greer v. Zurich Insurance Co.

441 S.W.2d 15 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1969 · Missouri

Holding: The Court held that an insurer who has assumed the defense of an insured cannot unilaterally withdraw if such withdrawal prejudices the insured. The duty to defend is independent of the outcome of the underlying litigation. This case dealt with an insurer's 'duty to defend' when there is a potential conflict between the insurer's interest and the insured's interest. The insurer defended the insured under a reservation of rights but later sought to withdraw, claiming the insured breached the cooperation clause. The insured argued that the insurer had waived its right to withdraw because it assumed the defense. The Supreme Court of Missouri reviewed the principles of the duty to defend and the duty of cooperation. The court held that an insurer cannot withdraw from a defense it has already undertaken if the withdrawal would cause prejudice to the insured's ability to mount a defense. Furthermore, the court emphasized that the duty to defend is broader than the duty to indemnify and is triggered by the allegations in the petition, regardless of the ultimate finding of liability. The insurer's attempt to withdraw was deemed improper because it did not provide the insured with adequate time to secure independent counsel.

## Gregg v. Georgia

428 U.S. 153 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1976 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the death penalty is not per se unconstitutional under the Eighth Amendment. A state's capital sentencing procedure is constitutional if it provides sufficient guidance to the jury through a bifurcated trial and required findings of aggravating circumstances. Following the decision in Furman v. Georgia, several states revised their capital punishment statutes to address concerns about arbitrary application. Georgia adopted a 'bifurcated trial' system, where the guilt phase and the sentencing phase are conducted separately, and the jury is required to find at least one 'aggravating circumstance' before imposing a death sentence. Troy Gregg challenged this new sentencing procedure, arguing that even with these safeguards, the death penalty remained cruel and unusual. The Supreme Court upheld the Georgia statute, ruling that the death penalty does not violate the Eighth Amendment if it is administered through a fair and structured process that channels jury discretion. The Court affirmed that capital punishment can serve legitimate penological goals of retribution and deterrence. The decision established the modern legal framework for the death penalty, confirming that states could impose death sentences if they established procedures that minimize the risk of arbitrary or discriminatory imposition.

Holding: The court held that the insurance policy was not ambiguous and the exclusion clause was enforceable. The summary judgment in favor of the insurance company was affirmed. This litigation arose from a dispute over the interpretation of an insurance contract. The insured sought coverage for property damage, but the insurer denied the claim, arguing that the loss was excluded under a specific 'peril' exclusion in the policy. The trial court granted summary judgment to the insurer, finding the language of the exclusion to be clear and unambiguous. The plaintiff appealed, arguing that the policy was ambiguous because the definition of the excluded peril conflicted with other provisions in the contract. The appellate court employed the standard rule for interpreting insurance policies: ambiguity is resolved in favor of the insured. The court analyzed the policy as a whole, looking for harmony between sections. It determined that while the exclusion was broad, it was not contradictory to the coverage provisions when read in the context of the entire agreement. The court reiterated that while insurance contracts are construed strictly against the insurer, a court cannot invent an ambiguity where none exists. The court affirmed the judgment, confirming that the insurer's denial was legally supported by the plain language of the policy document.

## Grieshaber v. State Farm Insurance Co.

## Griggs v. Duke Power Co.

## Grisham v. Grisham

599 S.W.3d 523 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: Use based on family permission is not adverse and cannot ripen into title or a boundary shift. Absent clear evidence that permission was revoked and the usage turned hostile, the claimant cannot prevail on adverse possession theories. This was a boundary dispute between family members involving a strip of land containing a shared shed. The defendants argued that they had acquired the land through adverse possession, or alternatively, that there was a boundary by acquiescence. The trial court found for the plaintiffs, ordering the shed removed. The appellate court reviewed the facts and found that the defendants' use of the shed was permissive, as it was a family arrangement. The court clarified that the doctrine of adverse possession requires 'hostile' use, and permissive use--regardless of how long it lasts--cannot be converted into adverse possession or a new boundary without a clear, hostile act. Because the defendants admitted the shed was placed there with the original owner's permission as a family benefit, they could not later claim that this use made them the owners of the land. The court affirmed the trial court's ruling, emphasizing that family permissiveness acts as a barrier to adverse possession claims.

## Grogan v. Garner

498 U.S. 279 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1991 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that the standard of proof for determining whether a debt is non-dischargeable under the fraud exception is the preponderance of the evidence. This standard applies regardless of the burden of proof required in state court fraud proceedings. The debtors sold stock in a company to the plaintiffs through fraudulent misrepresentations. The plaintiffs won a fraud judgment in state court and subsequently challenged the dischargeability of that judgment in the debtors' Chapter 11 bankruptcy. The issue was whether the 'preponderance of the evidence' standard or the 'clear and convincing' evidence standard should apply when determining if a debt is non-dischargeable due to fraud. The Supreme Court analyzed the Bankruptcy Code and concluded that there was no congressional intent to impose a higher burden of proof than the preponderance of the evidence, which is the standard typically applied in civil litigation. The Court explained that a creditor's interest in recovering a debt is secondary to the debtor's 'fresh start,' but that fresh start is

Second stored summary not meant to protect debtors who have committed fraud. By choosing the lower standard of proof, the Court made it easier for creditors to prove that a debt should not be discharged, furthering the policy of punishing fraudulent conduct.

## Gross v. FBL Financial Services, Inc.

557 U.S. 167 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2009 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Supreme Court held that a plaintiff bringing an age discrimination claim under the ADEA must prove that age was the 'but-for' cause of the employer's adverse action. It is not enough to show that age was a motivating factor. This case addressed the causation standard for age discrimination claims under the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA). Gross alleged that he was demoted because of his age. The Court held that ADEA claims require proof of 'but-for' causation, meaning age must have been the 'but-for' cause of the employer's adverse action, not just a contributing factor. This standard is more stringent than the 'mixed-motive' standard applicable to some Title VII claims.
