## In re Estate of A.G.

244 S.W.3d 762 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2008 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a holographic will lacking the required witnesses is invalid under Missouri probate law. It emphasized that courts cannot waive statutory requirements for will execution, regardless of the decedent's clearly expressed intent. The decedent left a holographic will that was handwritten, signed, but lacked formal witnessing required for standard wills in Missouri. The probate court refused to admit the document to probate. The beneficiaries named in the holographic will appealed, arguing that the document met the minimum requirements for a valid testamentary instrument under the law. The appellate court examined the Missouri statute regarding the validity of wills, noting that while some states permit holographic wills, Missouri has strict witnessing requirements for all wills. The court held that the absence of witnesses meant the document could not be admitted to probate, regardless of the clear intent of the testator. The court addressed the hardship caused by this rule but clarified that it was bound by the legislature's specific directives regarding the execution of wills. The decision underscores the rigid adherence to probate formalities in Missouri and the importance of having legal counsel oversee the execution of any estate planning documents to ensure they meet statutory requirements.

## In re Estate of A.G.M.

648 S.W.3d 917 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's ruling, holding that a pay-on-death beneficiary designation remains valid unless specifically changed in accordance with the institution's requirements. A general provision in a subsequent will is insufficient to override a specific non-probate beneficiary designation. The case involved a controversy regarding the distribution of assets held in a pay-on-death account. The decedent had established the account naming one sibling as the beneficiary but later executed a will that directed the residue of the estate to be divided equally among all siblings. After the decedent's death, the beneficiary of the account claimed the funds as a non-probate asset, arguing that the beneficiary designation was not overridden by the subsequent will. The other siblings argued that the decedent intended for the assets to pass through the estate according to the will. The trial court determined that, under Missouri law, a pay-on-death designation is a non-probate transfer that is generally not subject to a contradictory provision in a will. The Western District analyzed the relevant statutes governing non-probate transfers and the conditions under which such transfers may be set aside or invalidated. The court focused on the statutory requirement for specific writing or clear intent to change a beneficiary designation in non-probate assets.

## In re Estate of A.H.

936 S.W.2d 532 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1996 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that an estate is entitled to seek both actual and punitive damages under the Merchandising Practices Act. The deterrent purpose of punitive damages remains relevant and enforceable after the consumer's death. Following the primary holding on the survivability of claims, the court delved into the specifics of damages recoverable under the Missouri Merchandising Practices Act (MPA) by an estate. The litigation focused on whether the estate could recover not only the actual financial loss sustained by the decedent due to the deceptive practice but also punitive damages. The business argued that punitive damages are intended to punish a wrongdoer, which is a purpose that is frustrated if the defendant is only paying the victim's estate. The appellate court scrutinized the legislative intent and the statutory language of the MPA, which expressly provides for punitive damages as a mechanism to deter deceptive practices. The court held that the deterrent effect of punitive damages is preserved even when the original victim has died, as it prevents the defendant from profiting from their illegal conduct. This interpretation ensured that the MPA remained a potent tool for consumer protection, preventing entities from escaping the full financial consequences of fraudulent business tactics simply because the victim passed away before the litigation concluded. The decision reaffirmed the court's commitment to robust enforcement of the MPA as a deterrent against corporate misconduct in the state.

## In re Estate of A.H.

533 S.W.3d 240 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the decision, holding that the petitioner failed to present sufficient evidence of duress. It held that validly executed mediation agreements in probate cases are enforceable and not easily set aside. The case involved an appeal from a probate court's decision denying a petition to set aside a settlement agreement regarding an estate. The parties had entered into a mediation agreement resolving a dispute over the decedent's property, but the petitioner later claimed that the agreement was reached under economic duress. The trial court found the agreement valid and binding. The appellate court reviewed the standards for rescission based on duress, noting the high threshold for showing that one's free will was overborne. The

Second stored summary analysis addressed the role of mediation in resolving estate disputes and the policy preference for enforcing such settlements to avoid protracted litigation. The opinion also considered whether the probate court had the equitable authority to reconsider the settlement after its formal approval, particularly in light of the petitioner's delayed claims and the reliance interests of the other heirs.

## In re Estate of A.H.

148 S.W.3d 328 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while the ADA applies to public entities including courts, the probate court's appointment of a guardian did not violate the ADA because it followed state law in protecting the ward. The court determined the least restrictive alternative was considered. This case involves the application of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) and its interplay with state probate and guardianship laws. The litigants argued that the court's actions in appointing a guardian violated the ward's civil rights by failing to provide the least restrictive environment as mandated by the ADA and the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Olmstead v. L.C. The court analyzed whether state-level judicial proceedings are subject to the same civil rights mandates regarding disability as administrative agency actions. The discussion centers on whether a probate court is a public entity subject to the non-discrimination requirements of Title II of the ADA. This case is significant as it bridges the gap between traditional family law matters and federal disability rights legislation, highlighting the increasing relevance of civil rights law in guardianship proceedings.

## In re Estate of A.H. Voegele

85 S.W.3d 689 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2002 · Missouri

Also captioned In re Estate of Voegele

Holding: The court held that a mobile home remains subject to the motor vehicle title laws for the purposes of lien perfection, even if it is affixed to real property. The bank's lien noted on the title was superior. This case dealt with the priority of a security interest in a mobile home between a creditor and the estate. The creditor, a bank, had its lien noted on the certificate of title for the mobile home. The estate argued that because the mobile home was annexed to the real property, it had become a fixture and therefore should be governed by the real estate records rather than the motor vehicle title laws. The bank maintained that the motor vehicle title statute was the exclusive method for perfection, regardless of the physical status of the home. The court analyzed whether a mobile home remains a vehicle subject to title laws or becomes part of the real estate for security interest purposes. This involved interpreting the UCC provisions regarding fixtures and the specific motor vehicle statutes of Missouri. The court focused on the definitions of 'vehicle' and 'fixture' and the practical implications for lenders providing financing for manufactured housing units.

Second stored summary Holding: The court held that compliance with the motor vehicle title statute for perfecting a lien on a mobile home is sufficient and supersedes the general UCC filing requirements. Therefore, the bank's security interest was properly perfected despite the lack of a UCC-1 filing. This case involved a dispute over the priority of a security interest in a mobile home against the estate of a decedent. The creditor, a bank, held a perfected security interest in the mobile home through a notation on the certificate of title. The decedent's estate argued that the security interest was not properly perfected under the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC) because the bank failed to file a UCC-1 financing statement with the Secretary of State. The court had to determine whether the motor vehicle certificate of title act superseded the UCC filing requirements for perfection of a security interest in a mobile home. The bank argued that the certificate of title was the exclusive method for perfection, while the estate contended that the UCC's general filing provisions applied. The trial court held that the bank's security interest was superior because it complied with the motor vehicle statute, which governs the perfection of liens on titled vehicles. The appellate court reviewed the interaction between the Missouri UCC and the motor vehicle statutes. It emphasized that specific statutes governing motor vehicle titling act as an exception to the general filing requirements of the UCC regarding perfection.

## In re Estate of A.J.

105 S.W.3d 476 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the admission of the will to probate, holding that the defects in the self-proving affidavit did not invalidate the will. The court held that the core requirements for formal execution were satisfied by the witnesses' testimony. The matter involved a challenge to the admission of a will into probate based on allegations of improper execution. The witnesses to the will had signed the document, but the self-proving affidavit was improperly notarized. The appellants argued that this deficiency rendered the will invalid. The probate court admitted the will, finding that the requirements for the will's execution under Missouri law had been met, regardless of the defects in the self-proving affidavit. The appellate court reviewed the statutory requirements for the execution of a will, which involve the testator's signature and the presence of two witnesses. The court clarified that a self-proving affidavit is a separate procedural device that simplifies probate but is not a necessary condition for the validity of the will itself if the formal execution requirements are proved by witness testimony. The court affirmed the probate court's decision, noting that the will's validity was adequately established by the testimony of the witnesses who observed the testator sign the document.

## In re Estate of A.J. Pizzo

866 S.W.2d 919 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1993 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the bank's security interest remained valid and perfected despite the debtor's death. It further ruled that the UCC's provisions regarding secured transactions take precedence over general probate claim priorities for the specified collateral. This case arose from a probate proceeding where a creditor sought to enforce a security interest against assets held by the estate. The creditor, a bank, claimed a perfected security interest in the decedent's business equipment and inventory. The estate argued that the security agreement was insufficient because it lacked a proper description of the collateral or was never properly perfected before the decedent's death. The appellate court examined the requirements for an enforceable security agreement under Missouri law, focusing on the adequacy of the description in the security agreement and the validity of the financing statement filing. The case turned on whether the 'floating lien' theory applied to assets acquired post-death and how the UCC provisions interact with probate laws regarding the liquidation of assets for administrative expenses and creditors' claims. The court analyzed whether the bank's interest survived the transition of the business assets into the decedent's estate and if the statutory requirements for filing were met during the life of the debtor. This decision serves as a guide for reconciling secured interests with the administration of insolvent estates.

## In re Estate of A.M.

285 S.W.3d 367 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2009 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the creditor failed to obtain 'control' of the brokerage account as required by the UCC. Consequently, the creditor did not have a perfected security interest and was treated as a general creditor. This case involved a dispute over the perfection of a security interest in a brokerage account. The creditor held an interest in the account, but the estate argued that it had not followed the proper steps under the UCC to perfect the interest. The court looked at the rules for investment property and securities accounts, which are specifically governed by Article 8 and Article 9 of the UCC. The issue was whether the creditor had obtained 'control' of the account, which is the required method of perfection for such assets. The estate argued that the creditor merely relied on an unperfected security agreement. The court reviewed the requirements for 'control' under the UCC, including the necessity of a tripartite agreement between the broker, the creditor, and the debtor. The case highlighted the shift from physical collateral to intangible financial assets and the corresponding increase in the technical requirements for achieving a perfected security interest in modern commercial practice.

## In re Estate of A.M.D.

616 S.W.3d 483 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the decision, holding that the spendthrift provision was valid and enforceable. The assets within the trust were not part of the probate estate and were immune from the claims asserted by the estate administrator. The underlying litigation concerned the interpretation of a spendthrift trust provision and whether the assets of the trust could be reached by a creditor of the beneficiary. The estate administrator sought to satisfy claims against the decedent's estate by accessing the corpus of a trust established by the decedent's parent. The trial court determined that the spendthrift clause was effective in protecting the assets from the claims of the beneficiary's creditors, including the estate's claims for reimbursement. The appellate court analyzed the language of the trust instrument and the relevant Missouri statutes governing spendthrift trusts. The discussion focused on whether a beneficiary's interests in a discretionary trust constitute 'property' reachable by a probate estate. The court addressed the intersection of trust law and probate law, specifically looking at the Settlor's intent to shield the beneficiary from financial mismanagement or creditors. The court also touched upon the fiduciary duties of the trustee and the limitations imposed on creditors seeking to pierce the veil of a properly drafted trust document under Missouri law.

## In re Estate of A.M.M.

606 S.W.3d 678 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court held that the testator's inclusion of a survival requirement in the will constitutes a manifestation of contrary intent that displaces the default application of the anti-lapse statute. Consequently, the gift to the predeceased beneficiary failed, and the assets were properly distributed under the residuary clause. This litigation involved the interpretation of a will provision regarding the distribution of residuary assets. The testator provided that the residue should be divided among named beneficiaries, but a conflict arose when one beneficiary predeceased the testator. The personal representative sought guidance from the probate court on whether the anti-lapse statute applied to the specific language used in the will. The appellant, representing the heirs of the deceased beneficiary, argued that the testator's intent was for the gift to remain within the branch of the family. The trial court determined that the will's language creating a condition of survival effectively overrode the statutory anti-lapse protections. On appeal, the court reviewed the principles of will construction, noting that the primary goal is to discern the testator's intent from the four corners of the document. The court analyzed whether the specific survivorship clause constituted a 'contrary intent' sufficient to preclude the operation of Section 474.460 RSMo. The appellate court ultimately upheld the trial court's interpretation, finding that the clear language requiring survival meant the gift lapsed and fell into the residuary estate rather than passing to the deceased beneficiary's descendants, thereby affirming the court's strict adherence to the survivorship condition.

## In re Estate of A.S.

145 S.W.3d 520 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court held that the evidence was sufficient to warrant a trial on the merits. It reversed the directed verdict, noting that the capacity issue involved questions of fact for a jury. A contest was filed by distant relatives after a will was admitted to probate. The relatives argued that the testator was not of sound mind when he signed the document, citing his long-standing history of alcohol abuse. The appellate court reviewed the medical records and

Second stored summary the testimony of the witnesses present at the signing. The court addressed the 'lucid interval' doctrine, which allows for the admission of a will even if a testator suffers from recurring periods of diminished capacity, provided they were lucid at the specific time of execution. The court's analysis focused on whether the contestants met their burden of proving a lack of capacity at the specific moment of signing. The appellate court also scrutinized the trial court's decision to grant a directed verdict in favor of the estate, determining whether there was any evidence from which a reasonable jury could have inferred incapacity.

## In re Estate of Arens

890 S.W.2d 772 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1994 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the mobile home remained personal property subject to UCC filing requirements. Failure to properly perfect according to the relevant motor vehicle statutes rendered the security interest subordinate to the claims of the bankruptcy trustee. The dispute centered on the perfection of a security interest in a mobile home located on real property owned by the debtor. The creditor claimed a security interest in the mobile home through a document that was not filed as a fixture filing under the UCC. The estate argued that because the mobile home was occupied and connected to utilities, it should be treated as an improvement to the real estate, requiring a real estate mortgage filing to be valid against third-party creditors. The court analyzed whether the mobile home had lost its status as personal property. The court determined that the mobile home retained its status as personal property subject to Article 9 filing requirements, rather than real estate law. Because the creditor failed to comply with the proper perfection requirements for a vehicle/mobile home under Missouri statutes, the interest was unperfected against the bankruptcy estate. The decision highlights the distinction between perfection of security interests in mobile homes versus real estate improvements and the specific statutory requirements for titled vehicles that function as residences. It clarifies that simply placing a mobile home on land does not automatically convert the asset into real property for secured transaction purposes.

## In re Estate of B.C.

577 S.W.3d 120 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the probate court erred in failing to conduct an evidentiary hearing on the beneficiaries' specific allegations regarding missing property. The case was remanded to allow the beneficiaries to present evidence of the breach of fiduciary duty. This matter involved an objection to the final settlement of an estate. The beneficiaries of the estate alleged that the personal representative breached his fiduciary duty by selling estate assets at an undervalue and by failing to account for certain personal property items that were missing from the decedent's residence. The probate court approved the final settlement over the objections, finding that the assets were sold at a reasonable market price and that no evidence suggested a breach of duty. The beneficiaries appealed, contending that the court erred in failing to conduct an evidentiary hearing on the allegations of missing property. The appellate court examined the standard of review for probate accountings and the obligations of a personal representative to marshal assets and maximize value. The opinion focuses on the procedural requirements for notice and the necessity of addressing specific itemized objections in a formal evidentiary proceeding rather than via summary approval.

## In re Estate of B.C.

402 S.W.3d 108 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the dismissal, holding that the contestant failed to provide evidence of undue influence that overcame the testator's free agency. Opportunity to influence is not synonymous with the exercise of undue influence. A child of the decedent challenged the distribution of the estate, asserting that the will was product of undue influence by a sibling who was named the primary beneficiary. The trial court dismissed the claim, finding that the contestant had failed to establish a prima facie case of undue influence. On appeal, the contestant argued that the trial court ignored evidence of the beneficiary's constant presence and control over the decedent's finances. The appellate court reviewed the elements of undue influence, which include a person with the capacity to be influenced, a person who exercises that influence, and a result that clearly shows the effect of that influence. The court explained that while circumstantial evidence is admissible, the contestant must show that the influence destroyed the free agency of the testator. The record indicated that the decedent had independent legal advice and sufficient mental capacity to manage their own affairs. The appellate court affirmed the dismissal, clarifying that mere opportunity to influence is insufficient to invalidate a will. The decision underscores the high burden of proof required to contest a will on the basis of undue influence in Missouri probate law.

## In re Estate of B.C.

525 S.W.3d 412 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the award, holding that the minor child's allowance is a priority claim that cannot be diminished by administrative expenses or creditor claims. The case focused on the rights of a surviving minor child to an exempt property allowance under the Missouri Probate Code. The executor had argued that the allowance should be reduced because the estate was insolvent and there were other administrative expenses that required priority. The trial court ruled that the minor child's allowance was a priority claim that had to be satisfied from the available assets before general administrative expenses or creditor claims. The appellate court analyzed the statutory framework of the Missouri Probate Code regarding the priority of claims and allowances. The court evaluated whether the specific nature of the minor child's allowance, intended for basic subsistence, created an absolute priority over other claims. The opinion discusses the legislative purpose of the exempt property allowance in protecting dependents, confirming its status as a foundational element of Missouri's protective probate framework, and rejected the executor's attempt to prioritize administrative costs over the child's statutory entitlement.

## In re Estate of B.C.

385 S.W.3d 432 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the order, holding that funeral expenses are priority claims that must be satisfied. A personal representative lacks the authority to defer these payments indefinitely. The estate dispute arose regarding the reimbursement of expenses incurred by a family member who paid the decedent's funeral and burial costs. The claimant had sought payment from the estate, but the personal representative delayed, citing a lack of liquidity in the estate. The trial court ordered the payment to be prioritized as a funeral expense, which are preferred claims under Missouri law. The appellate court reviewed the classification of debts and claims against an estate. It confirmed that funeral expenses hold a high priority under the probate code and that the estate must satisfy these obligations before other lower-priority claims can be paid. The court rejected the representative's argument that they had the discretion to defer the payment based on cash flow, emphasizing the legal obligation to prioritize statutory claims, and affirmed the trial court's order requiring the estate to reimburse the claimant immediately.

## In re Estate of B.C.

477 S.W.3d 680 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a nominated personal representative should only be disqualified upon a clear showing of actual conflict or unsuitability. It affirmed that potential conflicts of interest are not a sufficient basis to override a testator's selection of a fiduciary. A daughter contested the appointment of her brother as personal representative of their father's estate, arguing that he had a conflict of interest due to his prior dealings with the father's business. The probate court appointed the brother, finding that he was better suited to

Second stored summary manage the complex business assets contained within the estate. The daughter appealed, alleging that the brother's conflict was so profound that it constituted a violation of the statutory qualifications for a personal representative under Missouri law. The appellate court examined the standard for removing or denying an appointment based on conflict of interest. It noted that, in Missouri, the preference is to appoint the individual nominated in the will unless there is a clear showing that they are unsuitable. The court held that mere speculation of future conflict is insufficient to disqualify a personal representative; rather, there must be evidence of present hostility or actual mismanagement that would impede the administration of the estate. Because the daughter failed to prove that the brother was incapable of fulfilling his duties impartially, the court affirmed the appointment, emphasizing the testator's right to choose their own fiduciary.

## In re Estate of B.C.

542 S.W.3d 321 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the trial court's order, holding that the court properly exercised its discretion in evaluating the conflicting evidence. The choice of valuation method was deemed reasonable and supported by the record. The case involved the valuation of a closely-held business interest held by the estate. A dispute arose between the residuary beneficiaries regarding the appraisal method used by the executor to determine the fair market value of the shares for tax and distribution purposes. One beneficiary contended that the executor's appraisal ignored intangible assets and goodwill. The trial court evaluated the competing expert witness testimonies regarding business valuation standards. The appellate court reviewed whether the trial court's acceptance of one expert's valuation over the other was an abuse of discretion. The decision turned on whether the appraisal met the 'fair market value' standard required by probate rules and whether the executor acted with due diligence in obtaining an appraisal that correctly reflected the value of the estate's interest for equitable distribution purposes.

## In re Estate of B.E.S.

552 S.W.3d 723 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The probate court did not abuse its discretion in denying the petition for removal of the personal representative. Potential conflicts of interest alone do not mandate removal unless there is clear evidence that the representative's actions have harmed or will harm the estate. This case involved a challenge to the appointment of a personal representative based on allegations of a conflict of interest. The family members of the decedent sought the removal of the personal representative, claiming that the representative's fiduciary duties conflicted with their personal business interests in an entity owned by the decedent. The probate court refused to remove the personal representative, finding no evidence of malfeasance or actual harm to the estate. The appellants argued on appeal that the mere appearance of a conflict should necessitate removal to protect the estate's assets and integrity. The appellate court performed an abuse of discretion review regarding the probate court's decision on the removal petition. The court analyzed the statutory grounds for removal under the Missouri Probate Code, emphasizing that removal is a drastic remedy to be applied only when necessary to protect the estate's interests. The appellate court held that while a potential conflict was present, the probate court's findings were supported by the record because the representative had acted in good faith and the assets were properly managed. The appellate court affirmed the decision, noting that personal animosity or potential conflict without proof of actual detriment to the estate is insufficient to warrant removal.

## In re Estate of B.G.

55 S.W.3d 832 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2001 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that partition in kind is the preferred method under Missouri law, and a sale should only be ordered if a physical division is impossible or causes substantial economic injury. It remanded the case to re-evaluate the partition options. A dispute arose between heirs regarding the partition of agricultural property that had been bequeathed to them as tenants in common in their father's will. One heir sought to force a sale of the property to realize his share of the inheritance, while the others wished to maintain the land as a working farm. The trial court ordered the sale, reasoning that a physical division of the land would be economically impractical given the layout of the property. The appellant argued that the trial court failed to adequately consider the historical value and the family's desire to keep the land in the family line. The appellate court reviewed the statutory provisions for partition, noting that in Missouri, the law generally favors the physical division of land unless it would result in significant waste or economic loss to the co-owners. It concluded that the trial court had relied too heavily on the convenience of a sale and had not adequately explored the feasibility of partitioning the land equitably among the heirs. The case was remanded to determine if a physical division was possible.

## In re Estate of B.G.S.

592 S.W.3d 411 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the prenuptial agreement was validly executed and that the spouse failed to meet the burden of proving duress or lack of disclosure. The lower court's decision was upheld. The matter concerned the validity of a prenuptial agreement during probate proceedings. The surviving spouse challenged the enforcement of the agreement, claiming it was executed under duress and lacked full financial disclosure, which are grounds for invalidating a marital contract. The trial court found the agreement valid, concluding that the decedent had made adequate disclosures and the spouse had sufficient time to consult with legal counsel. The spouse appealed, arguing that the trial court applied the wrong legal standard for assessing the fairness of the agreement. The appellate court reviewed the requirements for valid prenuptial agreements in Missouri, noting that fairness must be assessed at the time of execution. The court examined the evidence regarding the financial transparency and the voluntariness of the spouse's signature. It concluded that the trial court's factual findings were supported by the record and that no coercion or fraud occurred. The appellate court affirmed the decision, underscoring that parties to a prenuptial

Second stored summary agreement bear the burden of proving that they entered into the contract with full awareness of the other party's assets and the implications of the waiver of rights.

## In re Estate of B.H.

510 S.W.3d 605 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court held that a promissory note containing a recital of consideration is prima facie evidence of a binding contract. It held that the estate failed to present sufficient evidence to rebut this presumption, rendering the note an enforceable obligation. This matter involved a claim against an estate based on a promissory note signed by the decedent. The estate argued that the note was not supported by consideration, as it was given as a gift to a family member, and therefore was unenforceable against the estate's assets. The claimant argued that the note was a binding contract and that the recital of 'value received' within the note was sufficient to establish consideration. The appellate court evaluated the enforceability of promissory notes made by decedents to family members and the burden of proving consideration. The opinion contrasted the treatment of gratuitous promises with enforceable contractual obligations in the context of probate. The court considered whether the estate could introduce extrinsic evidence to show that the note was a gift and therefore lacked the consideration required to be a valid debt of the estate.

## In re Estate of B.H.

656 S.W.3d 282 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the judgment of the trial court. The court held that the evidence did not support a finding of an intent to defraud the surviving spouse. The appellant, a surviving spouse, filed a petition for an elective share, claiming that the decedent's inter vivos transfers to a revocable trust were intended to defraud the spouse of their statutory inheritance rights. The trial court rejected the claim, determining that the decedent had a legitimate estate planning purpose for the transfers and that there was no evidence of an intent to defeat the spouse's elective share. The appellate court reviewed the standards for evaluating 'illusory transfers' under Missouri law. The discussion centered on whether the trust assets should be 'clawed back' into the probate estate to calculate the elective share. The court analyzed the intent of the decedent and the extent of control retained over the trust assets. The opinion emphasizes the rigorous standard required to prove that inter vivos transfers were fraudulent as to a surviving spouse, distinguishing between legitimate asset protection and the intentional evasion of spousal support obligations under probate law.

## In re Estate of B.K.

512 S.W.3d 838 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, finding that the claimant did not meet the clear and convincing evidence standard required for inheritance by a non-marital child. The evidentiary requirements were deemed consistent with state law. This case concerned a petition to determine the rightful heirs of an intestate estate. The primary dispute was the standing of a child born out of wedlock to inherit from the decedent's estate. Under the relevant Missouri statutes, the claimant had to demonstrate a clear and convincing relationship to the decedent to inherit by intestate succession. The trial court denied the claim, stating that the biological testing offered by the claimant was inconclusive and that there was insufficient supporting documentation from the family records. The appellant challenged the evidentiary standards applied by the probate court, arguing that the court failed to consider testimony from relatives who acknowledged the claimant as the decedent's child. The appellate court examined the statutory requirements for proving parentage in probate proceedings, focusing on the balance between preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that the rights of children are protected. The review also addressed whether the trial court correctly evaluated the credibility of the witnesses and whether the evidentiary bar was set unreasonably high for the claimant.

## In re Estate of B.R.

489 S.W.3d 772 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court held that the trial court's finding of testamentary capacity was supported by substantial evidence. It affirmed the lower court's refusal to invalidate the will despite the allegations of influence. A daughter contested the probate of her father's estate on the grounds of lack of testamentary capacity and undue influence by a second spouse. The testator had changed his will shortly before his death while hospitalized. The appellate court reviewed the factors that determine mental capacity, such as understanding the nature and extent of one's property and the persons who are the natural objects of one's bounty. The court evaluated the testimony of the attending physicians and the attorney who drafted the final will. A significant portion of the appeal addressed the 'fiduciary' status of the spouse and how that affects the burden of proof in an undue influence claim. The court considered whether the evidence presented was sufficient to establish that the testator's free will was overborne. The decision also touched upon the necessity of expert testimony versus the probative value of lay witnesses in probate contests where mental health is a primary issue.

## In re Estate of Blodgett

147 S.W.3d 79 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: The judgment against the claimant was affirmed. The trial court correctly applied the Dead Man's Statute to exclude testimony concerning oral agreements made with the deceased party. This probate litigation involved a claim against an estate for services rendered to the decedent during their lifetime. The claimant argued that there was an oral contract for lifetime care in exchange for a significant portion of the decedent's estate. The estate representative denied the existence of such an agreement, asserting that the services were performed out of filial duty rather than a commercial arrangement. The evidence presented at trial included testimony regarding the decedent's promises to leave property to the claimant and the extent of the care provided over a decade. The central issue was the 'Dead Man's Statute' and the admissibility of the claimant's testimony regarding conversations with the deceased. The trial court disallowed significant portions of this testimony, which significantly weakened the claimant's case. On appeal, the claimant argued that the court misinterpreted the applicability of the statute and excluded crucial evidence that would have established the contract's existence. The appellate court examined the history and intent of the evidentiary rules governing claims against estates to ensure that only legitimate debts are satisfied while preventing fraudulent claims.

## In re Estate of Boatright

88 S.W.3d 500 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2002 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that Missouri does not recognize holographic wills that do not comply with the formal execution requirements of two witnesses. The court affirmed the lower court's decision to deny probate of the document. This case concerned the validity of a holographic will. After the decedent's death, a document purported to be a will was found in the decedent's personal belongings, written entirely in his handwriting but lacking the signatures of two witnesses, which is the standard requirement for a formal will under Missouri law. The trial court refused to admit the document to probate, ruling that it did not satisfy the

Second stored summary statutory requirements for the execution of wills. On appeal, the parties debated whether the document could be considered a valid holographic will under the state's statutes. Missouri generally does not recognize holographic wills unless they meet the requirements of a formal will, including the presence of two witnesses, unless specific exceptions apply under foreign law if the will was executed elsewhere. The appellate court reviewed the legislative intent behind the strict execution requirements, concluding that despite the testator's clearly expressed wishes, the failure to comply with the witness requirement rendered the document legally ineffective for passing property.

## In re Estate of Breyer

135 S.W.3d 575 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the security agreement's description of collateral was sufficiently broad to include the disputed assets. Furthermore, the creditor had maintained a valid, perfected security interest that took priority over the claims of the estate. This matter involved a dispute over the priority of claims against an estate's assets, specifically concerning secured creditors and the claims of the estate. The decedent had entered into a security agreement involving business assets, and following the death, conflicts arose regarding the classification of these assets and the validity of the security interests. The estate argued that certain assets were not covered by the security agreement or that the filings were insufficient. The secured creditor contended that its interest was fully perfected and entitled to priority over other claims against the estate assets. The court conducted an extensive review of the security agreement's language to determine the scope of the collateral, specifically whether it included after-acquired property. The case highlights the importance of precise description of collateral in security agreements and the necessity of maintaining proper perfection throughout the life of the security interest. The court weighed the competing interests of the probate estate and the secured party within the framework of Missouri's version of the Uniform Commercial Code.

## In re Estate of Breyer

713 S.W.2d 581 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1986 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the oral agreement was unenforceable because it failed to meet the requirements of UCC Section 9-203. Without a signed security agreement or possession of the collateral, no security interest was created. This case dealt with the enforceability of an oral security agreement. A claimant alleged that the decedent had granted a security interest in certain antiques as collateral for a loan, but there was no written security agreement signed by the debtor. The administrator of the estate disputed the claim, arguing that under UCC Section 9-203, a security interest is not enforceable unless the debtor has signed a security agreement that contains a description of the collateral. The court reviewed the strict requirements of Article 9 regarding the formation of an enforceable security interest. It addressed whether the 'possession' exception to the writing requirement applied in this case, as the claimant did not have physical possession of the antiques. The case emphasizes the necessity of a written document in creating a security interest when the secured party does not maintain possession of the collateral, protecting the estate from unsubstantiated claims by creditors.

## In re Estate of Bunting

893 S.W.2d 861 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 1995 · Missouri

Holding: Attachment of a security interest occurs when there is an agreement, value is given, and the debtor has rights in the collateral. Courts interpret the requirement for a written security agreement broadly to reflect the intent of the parties. This case explored the requirements for the attachment of a security interest. The court looked at whether there was a valid security agreement, the value given, and the debtor's rights in the collateral. The estate of the deceased debtor argued that the security agreement was invalid because it lacked a sufficient signature. The creditor, a bank, presented documentation signed by the debtor that clearly identified the collateral and the obligation. The court analyzed whether the electronic signature or the lack of a wet-ink signature in specific instances invalidated the agreement. The appellate court found that the documents, taken together, demonstrated the clear intent of the parties to create a security interest and that the statutory requirements for attachment had been met. The holding reinforces the principle that courts will look to the substance of the transaction rather than mere technicalities when determining whether a security interest has attached to the collateral.

## In re Estate of Bunting

311 S.W.3d 372 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2010 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a financing statement must be seriously misleading to be ineffective, and in this case, the errors in the debtor's name and collateral description rendered the filing insufficient. Consequently, the creditor failed to achieve a perfected security interest. The dispute involved a priority contest regarding a security interest in cattle. The creditor claimed a perfected security interest in the livestock, while the estate argued the financing statement was insufficient. The core issue centered on the description of the collateral in the financing statement and the debtor's name accuracy. The court examined the requirements for perfection under Article 9 of the UCC and whether the filing provided sufficient notice to other potential creditors. The trial court determined the security interest was not properly perfected due to errors in the financing statement, leading to an appeal by the creditor. The appellate court reviewed the statutory requirements for the naming of the debtor and the description of the collateral, emphasizing the objective nature of the notice filing system established by the UCC. The court found that because the financing statement did not reasonably identify the collateral or correctly name the debtor as required by Missouri's version of the UCC, the perfection was invalid.

## In re Estate of Bunting

311 S.W.3d 761 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2010 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the property remained part of the probate estate. The lack of formal delivery and recording before the grantor's death meant the transfer to the trust was never completed. This case involved a dispute over whether certain real property was an asset of the decedent's probate estate or whether it had been successfully transferred to a trust prior to the decedent's death. The beneficiaries of the estate argued that the deed transferring the property to the trust was defective due to a failure in delivery and recording during the decedent's lifetime. The trial court examined the law regarding the transfer of real estate to inter vivos trusts and the requirements for a valid delivery of a deed. The appellate court reviewed the evidence concerning the decedent's intent and the actions taken to effectuate the transfer. The case provides a detailed look at the formalities required to move real property into trust ownership, specifically addressing what constitutes a 'constructive delivery' of a deed and the impact of a grantor's failure to record the deed before their death.

## In re Estate of C.A.W.

19 S.W.3d 178 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2000 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the trusts were valid inter vivos transfers and were not a fraud on the surviving spouse's marital rights. The court affirmed the denial of the claim to include trust assets in the elective share calculation. This case involved a dispute over an elective share claim by a surviving spouse. The decedent had established several inter vivos trusts shortly before his death. The surviving spouse argued that these trusts were illusory and intended to defraud her of her elective share, seeking to have the assets of the trusts included in the probate estate for the purpose of calculating her statutory spousal share. The trial court ruled that the trusts were valid and that the assets were not part of the probate estate. The surviving spouse appealed, challenging the trial court's application of the 'fraud on the marital rights' doctrine. The appellate court examined the factors used to determine whether a trust is a valid transfer or a device to defeat marital rights, including the level of control retained by the settlor, the purpose of the transfer, and the timing of the creation of the trusts relative to the death and the onset of marital strain.

## In re Estate of C.H.

563 S.W.3d 839 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the denial of the claim, holding that the presumption of gratuitous services was not overcome. The evidence was insufficient to establish an implied contract for compensation. The estate dispute centered on a claim for compensation by a family member who provided long-term care for the decedent. The claimant argued that there was an implied contract for services, while the residuary legatees contended that the services were performed gratuitously, fueled by familial affection rather than a expectation of payment. The probate court denied the claim, stating that the claimant failed to provide evidence of an express agreement or the value of the services. The appellate court reviewed the standards for asserting claims against an estate based on quantum meruit. It noted that while Missouri law recognizes a presumption that services provided by family members are gratuitous, this presumption can be rebutted by showing that the claimant expected compensation at the time the services were rendered. The court examined the record for evidence of an understanding between the parties and found that the trial court properly applied the evidentiary burden, noting a lack of documented agreement or contemporaneous expectation of payment.

## In re Estate of C.J. v. Jones

295 S.W.3d 520 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2009 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that personal notice was required because the personal representative had knowledge of the heir's existence. Constructive notice through publication was insufficient to satisfy due process. An interested party filed a petition to set aside a decree of final distribution, alleging that they were not given proper notice of the probate proceedings despite being an heir at law. The personal representative argued that they had made a reasonable effort to locate all heirs through published notices in the local newspaper. The trial court denied the petition, finding that the personal representative complied with statutory notice requirements. On appeal, the court examined the constitutional requirements for notice to interested parties in probate. The appellate court reversed the trial court, holding that mere constructive notice through publication is insufficient when the personal representative has actual or constructive knowledge of an heir's identity and whereabouts. The duty to notify is a personal obligation, and failing to provide actual notice when the heir is easily identifiable constitutes a violation of due process. This case serves as a critical reminder that compliance with statutory notice does not override constitutional due process protections when the personal representative is aware of the existence of interested parties.

## In re Estate of C.K.

76 S.W.3d 287 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2001 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the removal and the order for reimbursement, holding that the trustee breached their fiduciary duty. The court held that even discretionary powers do not allow a trustee to commingle or misappropriate funds for personal use. This litigation involved the removal of a successor trustee based on the trustee's alleged failure to account for trust expenditures. The beneficiaries argued that the trustee used trust funds for personal travel and entertainment. The probate court found the trustee's explanations for the expenditures insufficient and ordered the trustee to reimburse the trust and be removed. The trustee appealed, arguing that the court failed to consider the trustee's broad discretionary powers granted under the trust instrument. The appellate court reviewed the fiduciary duty of a trustee, which requires that all expenditures be for the benefit of the trust and its beneficiaries. The court held that even with broad discretion, a trustee cannot use funds for personal purposes. The appellate court found that the evidence supported the trial court's conclusion that the trustee had breached their fiduciary duty and that removal was appropriate under the circumstances to prevent further loss to the trust assets.

## In re Estate of C.M.

495 S.W.3d 178 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the award, holding that the trial court properly exercised its discretion and that the family allowance is a protected statutory right. The case dealt with a family allowance claim made by a surviving spouse. The dispute arose when the decedent's children from a prior marriage challenged the amount requested, arguing it was excessive and unnecessary given the spouse's independent wealth. The trial court awarded a specific amount based on the statutory guidelines. The appellate court reviewed the statutory purpose of the family allowance, which is to provide for the support of the surviving spouse and minor children during the period of estate administration. The opinion explores the criteria for calculating the allowance, including the size of the estate and the standard of living maintained by the decedent. The court discussed the trial court's discretion in setting the allowance and whether it requires a specific finding of 'need' by the surviving spouse. The decision clarifies that the family allowance is a prioritized claim under the Missouri Probate Code, intended to prevent the destitution of the surviving spouse, regardless of their own separate financial assets.

## In re Estate of C.M.

412 S.W.3d 395 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's order approving the valuation methodology, finding no abuse of discretion. The court held that the probate court is entitled to weigh expert testimony as it deems appropriate and that the valuation was consistent with the testator's intent. This dispute arose during the administration of a large, complex estate involving multiple business entities. The decedent's will provided for the distribution of these entities to various family members. A disagreement occurred over the valuation of these entities for the purpose of tax allocation and distribution. The appellant argued that the probate court incorrectly accepted the valuations provided by the executor's experts, which excluded certain intangible assets. The probate court held that the methodology used was standard for the industry and within the realm of reasonable valuation methods. The appellate court reviewed the probate court's role in evaluating expert testimony, affirming that the court has broad discretion to accept or reject such testimony. The court noted that the probate court's task is not to determine the 'perfect' value but to ensure the distribution process is equitable and follows the testator's directive. The decision affirmed the trial court, emphasizing that in the absence of a clear showing of an error of law or a manifest abuse of discretion, the trial court's findings on complex asset valuation will be upheld.

## In re Estate of D.G.

428 S.W.3d 725 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The court reversed the lower court's distribution scheme, holding that Missouri statutes require per stirpes distribution in this context. The case was remanded for a calculation consistent with that finding. This litigation involved the determination of heirs when a decedent died intestate. A dispute arose between siblings and the children of a deceased sibling regarding the right to inherit real estate. The court had to interpret the Missouri statutes governing intestate succession, specifically the share allocated to the issue of a deceased heir. The trial court ruled that the inheritance should be divided per capita rather than per stirpes, which the appellants challenged. The appellate court examined the statutory rules of descent and distribution, finding that the trial court's application of the per capita rule was contrary to the legislative framework designed to preserve the shares of the decedent's branches of family. The court clarified the methodology for distribution, ensuring that the deceased sibling's descendants received their representative share. The case was remanded to the trial court with instructions to redistribute the estate assets in accordance with the statutory requirements for per stirpes succession.

## In re Estate of D.H.

852 S.W.2d 860 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1993 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that spendthrift trusts are valid and enforceable in Missouri, effectively shielding the beneficiary's interest from creditors. It affirmed the trial court's protection of the trust assets from attachment. This matter involved the interpretation of a spendthrift trust provision in the decedent's will. The creditors of one of the beneficiaries sought to reach the beneficiary's share of the trust to satisfy outstanding debts. The trustee refused to pay, citing the spendthrift clause, which prohibits the alienation of the interest by the beneficiary or their creditors. The creditors argued that the spendthrift clause was invalid because it lacked sufficient oversight and did not follow the standard Missouri format for such trusts. The trial court upheld the validity of the trust and denied the creditors' request for an attachment of the assets. The appellate court reviewed the history of spendthrift trust law in Missouri, noting that the state has a strong policy of protecting a settlor's right to control the distribution of their

Second stored summary assets. The court held that as long as the trust provides clear language preventing anticipation or alienation of benefits, the trust will be enforced against the claims of creditors, regardless of whether the beneficiary is personally indebted.

## In re Estate of D.S.

615 S.W.3d 897 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court, holding that the claimant failed to establish they were a 'reasonably ascertainable' creditor at the time notice was issued. The claim was properly barred by the statute of non-claims. The issue in this case was the timeliness of a claim filed against the estate. The claimant attempted to file a demand against the decedent's estate after the statutory period for filing claims had already expired, arguing that they had not received actual notice of the probate proceedings. The trial court dismissed the claim as time-barred. On appeal, the claimant argued that their status as a known creditor necessitated individual notice under the requirements of due process, rather than just the publication notice provided by the personal representative. The Eastern District analyzed the Missouri Probate Code regarding the obligations of the personal representative to identify and notify creditors. The court scrutinized the relationship between the decedent and the creditor to determine if the representative knew or should have known of the claim. The case provides significant clarity on the constitutional requirements for notice to creditors in probate estates within Missouri jurisdiction.

## In re Estate of D.T.K.

345 S.W.3d 305 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2011 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the probate court's refusal to compel distribution, holding that the spendthrift provision was valid and enforceable. The court held that a beneficiary has no right to alter the terms of a trust that explicitly prohibits alienation. This litigation involved the interpretation of a spendthrift trust provision within a will. The decedent's will created a trust for a beneficiary, which contained a spendthrift clause prohibiting creditors from attaching the assets. The beneficiary sought to compel a distribution of the corpus, arguing that the purpose of the trust had been frustrated. The probate court ruled that the trust was validly formed and that the spendthrift provision was enforceable, preventing the beneficiary from accessing the principal. The beneficiary appealed, contending that Missouri law allows for the modification of trusts when circumstances change significantly. The appellate court reviewed the law regarding spendthrift trusts, emphasizing the sanctity of the settlor's intent. The court found that there was no evidence of changed circumstances that would justify a deviation from the trust's original terms. The decision affirmed the probate court's judgment, reiterating that a beneficiary cannot unilaterally terminate or modify a spendthrift trust simply to access funds that the settlor specifically protected from dissipation.

## In re Estate of D.W. v. Wilson

430 S.W.3d 315 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the caretaker failed to overcome the presumption of undue influence arising from the confidential relationship. The assets were properly deemed part of the estate because the requirements for a valid gift were not met. This case centered on a petition to discover assets filed by the personal representative, alleging that the decedent's caretaker had converted various pieces of jewelry and cash during the decedent's final illness. The trial court found the caretaker liable and ordered the return of the property. The caretaker appealed, claiming that the assets were gifts inter vivos made by the decedent while the caretaker was providing services. The appellate court applied the standard for proving an inter vivos gift: donative intent, delivery, and acceptance. The court noted that the burden of proving a gift lies with the person asserting it, and because the caretaker stood in a confidential relationship with the decedent, a presumption of undue influence applied. The caretaker failed to rebut this presumption, as the evidence showed the caretaker had total control over the decedent's daily activities and finances during the period the alleged gifts occurred. Consequently, the appellate court affirmed the trial court's findings that the caretaker had breached their fiduciary-like position and that the transfer of assets was invalid. The ruling highlights the court's scrutiny of transactions between caregivers and vulnerable decedents.

## In re Estate of E.W.

173 S.W.3d 680 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2005 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that no-contest clauses are enforceable in Missouri unless the contestant can show good faith and probable cause for the challenge. Because the beneficiary failed this standard, the forfeiture was enforced. This litigation involved the interpretation of a 'no-contest' clause in a will. A beneficiary filed a claim to challenge the validity of certain bequests. The executor argued that the filing of the claim triggered the forfeiture provision of the will, effectively disinheriting the beneficiary. The beneficiary contended that the challenge was brought in good faith and with probable cause, and therefore should not invoke the no-contest clause. The trial court ruled that the clause was triggered, barring the beneficiary from inheriting. On appeal, the court analyzed the enforceability of no-contest clauses under Missouri law. It noted that such clauses are generally valid unless the challenge is brought in good faith and with probable cause, reflecting a public policy balance between honoring the testator's wishes and allowing beneficiaries to bring valid claims of wrongdoing. The court found that the beneficiary's claim lacked the requisite probable cause to exempt it from the no-contest clause.

## In re ESTATE of Elva H. FOSTER (Held), Deceased, Dorothy J. Busch, Adm. of James A. Ryan, Deceased, Edward C. Schneider and Harry A. Frank, Claimants, Appellants, v. Harry THEIS, Executor, and June Hunt Baker, Residuary Legatee, Respondents

290 S.W.2d 185 · St. Louis Court of Appeals · 1956 · Missouri

Citation record only - no summary is stored in the library for this case.

## In re Estate of F.C. Fechter

636 S.W.2d 342 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1982 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the bank's retention of the certificate of deposit was sufficient to constitute possession under the UCC. Consequently, the bank held a perfected security interest in the proceeds of the certificate. The estate of a decedent was involved in a dispute over whether a certificate of deposit (CD) was collateral for a loan. The bank held a security agreement executed by the decedent, which purportedly pledged the CD as security for various debts. After the decedent's death, the estate contested the bank's claim, arguing that there was no valid 'possession' of the collateral as required by the UCC for perfection of an interest in a security instrument. The bank argued that the physical retention of the CD by the bank as part of their internal banking procedures constituted 'possession' for the purposes of a perfected security interest. The court examined the requirements for perfection by control or possession under the Missouri UCC. The dispute turned on whether a bank's internal hold on a document it issued qualifies as possession of collateral to perfect a security interest, especially when the debtor did not have physical possession of the instrument during the term of the loan. The court analyzed Article 9 requirements for perfection in instruments and the role of 'possession' in securing financial interests against other creditors of an estate.

## In re Estate of F.L.

289 S.W.3d 215 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2009 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court held that the trial court's finding of testamentary capacity was supported by substantial evidence. The court concluded that the testimony of the drafting attorney and other witnesses provided a sufficient basis to uphold the validity of the codicil. The case involved a dispute over the validity of a codicil that altered the distribution of real estate. The plaintiffs alleged that the decedent lacked testamentary capacity at the time the codicil was executed, pointing to a history of dementia. The defendant maintained that the decedent was lucid and understood the nature of the transaction. The probate court found in favor of the defendant, relying on the testimony of the attorney who drafted the document. The plaintiffs appealed, arguing that the court failed to properly weigh evidence of the decedent's medical condition. The appellate court analyzed the standard for testamentary capacity, which requires the testator to understand the ordinary affairs of life and the nature and extent of their property. The court held that the evidence presented was sufficient to support the trial court's conclusion that the decedent possessed the required capacity. The appellate court affirmed the judgment, noting that the trial court is in the best position to assess the weight and credibility of the evidence regarding capacity.

## In re Estate of F.L.W.

936 S.W.2d 589 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1996 · Missouri

Holding: Perfecting a security interest in a deposit account requires strict adherence to the UCC's control requirements. Mere physical possession of a certificate of deposit is insufficient to perfect an interest if the statute demands a control agreement. This case involved a dispute over whether a security interest in a certificate of deposit was properly perfected by control. The creditor had obtained a possession-based interest in the certificate of deposit but failed to enter into a formal control agreement as required by the revised UCC statutes. The estate argued that the security interest was unperfected because the creditor's possession was not equivalent to the statutorily required 'control' over a deposit account. The court analyzed the transition from the old UCC to the revised Article 9, which shifted the focus to control agreements. The court held that the legislature intended for control to be the exclusive method of perfection for deposit accounts. Since the creditor relied on physical possession of the certificate without the necessary account control agreement, the perfection was invalid. This created a significant impact on the creditor's claim, as it left them in the position of an unsecured creditor. The case serves as an important lesson on the requirement to follow updated perfection procedures when dealing with financial instruments and bank accounts, noting that common law possession rules are often insufficient under the modern UCC framework.

The court looked at the intent requirement, analyzing whether the document was merely a planning list or an actual attempt to modify the testamentary disposition of the assets. The court emphasized the strict compliance required for holographic instruments to ensure that the decedent's true testamentary wishes are preserved against fraudulent or ambiguous claims.

## In re Estate of J.P.

644 S.W.3d 512 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the lower court's decision, holding that no valid inter vivos gift occurred and the items remained property of the estate. The litigation involved the challenge to a final settlement of an estate, specifically regarding the inclusion of certain personal property items. The appellant, a family member, claimed that specific heirlooms were promised as gifts inter vivos and should not be distributed as part of the residuary estate. The trial court determined that the requirements for a valid gift--intent, delivery, and acceptance--had not been met prior to the decedent's death. The appellate court reviewed the standard for proving inter vivos gifts, which requires clear and convincing evidence. The opinion discusses the rigor of the 'delivery' requirement, noting that physical or constructive possession must be transferred to the donee during the donor's lifetime. The court analyzed the testimony presented and found that the decedent had retained dominion and control over the items until death, thereby rendering any prior statements of intent as mere promises to make a future gift, which are unenforceable under Missouri law.

## In re Estate of J.R.

The estate proponents sought to prove the contents of the will through a PDF scan and testimony from the attorney who drafted it. The heirs at law argued that the loss of the original triggered a presumption of revocation that could only be overcome by clear and convincing evidence. The appellate court reviewed the requirements for 'lost will' proceedings under Missouri law. The focus was on the evidence required to rebut the presumption of

Second stored summary revocation, including the decedent's consistent declarations, the absence of any signs of destruction, and the attorney's testimony regarding the client's state of mind when the electronic copy was created and stored.

## In re Estate of K.J.

422 S.W.3d 290 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a prenuptial agreement waiving an elective share is unenforceable if there is no full and fair disclosure of financial assets at the time of signing. It confirmed the trial court's authority to invalidate such agreements. This case dealt with the petition for an elective share by a surviving spouse who had been omitted from the decedent's will. The executor argued that the spouse had waived the right to an elective share through a prenuptial agreement. The spouse challenged the validity of the prenuptial agreement, claiming that it was unconscionable and signed under duress. The trial court evaluated the disclosure of assets at the time the prenuptial agreement was executed. It found that the deceased spouse had failed to provide a full and fair disclosure of his financial situation, which is a requirement for a valid prenuptial agreement in Missouri. As a result, the trial court declared the agreement void and permitted the surviving spouse to claim the elective share. The executor appealed the decision, arguing that the spouse had access to financial information and that the agreement should be enforced. The appellate court affirmed, noting that the duty of disclosure is a prerequisite to the enforcement of any waiver of probate rights, and that the trial court's assessment of credibility regarding the duress and disclosure was supported by the evidence.

## In re Estate of K.L.

Holding: The court affirmed the decision that the no-contest clause did not apply. The trustee claimed that this action triggered the no-contest clause, which mandated the forfeiture of the beneficiary's interest in the trust. The trial court ruled that the beneficiary's lawsuit was brought in good faith to protect the trust assets and therefore did not violate the no-contest provision. The trustee appealed, arguing that the court was not authorized to create an exception for 'good faith' challenges when the trust language clearly prohibited any legal action against the trustee. The appellate court examined the validity and reach of no-contest clauses under Missouri law, focusing on whether such clauses could be enforced in a manner that prevents a beneficiary from seeking accountability for clear instances of fiduciary misconduct.

## In re Estate of K.T. v. State

Holding: The court held that the claim was correctly rejected for failing to meet the strict statutory service requirements. The estate rejected the claim, asserting that the nursing home had not followed the mandatory filing procedures under the probate code. Specifically, the estate argued that the claim was not served upon the personal representative within the time limits prescribed by statute. The nursing home contended that it had mailed a copy to the probate court clerk and that this should constitute constructive notice. The appellate court clarified that actual notice to the personal representative is a fundamental requirement for the validity of a creditor's claim in Missouri. Statutes governing claims against decedents are strict and procedural compliance is mandatory. The court held that reliance on filing with the clerk does not substitute for the duty to serve the personal representative directly. Because the statutory requirements were not strictly followed, the claim was properly disallowed as untimely. This decision reaffirms the importance of meticulous compliance with service requirements in probate litigation, as failure to do so will result in the loss of valid claims regardless of their underlying merit.

## In re Estate of Kester

The trial court ruled that the term 'farm property' was limited to the real estate and did not encompass personal property or business interests. The appellate court examined the principles of will construction, noting that courts must look to the plain language of the will to determine the testator's intent. If the language is unambiguous, the court cannot rewrite the will to reflect what the beneficiary believes the testator 'really meant'. The court found that the term was not ambiguous in its common and legal usage, thus excluding the disputed personal property.

## In re Estate of L.A.

The appellate court analyzed the state's statutes regarding the effect of divorce on beneficiary designations and whether those statutes applied to the particular policy in question. ## In re Estate of L.G.

Holding: The court held that a TOD deed is valid unless clear and convincing evidence demonstrates that the grantor lacked capacity or was subject to undue influence. The heirs-at-law challenged the deed, claiming that the decedent lacked the necessary mental capacity and was under the undue influence of the grantee, who was a caregiver. It held that the burden of proof rests on the challenger and that a mere showing of proximity or benefit to the grantee is not enough to presume undue influence without evidence of active interference in the decedent's free will. The appellant argued that the trial court erred in admitting evidence outside the four corners of the document, while the respondents contended that the ambiguity necessitated such evidence to prevent an absurd or unintended result. The appellate court analyzed the rules of construction applicable to Missouri wills, emphasizing the primary goal of effectuating the testator's true intent rather than relying solely on strict mechanical application of default rules.

## In re Estate of L.H. v. Estate

355 S.W.3d 505 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2011 · Missouri

The appellate court affirmed the decision, noting that Missouri courts have long held that temporary periods of confusion do not invalidate a will if the testator is lucid at the time of execution. The attorney's testimony, who observed the testator sign the document, was given significant weight as 'best evidence' of capacity. The court reiterated that probate courts are in the best position to assess the credibility of witnesses in these contests. The ruling confirms that the presence of medical conditions such as Alzheimer's does not automatically lead to a finding of incapacity, provided the testator meets the basic legal requirements at the moment of signing.

## In re Estate of L.M.K.
