The creditor argued that the settlement depleted estate assets that should have been used to pay their claim. The court explored the factors to be considered by the court in reviewing settlements, specifically whether the settlement is fair and in the best interests of the estate and its creditors. The opinion examines the due process rights of creditors in the context of probate settlements and the standard of review for trial court approval of such agreements. The court emphasized that the primary duty of the representative is to maximize the estate's value for the benefit of all interested parties, including creditors.

## In re Estate of L.R.

521 S.W.3d 622 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court reversed the appointment, holding that the statutory priority list must be followed unless a clear waiver exists. The appellate court examined the statutory preference for individuals seeking appointment as personal representative. The key issue was whether the surviving spouse had waived their right to priority through a prenuptial agreement. The court reviewed the terms of the agreement and the surrounding circumstances, determining that the agreement was ambiguous regarding the spouse's role in the estate's administration. The court concluded that the probate court should have strictly followed the statutory priority list absent a clear, unambiguous waiver in the prenuptial agreement, and remanded the matter to determine the spouse's eligibility for appointment.

The appellate court reviewed the evidence for 'clear and convincing' support for the finding of fraud. The court emphasized the need for a thorough factual determination of the decedent's solvency at the time of the transfer and whether the transaction left the estate with insufficient funds to pay its known obligations.

## In re Estate of Latimer

## In re Estate of Latimer

422 S.W.3d 465 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2014 · Missouri

## In re Estate of Long

A secured party filed a UCC-1 naming the debtor using a name that was slightly different from the name on the debtor's legal identification. The question presented was whether this discrepancy rendered the financing statement 'seriously misleading' under the UCC. The court considered the purpose of the financing statement, which is to provide notice to future creditors. The court engaged in an analysis of the 'standard search logic' provisions of the UCC and whether the filing was sufficient to put a reasonably diligent searcher on notice. The court determined that the variation was minor and not seriously misleading, thereby allowing the financing statement to remain effective and preserving the priority of the secured party. This case is frequently cited for the standard of determining whether a name error in a filing is fatal to the perfection of a security interest.

## In re Estate of M.B.

## In re Estate of M.R.

## In re Estate of M.R.

398 S.W.3d 602 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the dismissal, holding that the probate court lacked subject matter jurisdiction. Life insurance proceeds generally do not form part of the probate estate. This case dealt with an attempt to set aside a beneficiary designation on a life insurance policy. The challenger argued that the designation was changed by the decedent while the decedent was under undue influence by the new beneficiary. The estate administrator sought to recover the insurance proceeds for the estate, arguing that the change was invalid. The trial court held that the proceeds were not part of the probate estate and that the probate court lacked jurisdiction to determine the ownership of the insurance policy. ## In re Estate of M.R.

152 S.W.3d 308 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: A purchase money security interest must be perfected within the statutory grace period to enjoy priority over prior blanket security interests. Failure to meet this filing deadline results in the loss of super-priority status, and the standard first-to-file rule will apply. This matter involved the priority of security interests in various farm implements between a bank and a equipment manufacturer's financing arm. The conflict revolved around the perfection of PMSI (purchase money security interest) status. The manufacturer had filed its financing statement late, after the grace period allowed by the UCC. The bank argued that because the filing was late, the PMSI status was lost, and the bank's earlier-filed blanket lien took priority. The court reviewed the UCC requirements for PMSI perfection. It was determined that the grace period for filing a PMSI is a strict deadline. The court held that missing the deadline by even a short period deprives the creditor of the special 'super-priority' that a PMSI would otherwise enjoy. Therefore, the bank, having a prior-in-time filed financing statement that covered the equipment as after-acquired property, held the senior position. The court rejected the manufacturer's attempt to argue for an equitable exception, maintaining that the formalist requirements of the UCC are designed to provide certainty in commercial transactions, and those who fail to meet the filing deadlines must bear the consequences of losing their priority.

## In re Estate of Miller

Holding: The court held that the trustee's interpretation of 'comfort' was consistent with the testator's intent and that the trustee did not abuse their discretion. The court emphasized the deference given to broad discretionary powers in trust instruments. This case involved a dispute over the interpretation of a testamentary trust provision. The trustee argued that the language of the trust granted them broad discretion to invade the principal for the beneficiary's comfort. Other beneficiaries challenged the trustee's frequent distributions, arguing that they depleted the trust's remainder prematurely. The trial court held that the trustee's interpretation was consistent with the decedent's intent as expressed in the trust document. The appellate court reviewed the trust language using the 'four corners' rule, which requires courts to ascertain intent based on the document's text. The court determined that the word 'comfort' in the context of the decedent's directives encompassed a broader range of financial support than the challengers asserted. The court further noted that Missouri law provides significant deference to trustees when broad discretion is granted in the instrument, provided the trustee acts in good faith. Finding no evidence of bad faith or abuse of discretion, the appellate court affirmed the trial court's order. The decision serves as a guide for interpreting discretionary trust powers and the importance of specific language in defining the extent of a trustee's authority in the probate context.

## In re Estate of Miller

25 S.W.3d 611 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2000 · Missouri

Holding: An 'all accounts' description in a security agreement is sufficient to cover after-acquired accounts receivable. Specific mention of after-acquired property is not required if the general description of the collateral is comprehensive. The dispute was about whether a security interest in accounts receivable was properly perfected. The creditor had filed a financing statement, but the description of the collateral in the security agreement was somewhat ambiguous. The court examined whether the 'all accounts' language in the security agreement was sufficient to cover future accounts receivable, also known as 'after-acquired property.' The debtor argued that the security agreement did not explicitly mention after-acquired property, so it could not encumber such assets. The court analyzed the intent of the parties and the general commercial practices under the UCC. The court held that 'all accounts' is broad enough to include future accounts receivable unless specifically limited by the agreement. This affirmed the ability of creditors to secure blanket interests in fluctuating assets like accounts receivable, which is essential for working capital financing. The court's decision provides clarity on the interpretation of broad collateral descriptions in commercial loan agreements.

## In re Estate of Muehlheausler

590 S.W.2d 377 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1979 · Missouri

Holding: A security agreement's description of collateral is sufficient if it allows for the identification of the property. Specific serial numbers are not required as long as the description is not overly ambiguous. This case explored the requirements for the description of collateral in a security agreement. A lender had a security agreement that contained a broad description of assets, but the debtor argued that it was too vague to be enforceable. The court looked to the UCC standard, which requires that a description of collateral must simply make it possible to identify the items claimed. It rejected the 'serial number' requirement for all collateral, instead holding that a description like 'all farm machinery' or 'all office equipment' is sufficient if it reasonably identifies the property. The court held that the security agreement was valid because it provided enough information to allow a reasonable person to inquire further and identify the actual assets encumbered. This case established that Missouri courts favor a flexible approach to collateral description, focusing on whether a reasonably prudent party could determine the scope of the lien from the document provided.

## In re Estate of N.H.

450 S.W.3d 812 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed that the funds passed to the surviving sister. The evidence offered by the estate was insufficient to overcome the statutory presumption of joint tenancy. This matter involved the determination of whether certain bank accounts constituted a 'joint tenancy with right of survivorship' or were subject to probate as assets of the estate. The decedent had set up the accounts with their sister, but the signature cards were missing or incomplete. Upon the death of the decedent, the sister claimed the funds, while the estate argued the funds were part of the decedent's probate estate to be shared among all heirs. The trial court applied the statutory presumption that accounts held in multiple names are joint tenancies with survivorship rights, unless clear and convincing evidence proves otherwise. The estate challenged this, arguing that the decedent intended the funds to be held as a 'convenience' for managing daily bills rather than a transfer of interest. The appellate court reviewed the evidence required to overcome the statutory presumption of joint tenancy in bank accounts and whether the testimony of family members regarding the decedent's intent was sufficient to rebut this presumption in the absence of written documentation.

## In re Estate of P.D.

530 S.W.3d 596 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court remanded the case for further proceedings regarding the valuation of personal property. It held that a personal representative must provide adequate documentation for all assets included in the final settlement. A daughter contested the final distribution of her father's estate, arguing that the personal representative had undervalued real estate assets and improperly excluded certain personal property from the final accounting. The trial court had approved the final settlement over the objections of the daughter. The appellate court reviewed the procedures for approving a final settlement and the notice requirements for beneficiaries. The issue was whether the personal representative satisfied the duty of full disclosure regarding the estate's assets. The court analyzed whether the appraisal methods used for the real estate were reasonable and if the daughter was provided with an adequate opportunity to challenge the valuation before the final decree of distribution was entered. The appellate court found that while the representative had generally followed procedure, there were discrepancies in the inclusion of jewelry items that required further investigation. Consequently, the case was remanded to address these specific asset valuation concerns.

## In re Estate of P.G.

530 S.W.3d 601 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the finding of revocation, holding that the physical act of destruction coupled with the demonstrated intent to revoke satisfies the statutory requirements. The court ruled that the existence of a copy does not prevent the valid revocation of the original. The case focused on the revocation of a will through physical destruction. A prior will was produced by a beneficiary, but the executor of the estate argued that the decedent had revoked it by tearing the document before his death. Witnesses testified that the decedent expressed his intent to destroy the will and that the pieces of the document were found in his home. The trial court found the revocation to be valid, and the appellate court reviewed the requirements for revoking a will by act under Missouri law. The analysis centered on the 'animus revocandi'--the intent to revoke--and the sufficiency of the physical act. The court evaluated whether the destruction of the original will, while a copy remained intact elsewhere, was sufficient to revoke the testamentary intent expressed in the document. The appeal also addressed the presumptions that arise when a will last known to be in the testator's possession cannot be found.

## In re Estate of P.G. v. Jones

612 S.W.3d 230 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the self-proving affidavit does not satisfy the statutory requirement for two attesting witnesses on the will itself. The denial of probate was affirmed due to failure to meet formal execution standards. This appeal concerned the validity of a self-proving affidavit attached to a will that was otherwise missing the signature of a second witness. The probate court initially denied the will for probate, reasoning that it failed to meet the statutory requirement of two attesting witnesses. Proponents of the will argued that the presence of a properly notarized self-proving affidavit cured the lack of a second signature on the will instrument itself. The appellate court conducted a rigorous statutory interpretation of Missouri law regarding will execution. The court held that the self-proving affidavit serves as a separate instrument intended to facilitate probate rather than act as a substitute for the substantive requirements of valid will execution. Consequently, a will that lacks the signatures of two witnesses at the time of execution cannot be validated simply by the attachment of an affidavit, even if notarized. The court underscored that strict adherence to the formal requirements of will execution is essential to protect the integrity of the probate process and prevent fraudulent filings. The decision affirms that the self-proving affidavit is not a curative tool for defective execution under Missouri statutes.

## In re Estate of P.H.

372 S.W.3d 510 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, holding that the construction of the ambiguous will clause was supported by evidence. The court upheld the interpretation that favored in-kind distribution. This case involved a dispute over the interpretation of an ambiguous provision in a will regarding the distribution of an antique collection. One beneficiary argued that the collection was meant to be sold with proceeds divided equally, while another argued it was meant to be divided in kind. The trial court heard testimony regarding the decedent's past statements and the intent of the provision. The appellate court examined the ambiguity and held that the trial court was correct to consider the decedent's surrounding circumstances to resolve the conflict. The appellate court found that the trial court's construction of the will was reasonable and supported by the testimony regarding the decedent's lifelong collection practices. The court emphasized that probate courts should aim to implement the testator's intent in a manner that preserves the value of the assets involved. By affirming the distribution in kind, the court upheld the decision to keep the collection intact for the beneficiaries.

## In re Estate of P.L. Hiles

572 S.W.2d 159 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Kansas City District · 1978 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the security interest in the original collateral extends to the identifiable proceeds of that collateral. The bank's claim against the estate for the proceeds of the sold livestock was valid. This probate case involved a bank's claim against an estate for assets that were pledged as collateral. The bank had a security interest in the decedent's livestock and equipment. Upon the decedent's death, the estate administrator argued that the bank's security interest did not attach to the proceeds of the livestock sold after the date of death. The bank argued that its security agreement explicitly included 'proceeds' of the collateral, and therefore, its interest followed the funds regardless of the sale or the death of the debtor. The court examined the UCC definitions of 'proceeds' and the rules regarding the continuation of security interests in identifiable cash proceeds. The case required a determination of whether the bank's perfected interest remained enforceable against the personal representative of the estate and if the proceeds remained 'identifiable' as required by Article 9 for a security interest to continue after the disposition of the original collateral.

## In re Estate of P.S.

399 S.W.3d 601 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court held that the unsigned trust amendments were invalid and could not be incorporated into the will. The distribution was ordered according to the last validly executed trust instrument. The controversy centered on the interpretation of a pour-over will and its relationship with an inter vivos trust. The decedent had created a trust that named certain beneficiaries but then executed a will that directed all assets to be distributed under the terms of a different document, which the parties disagreed was the 'intended' trust instrument. The probate court had to determine which documents were properly incorporated by reference into the will. The dispute was complicated by the existence of multiple amendments to the trust that were not properly signed or notarized according to the trust's own amendment procedures. The court had to evaluate the validity of these amendments and their effect on the final distribution of the estate. The appeal addressed the legal standards for incorporation by reference and the extent to which the court can rely on the decedent's known financial plans versus the strict adherence to the formal requirements of trust modification and testamentary documents under Missouri statutes.

## In re Estate of P.V.

388 S.W.3d 601 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The court reversed the trial court, holding that the failure to meet the statutory requirement of having two credible witnesses observe the signing invalidated the will. The court held that strict compliance with the execution statute is mandatory. The case involved a dispute over the validity of a signature on a will. The decedent's signature was witnessed by two individuals, but one witness later testified that they did not see the decedent sign the document and did not believe the decedent knew what they were signing. The trial court admitted the will to probate after the proponent provided evidence of the decedent's long-standing testamentary plan. The contestants appealed, arguing that the statutory requirements for proper execution were not met because one of the witnesses did not actually attest the signing as required by law. The appellate court analyzed the statutory requirements for the execution of a formal will in Missouri. The court focused on the 'strict compliance' doctrine, discussing whether the testimony of an 'interested' witness could be impeached and whether the lack of a formal attestation clause affected the presumption of validity.

## In re Estate of Parker

595 S.W.3d 520 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: A deed remains invalid if it is not delivered during the grantor's lifetime. Because the grantor maintained control and only intended the deed to be effective upon death, it failed as a testamentary instrument. This case involved a dispute over the ownership of real property following the death of the owner. The central issue concerned whether a deed executed by the decedent was validly delivered during her lifetime or if it was an invalid testamentary disposition. The decedent had executed a warranty deed conveying the property to her children but kept the deed in her possession, intending for it to be recorded only upon her death. The court examined Missouri law regarding the delivery of deeds, which requires an intention by the grantor to part with control of the deed and to pass title immediately. The evidence presented indicated that the decedent never relinquished control of the deed during her life and clearly intended for the transfer to occur only posthumously. Because the deed did not meet the legal requirements for a present conveyance of interest, it functioned as an attempted testamentary disposition that failed to comply with the Statute of Wills. Consequently, the property remained part of the decedent's estate, and the trial court's ruling in favor of the estate was affirmed.

## In re Estate of Parker

Holding: The court held that the definition of 'merchandise' under the MPA is broad enough to include certain financial services. The estate's claim under the MPA was permitted to proceed. The estate alleged that the financial advisor engaged in deceptive practices by recommending high-risk investments without explaining the potential for loss. The financial institution argued that the MPA does not apply to the sale of financial products, as they are not 'merchandise'. The court analyzed the definition of merchandise within the context of investment services. This case was significant for determining whether financial services and advisory activities are encompassed by the MPA, a question that has frequently arisen in Missouri courts as the definition of 'merchandise' has been interpreted to be quite expansive.

## In re Estate of R.C.M.

285 S.W.3d 395 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2009 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that strict compliance with the motor vehicle lien statutes is required for perfection. Because the lien was not properly noted on the title, the security interest was not perfected against the estate. This case arose from a dispute between a secured creditor and the personal representative of an estate regarding the enforceability of a security interest in titled property. The decedent had pledged a motorcycle as collateral for a loan. After the death of the debtor, the personal representative argued that the security interest was not perfected because the lien was not correctly noted on the certificate of title as required by the Missouri Department of Revenue. The secured creditor contended that it had substantially complied with the requirements and that the estate had actual knowledge of the lien. The court explored the interplay between UCC perfection rules and the specific statutory procedures for motor vehicle title liens. It addressed whether equitable arguments, such as actual notice, could overcome a failure to comply with strict statutory perfection requirements. The case highlights the rigor required in perfecting interests in titled motor vehicles and the limited circumstances where substantial compliance might be accepted by the court.

## In re Estate of R.L.

488 S.W.3d 762 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the probate court did not abuse its discretion in appointing a neutral fiduciary. The court found that the presence of extreme conflict between heirs serves as a valid justification for bypassing statutory priority to ensure the estate is managed impartially. The case involved an appeal from a probate court's decision regarding the appointment of a personal representative. The decedent died intestate, and multiple family members petitioned for letters of administration. The probate court selected a third-party professional fiduciary over the competing family members, citing ongoing animosity and conflict among the heirs that threatened the efficient administration of the estate. On appeal, the heirs argued that the probate court abused its discretion by bypassing the statutory preference for relatives in the appointment process. The appellate court examined Missouri statutes regarding the priority of appointment, which prioritize the surviving spouse, children, and other heirs, but grant the court discretion to pass over these individuals if the circumstances warrant. The analysis highlighted the trial court's authority to evaluate the fitness of applicants and the necessity of neutral management when family disputes reach a level of dysfunction that prevents the timely settlement of debts and asset distribution.

## In re Estate of R.L. R.

843 S.W.2d 394 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1992 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the mobile home remained a chattel rather than a fixture, and therefore the UCC financing statement was the correct method of perfection. Consequently, the creditor's interest was valid and superior to the estate claims. The dispute involved the status of a lien on a mobile home after the death of the owner. A creditor argued that its security interest in the mobile home survived and had priority over the claims of the estate beneficiaries. The court examined whether the mobile home was properly classified as consumer goods or real property, as this classification affects how a security interest is perfected. The creditor had filed a UCC financing statement, but the estate argued that because the mobile home was affixed to the land, the security interest should have been perfected as a real estate mortgage. The court analyzed the statutory definitions of fixtures and the requirements for perfecting an interest in a fixture under the UCC. The case required a detailed review of the physical connection between the mobile home and the land to determine if the UCC perfection was valid or if a real estate filing was required. The appellate court weighed the arguments based on Missouri's fixture filing statutes.

## In re Estate of R.P.

288 S.W.3d 750 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2009 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the trial court acted within its discretion in appointing the successor. It affirmed the appointment, finding the chosen representative had the requisite neutrality and skill to manage the assets. This case dealt with the appointment of a successor personal representative. A conflict arose when the original executor died mid-administration. Two groups of heirs proposed different candidates, each arguing their nominee was better suited to manage the complex real estate holdings remaining in the estate. The appellate court examined the statutory preference for individuals nominated in the will versus those preferred by the majority of the beneficiaries. The court looked at the discretion granted to probate courts in selecting a representative when the original nominee is unavailable. The analysis focused on whether the trial court gave proper weight to the beneficiaries' preferences and whether the chosen representative had a conflict of interest due to their involvement in the ongoing estate litigation. The court emphasized the goal of efficient administration and the need to avoid further animosity between the heirs, which was a significant factor in the selection process conducted by the probate court judge.

## In re Estate of R.S.

142 S.W.3d 789 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that in cases involving a fiduciary or confidential relationship, a presumption of undue influence arises upon the exercise of that influence, shifting the burden to the beneficiary to prove the validity of the transaction. It remanded for proper application of the burden of proof. The case involved a challenge to an amendment to a trust made by the grantor when they were allegedly subject to undue influence. The primary beneficiary of the original trust sought to invalidate the amendment, which had diverted a significant portion of the trust assets to a new caretaker. The trial court found that the amendment was valid and denied the challenge, leading to an appeal by the original beneficiary. The appellate court examined the elements of undue influence, including the existence of a confidential relationship, the exercise of influence, and a resulting unnatural disposition of assets. It found that the caretaker had held a position of trust and had actively participated in the creation and execution of the trust amendment. The court held that under these circumstances, a presumption of undue influence arose, shifting the burden of proof to the proponent of the amendment to prove its fairness. The case was remanded for the trial court to apply this shifted burden of proof, noting that the trial court had incorrectly required the challenger to prove the influence in the first instance.

## In re Estate of R.T.

472 S.W.3d 624 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the trial court's judgment, holding that the challenger failed to rebut the presumption of validity. The evidence of capacity at the time of account creation was considered sufficient. This probate litigation focused on the validity of a joint bank account with a right of survivorship established shortly before the decedent's death. The appellant claimed the account was created through fraud and undue influence, alleging that the bank employee failed to verify the decedent's capacity. The trial court found no evidence of undue influence or lack of capacity. On appeal, the court scrutinized the evidentiary requirements for challenging a non-probate transfer. It noted that the burden rests on the challenger to produce clear and

The appellate court found that the evidence presented by the challenger was speculative and insufficient to overcome the statutory presumption that the account holder intended the survivorship arrangement. The court affirmed the judgment, noting the high threshold for challenging such financial instruments in the absence of documented coercion or evidence of incompetence at the time of the bank transaction.

## In re Estate of Reimer

897 S.W.2d 163 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1995 · Missouri

Holding: A description of 'all equipment' in a security agreement covers subsequently acquired equipment. The court held that broad categories provide sufficient notice under the UCC. This case dealt with the scope of a security interest in business assets, specifically the 'inventory' classification. A bank claimed a security interest in the business's 'inventory and equipment.' The business later purchased specialized computer equipment, and the bank asserted that this was covered by their existing security interest. The court analyzed whether the computer hardware constituted 'equipment' or 'inventory' and if the description was broad enough to encompass it. The court held that the language 'all equipment' is a sufficiently broad description to capture future items purchased for business use. The court reaffirmed that the UCC's notice-filing system is intended to warn other creditors that a lien exists on a particular category of assets, and once that warning is provided, the specific sub-types of that category do not need to be individually listed to be covered. The case provides significant protection to lenders who utilize broad collateral descriptions in their financing statements.

## In re Estate of S.C.

355 S.W.3d 510 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2011 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the denial of the spouse's claim, holding that the elective share applies only to probate assets under current Missouri law. The revocable trust was found to be beyond the scope of the elective share calculation. This litigation involved the determination of elective share rights of a surviving spouse when the decedent's assets were largely held in a revocable trust. The spouse argued that the trust assets should be included in the 'augmented estate' for the purpose of calculating their elective share, as the trust was essentially a will substitute that depleted the probate estate to the detriment of the spouse. The trustee contended that the trust was a separate legal entity and that the elective share only applied to assets probate-controlled. The trial court sided with the trustee, adhering to a strict interpretation of the Missouri elective share statutes existing at the time. The surviving spouse appealed, arguing that the court should apply a broader, modern interpretation of marital rights that accounts for non-probate transfers like revocable trusts. The court evaluated the legislative history of the elective share statutes and the distinction between probate assets and assets subject to the surviving spouse's elective claim under prevailing Missouri law.

## In re Estate of S.C.

98 S.W.3d 623 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: A security interest in a fixture must be perfected by a fixture filing in the land records. A standard UCC-1 financing statement is ineffective to perfect an interest in a structure that has become legally classified as a fixture to real property. The court heard a case concerning a creditor's attempt to enforce a security interest in a mobile home that was partially affixed to the land. The creditor held an interest in the mobile home as personal property, while the estate argued it had become part of the real estate and therefore the creditor's UCC filing was ineffective. The court applied the 'fixture' test, considering the method of attachment, the adaptability of the use, and the intent of the party making the annexation. The court found that because the mobile home was mounted on a permanent foundation and tied to residential infrastructure, it had ceased to be personal property. However, the creditor had not filed a fixture filing in the real estate records, having only filed a standard UCC-1 financing statement. The court held that a standard UCC filing is insufficient to perfect an interest in a fixture. Because the creditor did not comply with the fixture filing requirements, they lost their secured status as against other parties with an interest in the land. The case emphasizes the crucial distinction between perfection under the UCC for personal property and the specific requirements for fixtures attached to real estate.

## In re Estate of S.J.K.

## In re Estate of S.K.

## In re Estate of S.K.

The beneficiary sought to challenge the trustee's accounting, but the trustee argued that the challenge triggered the no-contest clause, causing the beneficiary to forfeit their interest. ## In re Estate of S.M.

The estate executor excluded the adopted-away child from the distribution, interpreting the term 'children' as only those who maintained a legal relationship with the decedent at the time of death. It noted that the law seeks to avoid ambiguity by interpreting terms based on the relationship at the time of the testator's death, but it must also respect the clear intent of the testator if expressed elsewhere in the document. The court found that the will did not define 'children' specifically, and thus the court must apply the default rules under Missouri law, which do not automatically terminate inheritance rights based on adoption in this specific context. Consequently, the court held that the adopted-away child was entitled to a portion of the residuary estate.

## In re Estate of S.W.

## In re Estate of Scott

Holding: The court held that the bank's security interest was properly perfected because it had complied with the Missouri motor vehicle title statutes. Vehicle perfection is governed by the title law rather than the general UCC filing rules. This matter involved a challenge to the perfection of a security interest in a vehicle. A bank provided a loan for the purchase of a motor vehicle and claimed a perfected lien on the title. A dispute arose among heirs and creditors regarding the validity of that lien when the title was not properly processed by the state motor vehicle department before the debtor's death. The court had to determine if the UCC rules for perfection or the specific provisions of the Missouri motor vehicle statute controlled the perfection process. The opinion clarifies the relationship between the UCC's general filing rules and the vehicle-specific title laws. The court examined whether the bank had taken all necessary steps to perfect its interest under the statutory scheme applicable to motor vehicles, noting that compliance with title statutes generally preempts the UCC filing requirements for vehicles. The decision is vital for understanding how secured parties must navigate state-specific titling procedures to ensure their interest is enforceable against subsequent purchasers or estate representatives.

## In re Estate of Shroyer

173 S.W.3d 348 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2005 · Missouri

Holding: Minor inaccuracies in a financing statement that do not seriously mislead a searcher do not invalidate perfection. Security interests remain enforceable against the estate of a deceased debtor. This probate matter examined whether a creditor's security interest survived the death of the debtor and the subsequent transfer of assets. The estate argued that the security interest was not properly perfected because of errors in the financing statement regarding the debtor's middle name and address. The court applied the 'substantial compliance' test, determining whether the inaccuracies were so significant that a reasonable searcher would be unable to find the record. The court found that the UCC's filing system is designed to provide notice, and because the errors were minor and did not obscure the identity of the debtor or the existence of the lien, the filing was effective. The court further held that death does not terminate a security interest; rather, the interest remains attached to the collateral held by the estate. The ruling reinforced the liberal construction of UCC perfection requirements in Missouri to prevent the invalidation of security interests due to minor, non-prejudicial clerical errors.

## In re Estate of T.B. v. Clerk

225 S.W.3d 422 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2007 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the filing in the wrong county did not preserve the claim. The non-claim statute is an absolute bar to untimely or misfiled claims. A creditor attempted to file a claim against an estate, but the claim was filed in the wrong county. After the statutory period for filing claims expired, the creditor sought to transfer the claim to the proper probate court. The trial court denied the transfer, finding that the filing was null and void due to lack of jurisdiction. On appeal, the creditor argued for the application of equitable principles to allow the transfer. The appellate court held that filing a claim in the wrong county does not toll the non-claim statute. The non-claim statute is a strict jurisdictional requirement that serves the public interest in the finality of probate. The court emphasized that the burden is on the creditor to identify the correct court and file within the prescribed time limit. Because the jurisdictional threshold was not met, the court had no authority to allow the transfer of the claim. This case is a strict application of procedural rules in Missouri probate law, emphasizing that there is no 'grace period' for procedural errors by creditors.

## In re Estate of T.D.

528 S.W.3d 432 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the family member presumption is rebuttable by evidence demonstrating an expectation of compensation. It remanded the case, instructing the trial court to evaluate whether the specific evidence provided by the claimant established an enforceable agreement. The dispute involved the reimbursement of expenses incurred by a family member who provided care for the decedent prior to their death. The family member filed a claim against the estate for the value of the services rendered, citing an informal agreement with the decedent. The estate rejected the claim, arguing that the services were gratuitous and that no formal contract for payment existed. The probate court entered judgment against the claimant, finding that the 'family member presumption' applied, meaning that services rendered by family members to one another are presumed to be gratuitous in the absence of a clear, express contract. The appellate court reviewed the application of this presumption and analyzed the evidence provided by the claimant, which included handwritten notes and witness accounts of the decedent's intent to pay. The court held that while the family member presumption exists to prevent fraudulent claims against estates, it can be rebutted by evidence of a specific agreement or an expectation of compensation clearly communicated between the parties. The court remanded the matter for the trial court to determine if the claimant provided sufficient evidence to rebut the presumption.

## In re Estate of T.K.

560 S.W.3d 442 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court reversed the probate court's decision, holding that evidence of separation alone does not satisfy the statutory definition of abandonment. It held that the estate failed to prove that the spouse acted with the intent to permanently abandon the marriage. This case dealt with the petition for an elective share filed by a surviving spouse who had been separated from the decedent for several years prior to death. The decedent's estate argued that the spouse had abandoned the decedent, thereby forfeiting her right to an elective share under Missouri law. The probate court conducted an evidentiary hearing on the nature of the separation and the duration of the estrangement. The appellate court reviewed the statutory definition of abandonment and the degree of proof required to deny a spouse their legal inheritance rights. The opinion analyzed whether mere living apart, in the absence of formal legal separation or divorce, constitutes abandonment sufficient to bar a spouse's claim. The analysis also considered whether the spouse's lack of financial support or communication during the years preceding the decedent's death met the threshold for disqualification under the probate code.

## In re Estate of T.S.

455 S.W.3d 490 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that federal law preempts state law in this context, allowing the named beneficiary to collect the retirement funds. The waiver in the divorce decree was insufficient to override the plan's beneficiary designation under ERISA.

Second stored summary This case addressed the effect of a divorce on beneficiary designations in a non-probate asset. The decedent had a 401(k) plan naming their former spouse as the beneficiary, but the dissolution decree contained a provision waiving all claims to the other party's retirement assets. The decedent failed to update the beneficiary designation form before their death. The former spouse claimed the funds as the named beneficiary. The decedent's estate argued that the waiver in the dissolution decree was legally binding. The court analyzed the federal preemption issues regarding ERISA-governed plans and state law regarding the impact of divorce on beneficiary designations. The court examined whether Missouri's revocation-on-divorce statute could reach retirement accounts that are subject to federal preemption, focusing on the recent developments in federal case law concerning beneficiary rules.

## In re Estate of T.W.

440 S.W.3d 210 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the trial court's fee award, holding that the court properly exercised its discretion in balancing the complexity of the estate against the results achieved. It held that the fee was reasonable under the circumstances of the case. The case centered on a dispute over the executor's fee. The estate was highly complex, involving numerous real estate holdings and ongoing business interests. The executor requested a fee exceeding the statutory guidelines, arguing that the time and effort expended warranted additional compensation. The beneficiaries objected, arguing that the executor's performance was subpar and that the fee should be limited to the standard amount. The probate court granted a fee that was higher than the guidelines but lower than the requested amount. The appellate court reviewed the standard for determining reasonable compensation for fiduciaries. The opinion assessed whether the trial court gave proper weight to the factors prescribed by Missouri law, such as the complexity of the estate, the skill employed by the executor, and the results achieved for the beneficiaries. The court provided guidance on when departures from the standard guidelines are permissible in estate administration.

## In re Estate of T.W.

412 S.W.3d 890 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court held that the prenuptial agreement was valid and binding. It affirmed the denial of the elective share, finding the agreement met all requirements for enforceability. This matter involved an application for a spousal elective share against the decedent's estate. The surviving spouse filed for her elective share under Missouri law, but the estate argued that she had waived this right through a prenuptial agreement executed decades earlier. The appeal focused on the validity of that prenuptial agreement, specifically whether there had been full and fair disclosure of assets at the time of signing. The appellate court analyzed the shifting burdens of proof in disputes over marital contracts and the level of scrutiny the court applies when one spouse is left with nothing. The court discussed the 'unconscionability' standard as it applies to prenuptial agreements in the context of a death, as opposed to a divorce. The decision provided clarity on when a prenuptial agreement can effectively bar a spousal elective share and the extent of the duty of disclosure required to enforce such an agreement in the probate context.

## In re Estate of Thomas

648 S.W.3d 810 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the trial court's decision, holding that the proponents of the will met their burden of proving testamentary capacity. The evidence showed that the decedent understood the nature of his estate and the objects of his bounty at the time of execution. The decedent left a will that was contested by his children, who alleged lack of testamentary capacity and undue influence. The trial court found in favor of the estate, determining that the decedent possessed the required mental capacity at the time of execution. The children appealed, arguing that the court failed to properly weigh evidence of the decedent's cognitive decline and potential manipulation by the beneficiary. The appellate court examined the standard for testamentary capacity, noting that a testator must only understand the ordinary affairs of life, the nature and extent of their property, and the natural objects of their bounty. The record showed substantial medical testimony and lay witness accounts confirming the decedent was lucid when signing the document. The appellate court reviewed the trial court's findings for clear error and found that the trial court's assessment of credibility was within its discretion. The court emphasized that even if the decedent suffered from periods of confusion, they were not necessarily present during the specific moment the will was executed. The judgment upholding the will's validity was affirmed, reinforcing the high threshold for overturning testamentary intent based on capacity arguments.

## In re Estate of Thomas

648 S.W.3d 911 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the trial court erred in its analysis of the presumption of undue influence. It remanded the case for a new trial, finding that the trial court failed to properly weigh the evidentiary burden shifted to the respondent. The dispute involved the validity of a beneficiary designation on a payable-on-death account. After the decedent's death, the family disagreed on whether the decedent possessed the requisite mental capacity to modify the account designation shortly before passing. The trial court admitted evidence regarding the decedent's medical history and testimony from non-expert witnesses concerning cognitive decline. The appellate court reviewed the evidentiary rulings, particularly focusing on the admission of hearsay and the weight afforded to expert versus lay testimony. The core issue was whether the trial court abused its discretion in determining that the decedent was under undue influence when updating the account. The appellate court analyzed the burden of proof required to establish a confidential relationship and the resulting presumption of undue influence. Ultimately, the court explored whether the trial court correctly applied the standards set forth in established Missouri statutes regarding the mental capacity to execute contracts versus testamentary capacity, noting that the standards for lifetime transfers differ from those for wills.

## In re Estate of Thompson

954 S.W.2d 694 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1997 · Missouri

Holding: A mobile home is generally classified as personal property subject to UCC Article 9 unless it is physically integrated into the land to such a degree that it qualifies as a fixture under state law. Failure to perfect an interest in a mobile home under the UCC renders the security interest unperfected, even if a real estate deed of trust was filed. This case involved the determination of the validity and attachment of a security interest in a mobile home located on real property. The creditor attempted to assert a secured claim against the estate of the deceased, claiming an interest in the structure. The dispute centered on whether the mobile home should be considered personal property subject to UCC Article 9 or if it had become a fixture, thus subject to real property law. The court examined the intent of the parties at the time of the mobile home's placement on the land and the degree of annexation to the property. Missouri law requires specific indicators, such as the removal of wheels and connection to permanent utilities, to classify a mobile home as a fixture. The creditor had failed to file a UCC-1 financing statement, assuming the interest was covered by a real estate deed of trust. However, because the structure remained a mobile home under statutory definitions, the court held that it was personal property. Since the creditor did not comply with the perfection requirements of the UCC, the security interest remained unperfected. Consequently, the claim was treated as an unsecured debt against the estate. The case highlights the distinction between fixture filings and standard personal property perfection under the UCC.

## In re Estate of Thompson

599 S.W.3d 244 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the property passed outside of the probate estate to the surviving joint tenant regardless of the conflicting provisions in the will. The legal title to the property was unaffected by the testator's testamentary intent. The survivorship interest controls. The case concerned a dispute regarding the interpretation of a will involving the distribution of real estate. The testator had bequeathed the family residence to one child, while leaving other assets to the remaining children. The dispute arose when it was discovered that the title to the residence was held in a joint tenancy with a right of survivorship between the testator and the child who was supposed to receive the property via the will. The other heirs argued that the property should have been considered part of the probate estate and divided equally. The legal battle centered on whether the joint tenancy agreement superseded the provisions of the will. The court analyzed the principles of real property law concerning survivorship interests and the rules governing probate assets. The appellate court examined whether extrinsic evidence of the decedent's intent could be used to challenge the legal effect of a property deed. The decision underscores the importance of carefully coordinating estate planning documents with the legal titling of real property assets to avoid unintended inheritance consequences.

## In re Estate of W.C.

223 S.W.3d 898 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2007 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the dismissal, holding that the non-claim statute is mandatory and cannot be waived by the personal representative. The court held that the probate court correctly applied the jurisdictional deadline to the late-filed claim. The dispute involved the status of a creditor's claim against an estate. The claimant filed the claim after the statutory period had expired but argued that the personal representative's actual notice of the debt waived the filing requirement. The probate court dismissed the claim as time-barred. The claimant appealed, asserting that the personal representative's behavior constituted a waiver or estoppel. The appellate court reviewed the non-claim statute, explaining that it serves as a strict bar to late claims to ensure that estates can be settled efficiently. The court clarified that the personal representative does not have the legal authority to waive the statutory filing deadline, as it is a jurisdictional requirement imposed by the legislature to provide finality to estate settlements. The decision confirmed that regardless of the representative's knowledge of the debt, a creditor must comply with the strict statutory timeline to maintain a claim against the assets of the estate.

## In re Estate of W.C.

355 S.W.3d 520 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2011 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that unambiguous survival clauses in wills are enforceable and must be strictly applied. It determined that the spouse's death before the designated timeframe precluded their estate from inheriting under the will. This litigation involved the interpretation of a 'simultaneous death' clause in the decedent's will. The testator and his spouse died in a car accident, and the court had to determine if the spouse survived the testator by the time period required by the will to inherit the estate. The will stated that the spouse must survive the testator by 30 days to inherit. The medical evidence indicated that the spouse lived for approximately 28 days in a persistent vegetative state before passing away. The executor sought to exclude the spouse from the estate, while the spouse's estate sought to include the assets, arguing that 'survival' should not be interpreted as 'consciousness.' The trial court ruled that the spouse failed to survive by the 30-day period. The appellate court affirmed, holding that the clear, unambiguous language of the will controlled. The court noted that testamentary intent is the primary guide in probate, and if a testator specifies a survival period, that period must be strictly adhered to, regardless of the perceived fairness of the outcome. The definition of survival in this context did not require consciousness but simply life, which ended before the 30-day mark.

## In re Estate of W.C. Roney

139 S.W.3d 634 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2004 · Missouri

Holding: Perfection of a security interest in a motor vehicle is governed by the state's certificate of title statutes. Once a lien is properly noted on the certificate of title, the security interest is perfected, and this provides constructive notice that satisfies the requirements for secured status. The case involved a dispute between a bank and an estate over a vehicle that served as collateral for a loan. The bank held a title lien, but the debtor had filed for bankruptcy before the creditor could fully realize the asset. The issue centered on whether the certificate of title's recordation satisfied the perfection requirements for a vehicle under Missouri law, which displaces some UCC filing requirements. The court examined whether the bank had properly noted its lien on the title as mandated by Missouri's motor vehicle registration statutes. The estate challenged the validity of the lien, arguing that the bank had failed to maintain proper records and that the lien had lapsed. The court reviewed the timing of the registration and the renewal requirements under the relevant statutes. It was determined that even if the bank's internal files were disorganized, the public notice provided by the properly endorsed certificate of title was sufficient to perfect the interest against third-party claims. The court applied the rule that a lien noted on a certificate of title acts as constructive notice, thereby fulfilling the policy goals of the UCC's perfection requirements. The decision affirmed that specific statutory procedures for motor vehicles take precedence over the general UCC-1 filing requirements for other types of collateral.

## In re Estate of W.R.

The decedent left a will that failed to specify what would happen if a beneficiary died before the testator. One of the primary beneficiaries, a sibling, died before the testator, leaving children. The issue was whether the share of the deceased sibling passed to the sibling's children via the anti-lapse statute or whether it reverted to the residuary estate. The trial court applied the anti-lapse statute, distributing the share to the children. The residuary legatees appealed, arguing that the statute was inapplicable because the will contained a residuary clause that demonstrated a contrary intent. The appellate court reviewed the legislative history and purpose of the anti-lapse statute, concluding that it applies unless the will provides a clear and unambiguous alternative distribution scheme that effectively supersedes the statute. The court determined that the will did not contain sufficient language to defeat the statute's application.

## In re Gouveia

135 F.3d 1166 · United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit · 1998 · Federal

Holding: The Seventh Circuit held that the Rooker-Feldman doctrine does not prevent a bankruptcy court from exercising its avoidance powers under the Bankruptcy Code to invalidate a transfer, even if that transfer was mandated by a state court judgment. This case involved a dispute over whether a bankruptcy trustee could avoid a transfer of property that occurred under a state-ordered judgment lien. The debtor argued that the lien was invalid under state law, while the creditor maintained that the bankruptcy court lacked the jurisdiction to review the validity of a final state court judgment. The Seventh Circuit analyzed the 'Rooker-Feldman' doctrine, which prevents lower federal courts from reviewing final state court judgments. However, the court distinguished between direct appeals of state court decisions and the exercise of the bankruptcy court's specific statutory powers, such as the power to avoid preferences or fraudulent transfers. The court held that the bankruptcy court possesses independent jurisdiction to evaluate whether a transfer of property to a creditor meets the requirements of the Bankruptcy Code, even if that transfer was authorized by a state court order. This allows the bankruptcy court to ensure that all creditors are treated fairly according to the uniform rules of the federal system.

## In re Jevic Holding Corp.

580 U.S. 451 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2017 · Federal

Holding: The Supreme Court held that a bankruptcy court may not approve a structured dismissal that provides for distributions of assets that violate the Bankruptcy Code's established priority rules. Equitable powers do not grant judges the authority to bypass statutory priorities. Jevic Holding Corporation filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. During the case, the bankruptcy court approved a 'structured dismissal' that settled the dispute but distributed assets in a way that violated the priority rules of the Bankruptcy Code--specifically, it paid junior creditors while skipping over certain priority wage claims. A group of employees challenged the plan, arguing that bankruptcy courts cannot approve settlements that deviate from the statutory priority scheme. The Supreme Court addressed whether a bankruptcy court has the authority to approve a distribution of assets that violates the 'absolute priority rule' in a dismissal. The Court held that while bankruptcy courts have broad equitable powers, those powers cannot override the explicit priority provisions established by Congress. The decision clarified that a structured dismissal cannot be used as a shortcut to favor some creditors over others in a manner that contradicts the fundamental requirements of the Bankruptcy Code, thereby protecting the integrity of the priority hierarchy in liquidation.

## In re Jones

638 F.3d 901 · 8th Cir. · 2011 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Eighth Circuit affirmed the bankruptcy court's confirmation of the Chapter 13 plan. The court found that the debtor's valuation of the collateral was reasonable and that the plan provided the creditor with the present value of its secured claim. Therefore, the cramdown provision was properly applied, and the creditor's objection was overruled. A Chapter 13 debtor proposed a plan wherein a secured creditor's claim would be paid off over the plan's duration, with interest. The creditor objected, arguing its claim should be treated differently due to the collateral's depreciation. The debtor argued the plan complied with 11 U.S.C. § 1325(a)(5)(B), allowing for cramdown. The bankruptcy court confirmed the plan, and the creditor appealed.

## In re Kismet Products, Inc.

221 F.3d 983 · United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit · 2000 · Federal

Holding: Claims in a Chapter 7 bankruptcy must follow the strict priority hierarchy set forth in the Bankruptcy Code. Courts may not create equitable priorities that contradict statutory mandates. Super-priority status must be expressly provided for in the Code to be recognized in a liquidation proceeding. This case involved a Chapter 7 liquidation and the determination of the priority of claims. A creditor asserted a super-priority claim based on a previous court order in a failed Chapter 11 proceeding. The bankruptcy trustee argued that the claim should be treated as a general unsecured claim because the prior reorganization was unsuccessful and the assets were insufficient. The Seventh Circuit analyzed the priorities established under Section 507 of the Bankruptcy Code. The court addressed the tension between the policy favoring successful reorganization and the need for fair liquidation in Chapter 7. The court held that unless a specific statutory exception provides for a super-priority status, the administrative expenses and general claims must follow the hierarchy of the Code. The court refused to create a 'common law' priority that would contradict the express language of the Bankruptcy Code.

## In re Knight

370 F.3d 1030 · United States Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit · 2004 · Federal

Holding: The anti-modification provision of Section 1322(b)(2) applies to any claim secured by the debtor's principal residence, even if the property is used for rental purposes. The statute does not allow for the cramdown of such mortgages in Chapter 13 plans. The nature of the property as a principal residence triggers the protection for the creditor. The debtors filed for Chapter 13 bankruptcy and attempted to use the 'cramdown' provision to reduce the amount owed on a loan secured by their primary residence. The creditor argued that Section 1322(b)(2) prohibits any modification of a claim secured solely by a security interest in real property that is the debtor's principal residence. The debtors argued that the loan was actually a business loan because the property was used for rental purposes, thus taking it outside the protection of the anti-modification clause. The Tenth Circuit examined the nature of the security interest. The court held that the plain language of the statute protects any claim secured by the debtor's principal residence, regardless of whether the property also serves an investment function. The court emphasized that the statute focuses on the security interest itself rather than the usage of the property.

## In re Krystal Cadillac Oldsmobile GMC Truck, Inc.

337 F.3d 314 · United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit · 2003 · Federal

Holding: The Third Circuit held that a confirmed bankruptcy order approving a settlement agreement is a final judgment and is subject to the doctrine of res judicata. A debtor cannot seek to reject an agreement once it has been assumed through a court-approved, final settlement. The debtor, a car dealership, reached a settlement agreement with a manufacturer to assume a franchise agreement. The bankruptcy court approved the settlement, and the debtor began operating under the agreement. Later, the dealership attempted to reject the agreement, arguing that it was an executory contract. The manufacturer argued that the order approving the settlement had become final and that the doctrine of res judicata barred the debtor from challenging the assumption of the agreement. The Third Circuit examined whether an order approving a settlement and the assumption of an executory contract can be undone once the time for appeal has passed. The court concluded that the bankruptcy court's order was a final judgment on the merits. Because the dealership had already benefited from the settlement, allowing them to rescind the contract after the fact would undermine the finality of bankruptcy court orders and prejudice the other party, who had performed its obligations under the agreement.

## In re Marrama

549 U.S. 365 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2007 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Supreme Court held that a bankruptcy court may deny a debtor's motion to convert a Chapter 7 case to Chapter 13 if the debtor has acted in bad faith or engaged in fraud. The right to convert is not absolute when it would facilitate an abuse of the court's process. Robert Marrama sought relief under Chapter 7 but later attempted to convert his case to Chapter 13. The lower courts denied his motion to convert, citing his bad faith conduct, including concealing assets from the bankruptcy court. Marrama argued that under the plain language of the Bankruptcy Code, a debtor has an absolute right to convert their case from Chapter 7 to Chapter 13 at any time, provided the debtor is eligible to be a debtor under Chapter 13. The Supreme Court reviewed the provision and considered whether a bankruptcy judge has the discretion to deny a conversion based on the debtor's fraudulent conduct. The Court analyzed the inherent authority of the bankruptcy court to prevent the abuse of the bankruptcy process. It concluded that allowing a debtor who acted in bad faith to convert to Chapter 13 would be inconsistent with the statute's requirement that the debtor act in good faith. The Court affirmed that bankruptcy courts have the power to deny conversion if the debtor's conduct violates the spirit of the bankruptcy system.

## In re Marriage of A.J.W. and N.L.W.

647 S.W.3d 532 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's award of joint legal and physical custody and the established visitation schedule, finding it to be in the children's best interest. The child support order, including the imputation of income, was also affirmed. This appeal concerned a divorce decree that included orders for child custody, child support, and division of marital property. The mother appealed the custody award, arguing the trial court erred in granting joint legal and physical custody and the specific week-on/week-off schedule, contending it was not in the children's best interest due to the parents' acrimonious relationship. The father cross-appealed the child support calculation, arguing error in the imputation of income. The appellate court reviewed the evidence concerning the children's adjustment, the parents' capacity to co-parent, and the statutory factors for determining the best interests of the child. The court affirmed the joint physical custody award and schedule, finding it served the children's best interests despite the conflict. The child support calculation, including the imputation of income, was also affirmed.

## In re Marriage of A.L. v. T.L.

585 S.W.3d 810 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's denial of the modification. It held that the father failed to show a substantial and continuing change in circumstances, as the expenses he cited were foreseeable at the time of the original support order. This appeal centered on the trial court's denial of a motion to modify child support based on the father's claim of 'extraordinary expenses' related to his visitation time. The father argued that his costs for transporting the children between states and the expenses incurred during his extended summer visitation constituted a 'significant change in circumstances' justifying a reduction in his monthly child support payment. The trial court found that these costs were anticipated at the time of the original decree and did not constitute an unforeseen change. The appellate court reviewed the trial court's decision under the abuse of discretion standard, noting that the trial court must look for a change that is substantial and continuing. The court upheld the trial court's finding that the father's transportation costs were not unforeseen and that the current child support amount was sufficient to cover these needs. The decision confirms that recurring or anticipated costs, even if significant, do not automatically qualify for a modification of child support if they were part of the initial financial landscape established during the dissolution.

## In re Marriage of A.L.W. and D.W.

412 S.W.3d 403 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's classification of the property. It held that the party asserting the separate property interest failed to meet the burden of proof through clear and convincing evidence. This divorce case concerned the characterization of real estate purchased during the marriage using funds that one party claimed were a gift from a parent. The trial court classified the home as marital property, resulting in an equal division of the equity. The husband appealed, arguing that the down payment came from his non-marital inheritance and that this portion should have been set aside as his separate property. The appellate court analyzed the principles of tracing assets in divorce proceedings. It noted that when separate property is commingled with marital property, the burden is on the party claiming the separate interest to prove the source of the funds by clear and convincing evidence. The court found that the husband failed to produce sufficient bank records or other documentation to definitively trace the funds from his inheritance to the purchase of the home. As a result, the court concluded that the trial court did not err in treating the home as marital property subject to division.

## In re Marriage of A.R. and R.R.

457 S.W.3d 839 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the trial court's finding that the former husband was in contempt for failing to pay child support and maintenance as ordered. However, the court reversed the modification of maintenance, finding insufficient evidence of a substantial change in circumstances to warrant such a modification. This appeal concerned a post-dissolution contempt action related to child support and maintenance obligations. The former wife filed a motion seeking to hold the former husband in contempt for failing to pay the full amount of court-ordered child support and maintenance. The trial court found the husband in contempt, ordered him to pay arrearages, and modified his maintenance obligation. The husband appealed, arguing that the trial court erred in finding him in contempt and in modifying his maintenance without sufficient evidence of a change in circumstances.
