## Laut v. City of Arnold

491 S.W.3d 248 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2016 · Missouri

3 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that the City of Arnold failed to provide a specific, legally sufficient justification for withholding the requested documents. It affirmed that governmental bodies must clearly articulate which statutory exemption applies to each specific document withheld. This case involved a citizen's request for records related to a city investigation into police misconduct. The City of Arnold refused to produce several documents, citing various Sunshine Law exemptions, including personnel records and litigation-related privilege. The requester challenged these denials, arguing that the public interest outweighed the City's claim of confidentiality. The core issue on appeal was whether the trial court correctly applied the balancing test for nondisclosure and whether the City had acted with the requisite intent to violate the Sunshine Law. The appellate court reviewed the administrative process used by the City to determine if they had complied with the statutory requirements for closing a meeting or denying a record request. The case is significant because it clarifies the burden of proof placed on a governmental body when it invokes exemptions to deny access to public documents, particularly those involving public safety officials and internal administrative reviews. The court emphasized that vague assertions of confidentiality are insufficient to overcome the presumption of openness established by the Missouri Sunshine Law.

## Lazaroff v. Culver

17 S.W.3d 608 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2000 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a landlord has a duty to maintain common areas in a reasonably safe condition. It affirmed that the evidence was sufficient for a jury to conclude the landlord had constructive notice of the dangerous carpet. This case dealt with a slip and fall injury occurring on the premises of a residential landlord. The plaintiff, a guest of the tenant, tripped over a loose carpet in a common area of the apartment complex. The main dispute was whether the landlord had received adequate notice of the carpet's condition. The court focused on the 'duty to repair' within common areas that are reserved for the use of multiple tenants. It examined the requirements for constructive notice and whether the duration of the defect was sufficient to constitute negligence by the management company. The decision clarifies the extent to which landlords are obligated to inspect and remediate common areas, emphasizing that constructive notice remains a vital component of the plaintiff's burden in premises liability cases in Missouri.

## Ledbetter v. Goodyear Tire & Rubber Co.

550 U.S. 618 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2007 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The time limit for filing a pay discrimination claim begins at the date the initial discriminatory pay decision is made. This ruling restricted the ability of plaintiffs to challenge long-term pay disparities unless they act within the short window following the initial decision. Lilly Ledbetter discovered late in her career at Goodyear that she had been paid significantly less than her male counterparts for many years. She sued under Title VII, arguing that the pay disparity resulted from discriminatory performance evaluations conducted years earlier. The Supreme Court held that the statute of limitations for filing an EEOC charge regarding discriminatory pay begins at the moment the discriminatory pay decision is initially made, not each time a paycheck is issued. Consequently, Ledbetter's claim was barred as untimely because she failed to file within 180 days of the original discriminatory salary setting. This decision triggered widespread public criticism and eventually led Congress to pass the Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act of 2009, which effectively overturned this ruling by clarifying that each discriminatory paycheck constitutes a separate violation for the purpose of the statute of limitations.

## Lee v. Monsanto Company

415 S.W.3d 122 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a safety violation penalty requires clear proof of intentional, willful misconduct by the employee. If the employer does not consistently enforce the rule, the penalty will not be applied. A laboratory worker alleged chemical exposure resulted in skin sensitivities. The employer denied liability, claiming the employee failed to properly follow safety protocols for handling chemicals, which was a violation of company policy. The employer sought to reduce the award by 15% pursuant to the 'willful misconduct' or 'rule violation' penalty under Missouri law. The Commission denied the reduction, finding the employee's deviation from safety protocols was unintentional and that the employer failed to enforce the safety policy consistently. The employer appealed the refusal to apply the penalty. The appellate court reviewed the requirements for a safety violation penalty, noting that the employer must show the claimant knowingly and intentionally violated a rule. The court held that the evidence supported the Commission's finding that the rule was not strictly enforced, and therefore, the penalty was not mandatory. The court affirmed the full award, emphasizing the burden on the employer to prove the 'willful' nature of the misconduct.

## Leegin Creative Leather Products, Inc. v. PSKS, Inc.

551 U.S. 877 · U.S. Supreme Court · 2007 · Federal

4 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Supreme Court overruled the per se ban on vertical price-fixing agreements, holding that they are to be evaluated under the rule of reason. This decision allows manufacturers more flexibility in setting minimum prices with their distributors. This case fundamentally changed the legal standard for vertical price-fixing, overruling a century of precedent established in Dr. Miles Medical Co. v. John D. Park & Sons Co. The case involved Leegin, a manufacturer of women's apparel and accessories, which refused to sell its products to retailers that discounted below a suggested retail price (SRP). PSKS, a retailer, challenged this policy under the Sherman Act. Historically, all vertical price-fixing (resale price maintenance) was considered per se illegal. However, the Supreme Court held that such agreements should instead be evaluated under the 'rule of reason' analysis. The Court reasoned that manufacturers may use resale price maintenance to promote interbrand competition, improve services, and prevent free-riding by discounters. The ruling shifted the burden of proof to the plaintiff to demonstrate that a manufacturer's pricing policies result in an unreasonable restraint of trade that outweighs potential pro-competitive benefits, effectively making it more difficult for retailers to successfully challenge manufacturer pricing mandates.

## Lemp Brewing Co. v. Union Electric Co.

309 S.W.2d 680 · Missouri Court of Appeals, St. Louis · 1958 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that 'as is' clauses in commercial leases are valid and enforceable. Such clauses effectively shift the risk of mechanical failure from the landlord to the tenant. This case addressed whether a landlord could be held liable for damages caused by the failure of a heating system that was leased along with the commercial building. The tenant argued that the landlord had an implied duty to provide a functional HVAC system as a component of the leased premises. The landlord, however, pointed to a 'take the premises as is' clause in the commercial lease agreement. The court weighed the language of the 'as is' clause against the general duty of a landlord to provide a safe structure. It concluded that in a commercial context, parties are free to allocate the risk of equipment failure through an 'as is' clause. Because the tenant had the opportunity to inspect the property and the system prior to signing the lease, the 'as is' provision was held to be valid and binding, relieving the landlord of any obligation to fix the HVAC system.

## Lester v. McClatchy Newspaper, Inc.

601 S.W.3d 301 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the trial court erred in granting summary judgment by failing to apply the correct economic realities test. It remanded the case to determine if the worker was an employee under the MMWL. The court emphasized that contractual labels do not override the actual control exercised by the employer. The plaintiff, a delivery driver, sought recovery for unpaid wages, arguing that the employer's compensation structure violated Missouri law by failing to account for all hours worked during the delivery process. The central issue was whether the plaintiff was an independent contractor or an employee under the 'economic realities' test, which determines coverage under the Missouri Minimum Wage Law. The employer maintained that the driver operated as an independent contractor, thus exempting them from wage and hour requirements regarding minimum wage and overtime. The trial court held that the driver was an independent contractor, leading to the dismissal of the wage claims. Upon review, the appellate court analyzed the level of control the newspaper exerted over the means and methods of the delivery, including routing instructions, specific equipment requirements, and the degree of independence the driver exercised in performing the job. The court noted that while some factors suggested independence, the restrictive nature of the contractual provisions indicated an employer-employee relationship for the purposes of the MMWL. The appellate court concluded that the trial court applied an incorrect legal standard when evaluating the totality of the circumstances surrounding the working relationship and remanded the matter for further evaluation of the statutory definitions of employee.

## Lester v. McDaniel

456 S.W.3d 873 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2015 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that an express easement is not abandoned by mere non-use. The defendants' obstruction of the easement was improper as no intent to abandon was proven. This litigation involved the creation and termination of an easement by deed. The plaintiffs held a deeded easement for a driveway, but the defendants installed a fence that blocked access, claiming the easement had been abandoned due to non-use for several years. The appellate court examined the legal standards for abandonment of an express easement. It is well-settled in Missouri that an easement created by a grant in a deed cannot be extinguished by mere non-use, regardless of the duration, unless there is also a clear and unequivocal act demonstrating an intention to abandon the right. The defendants argued that the plaintiffs' failure to use the driveway for over a decade constituted abandonment, but the court disagreed, citing the lack of evidence of any intent to surrender the easement rights. The opinion reiterates that the law protects express property interests from being lost simply through inactivity. The

Second stored summary court ordered the removal of the fence and restored the plaintiffs' access, emphasizing that express easements are robust property rights that require explicit actions to terminate.

## Lester v. Sayles

850 S.W.2d 855 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1993 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the 'loss of chance' theory of causation is not recognized in Missouri medical malpractice law. Recovery requires proof that the defendant's negligence was a direct and proximate cause of the injury. This medical malpractice and negligence case involved the standard of care for emergency room personnel in diagnosing a life-threatening condition. The plaintiff alleged that the medical staff failed to timely diagnose and treat a condition, leading to permanent injury. The central dispute was the 'loss of chance' doctrine and whether Missouri law permits recovery for the loss of a chance of a better outcome, even if the final result was not 'more likely than not' caused by the negligence. The court examined the policy implications of expanding causation standards in medical negligence cases. The appellate court reviewed expert testimony and the jury instructions used at the trial level to determine if the standard for causation had been properly applied to the clinical setting. The case provides critical guidance on how Missouri courts handle causation and the standard of proof required in complex medical negligence litigation, particularly when the plaintiff's health outcome was already compromised by a pre-existing medical condition.

## Levin v. Levin

43 S.W.3d 337 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2001 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the breach of the lease terms was material, regardless of the family relationship. It affirmed the eviction of the defendant for non-payment of rent. This case involved a family-owned commercial property where a dispute arose between relatives regarding a long-term lease. One relative, who was both a part-owner of the property and a tenant, failed to pay the agreed-upon rent to the entity holding the property title. The other owners sued for breach of contract and sought to terminate the lease based on the default. The defendant argued that the rent payments were offset by contributions made to the property's upkeep and that the lease terms were essentially an internal family arrangement that allowed for flexible payment schedules. The appellate court examined the fiduciary duties of the parties involved in the ownership and leasing of the property. The case presented complex issues regarding the intersection of property law, contract enforcement, and family law considerations. The court had to determine whether the failure to pay rent constituted a material breach that justified the eviction of a family member from the commercial space they operated their business from.

## Lewis v. Ameren Missouri

673 S.W.3d 811 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2023 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the Commission's decision, holding that mandatory overtime must be included in the calculation of an employee's average weekly wage. The court held this accurately reflects the lost earning potential of the injured worker. The claimant, a lineman, sustained an electrical burn injury. The case involved a dispute over the calculation of the 'average weekly wage' for the purpose of temporary total disability (TTD) payments. The employer argued that the calculation should only include base pay, while the claimant argued it should include significant overtime hours that were a regular and expected part of his employment contract. The Commission sided with the claimant, including the average overtime pay in the calculation. The employer appealed, arguing that the statute was interpreted too broadly. The appellate court reviewed the statutory provisions for calculating wages, which focus on the earnings the employee would have received had they not been injured. The court found that because overtime was a mandatory and constant aspect of the claimant's employment, excluding it would result in a misrepresentation of his actual earning capacity. The court affirmed the Commission's inclusive approach to calculating the weekly wage.

## Lewis v. City of Kansas City

420 S.W.3d 690 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that interpersonal work conflicts do not constitute an extraordinary event for mental injury claims. The denial was affirmed. The claimant, a municipal employee, alleged that she suffered a mental injury due to harassment by her supervisor. The Commission denied the claim, finding that the alleged injury did not meet the definition of a 'mental injury' under the Act because it did not result from an 'extraordinary and unusual' work-related event, but rather from routine interpersonal conflicts. The claimant appealed, arguing that the harassment was sufficiently egregious to constitute an unusual event. The appellate court reviewed the statutory language in Section 287.120, which distinguishes between ordinary stressors and extraordinary events. The court agreed with the Commission's finding that the work environment, while unpleasant, did not rise to the level of an 'extraordinary and unusual' occurrence that would justify compensation for a mental injury. The court emphasized that the legislature intended to limit compensation for purely mental claims to avoid opening the door to claims stemming from normal workplace frictions. Thus, the court affirmed the denial of benefits, holding that the Commission correctly applied the high threshold required by the statute.

## Lewis v. Healthcare Facility

598 S.W.3d 601 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court held that an employer's valid business reason for a layoff does not automatically immunize it from a claim of retaliatory discharge if the timing and facts suggest that an employee was targeted due to protected whistleblowing activity. Lewis was an employee at a nursing home who claimed she was fired for reporting that residents were not being fed properly, which she alleged violated state licensing regulations. The employer maintained that the facility was facing severe financial strain and was forced to reduce staff, leading to the elimination of the plaintiff's position. The trial court found in favor of the employer, ruling that the plaintiff could not overcome the employer's evidence of financial necessity. The appellate court reviewed the record and noted that while the employer's financial situation was indeed dire, the timing of the plaintiff's discharge--just two days after her report to the state licensing board--was highly suspicious. The court concluded that a reasonable jury could find that the employer used the layoff as a cover for retaliation. Therefore, the court reversed the lower court's judgment and remanded the case, holding that the existence of a valid business justification does not insulate an employer if a jury concludes that the retaliatory intent was the motivating force behind the selection for layoff.

## Liberman v. City of Kansas City

893 S.W.2d 860 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1995 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the litigation exemption under the Sunshine Law is restricted to discussions of legal strategy and risks. It cannot be used to hide general policy decisions just because they are tangentially related to a lawsuit. In this case, a citizen challenged the city's practice of holding closed meetings to discuss a redevelopment plan. The city argued that the litigation exemption applied because the city was involved in a pending lawsuit regarding the project. The court examined the scope of the litigation exemption under the Sunshine Law, which allows for closed meetings to discuss legal actions and settlement negotiations. The court ruled that the existence of a lawsuit does not grant the city a 'blanket permit' to discuss everything related to the subject of that lawsuit in secret. It determined that the exemption is limited to matters where the body is engaged in active litigation or is preparing for imminent litigation, and that the closed-door discussions must be strictly confined to legal strategy and case risks. The court cautioned against using litigation as a 'catch-all' to shield controversial administrative decisions from public scrutiny, as this would undermine the intent of the Sunshine Law to keep governmental decision-making processes transparent.

## Liggins v. Arch Coal, Inc.

395 S.W.3d 594 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while federal safety reporting can support a public policy claim, the plaintiff must provide evidence that the discharge was directly motivated by that report. The evidence presented was insufficient to overcome the legitimate, non-discriminatory reason provided by the employer. The plaintiff, an employee at a coal mining facility, filed a wrongful termination suit alleging that his firing was in violation of public policy because he was terminated after reporting safety violations to the Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA). The employer contended that the termination was due to a reduction in force and internal restructuring. The legal issue was whether reports to federal agencies concerning safety constitute a clear public policy mandate in Missouri that protects an employee from at-will discharge. The appellate court examined the requirements for the public policy exception, confirming that the policy must be rooted in clear constitutional or statutory authority. The court considered whether federal regulations, such as those governing mine safety, can serve as the basis for a Missouri wrongful discharge claim. The court analyzed the evidence regarding the timeline of the reporting and the subsequent termination. The court concluded that while the public policy exception exists, the plaintiff failed to provide sufficient evidence that his reporting was the actual motivation for the termination as opposed to the company's stated economic restructuring plan.

## Linegar v. Armour of America, Inc.

909 F.2d 1150 · United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit (Applying Missouri Law) · 1990 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a product is not defectively designed merely because a safer, but less practical, alternative exists. The design must be evaluated in the context of the product's intended use and performance requirements. Linegar involved a wrongful death action brought by the family of a police officer killed while wearing a bulletproof vest manufactured by the defendant. The central claim was that the vest was defectively designed because it did not provide coverage for the entire torso, specifically leaving the side areas exposed. The case centered on the 'risk-utility' analysis, where the court weighed the trade-offs between coverage, weight, and flexibility of the armor. The manufacturer argued that to provide full coverage would have rendered the vest too heavy and uncomfortable for practical use by officers, thus reducing its effectiveness in the field. The court analyzed whether a design is 'unreasonably dangerous' when the manufacturer makes conscious trade-offs between safety and performance. The decision is frequently used to discuss the limitations of design defect claims when the product is designed for a specific purpose that mandates compromise on certain safety features, provided the risks are not hidden from the user.

## Linegar v. Armour of America, Inc.

906 F.2d 1150 · United States Court of Appeals, Eighth Circuit (applying Missouri law) · 1990 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a product design that balances competing interests like comfort and protection is not automatically 'unreasonably dangerous.' It ruled that the plaintiff must prove that the chosen trade-off was unreasonable. A police officer was shot in the chest while wearing a protective vest that did not cover the side of his torso. The vest was designed to be concealable, which the manufacturer argued was necessary for law enforcement usage, requiring a trade-off in the amount of coverage. The plaintiff argued the vest was defectively designed because it left too much of the chest area unprotected. The federal court applying Missouri law analyzed whether the product was 'unreasonably dangerous.' The case involved a detailed discussion of the risk-utility balancing test, specifically weighing the need for mobility and concealability against the need for maximum ballistic protection. The court concluded that a product is not defectively designed simply because there is a safer, bulkier alternative that would have prevented the injury, especially when the current design serves a different, equally valid utility. This case serves as a leading authority on design

Second stored summary trade-offs in protective equipment and the burden of the plaintiff to prove a safer alternative that doesn't compromise the product's primary utility.

## Lipton Realty, Inc. v. St. Louis Housing Authority

705 S.W.2d 565 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1986 · Missouri

Holding: The classification of a property management firm as an agent rather than an independent contractor depends on the degree of control retained by the principal. Because the housing authority exercised extensive control over daily operations, the management firm functioned as an agent, thereby implicating sovereign immunity protections. This litigation arose from a dispute between a private property management entity and a public housing authority regarding the interpretation of contractual obligations under a management agreement. The core of the case involved the scope of the housing authority's liability for property damage and the extent of the management company's operational responsibilities. The dispute centered on whether the management firm was an independent contractor or an agent of the authority, which would dictate the applicability of sovereign immunity. The court performed a rigorous analysis of the management contract's language, noting that the degree of control reserved by the housing authority was the defining factor in establishing the legal relationship. The court examined Missouri case law regarding the distinctions between service contracts and agency relationships, ultimately determining that the operational oversight maintained by the authority was sufficient to create an agency relationship. This classification was pivotal, as it allowed for the application of immunity principles that would have been unavailable had the entity been deemed an independent contractor. The decision highlighted the importance of clear drafting in government contracts, specifically regarding the delegation of management duties.

## Lister v. Breeden

969 S.W.2d 834 (Mo. App. W.D. 1998) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1998 · Missouri

Holding: The Court of Appeals affirmed the trial court's judgment. The court held that the evidence presented did not establish that the Listers' use of Breeden's property was adverse. Instead, the court found evidence suggesting the use was initially permissive, arising from neighborly accommodation. Once use is shown to be permissive, it cannot become adverse without a clear repudiation of the owner's rights. The court concluded that the Listers failed to meet the burden of proving adverse use for the prescriptive period. This case involved a dispute over prescriptive easements claimed by adjoining landowners. The Listers and Breeden owned adjacent properties. The Listers claimed they had acquired a prescriptive easement over a portion of Breeden's land for access to a driveway and utility lines. To establish a prescriptive easement, the Listers had to prove continuous, uninterrupted, adverse, and open use of the property for the statutory period. Breeden argued that the use was permissive, not adverse, and therefore could not ripen into a prescriptive easement. The trial court found that the use was indeed permissive and denied the claim for a prescriptive easement.

Holding: The court held that the entire amount of the lease agreement was not subject to sales tax at the time of execution. Tax is only applicable to the periodic payments as they are made. The taxpayer argued that the tax should be applied only to the periodic lease payments, whereas the Director of Revenue argued that the total value of the lease agreement was taxable at the inception of the contract. The case centered on the interpretation of the sales tax statute regarding the 'sale' of property via a lease-purchase agreement. The taxpayer claimed that the statutory definitions favored an installment-based tax collection rather than a lump-sum tax. The court evaluated the structure of the lease agreements to determine the true nature of the transfer of property. This case was significant for its analysis of timing for tax collection in lease-purchase scenarios and the impact of contractual terms on the taxpayer's liability. The decision offered clarification on whether a lease is a taxable event at

## Lockheed Corp. v. Spink

517 U.S. 882 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1996 · Federal

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Court held that an employer does not act as a fiduciary when amending a plan, and therefore is not subject to ERISA's fiduciary duties during the amendment process. It also held that conditioning benefits on a release of claims is not a prohibited transaction. Lockheed amended its retirement plan to offer increased benefits to employees who signed a release of employment-related claims. A former employee challenged this amendment, arguing that the employer acted as a fiduciary and that the requirement of a release of claims was a prohibited transaction under ERISA Section 406. The Court reviewed whether the act of amending a plan is a fiduciary function and whether the exchange of plan benefits for a release of claims constitutes a prohibited transaction. The Court concluded that an employer acts as a settlor when amending a plan, meaning the act is not subject to fiduciary duties. Furthermore, the Court held that the provision of benefits conditioned on a release of claims did not fall under the prohibited transaction rules, as the employer was not using plan assets for its own benefit in a way that violated the statute.

## Loehr v. Missouri Department of Corrections

580 S.W.3d 632 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2019 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that if an employer fails to provide adequate medical care, the employee may choose their own doctor at the employer's cost. It affirmed the Commission's findings on the employer's breach of duty. This case involved an appeal regarding the reimbursement of medical expenses under the workers' compensation system. The claimant argued that the employer should reimburse her for medical treatment obtained from a provider of her choice after the employer refused to provide care. The employer argued that it had provided a panel of physicians and that the claimant was required to use the provided list. The Commission found that the employer's panel was inadequate and that the employer had failed to offer prompt medical care, thus justifying the employee's choice of an alternative provider. The employer appealed, challenging the Commission's ruling on the adequacy of the medical panel. The Western District reviewed the evidence and confirmed that the employer failed to fulfill its statutory duty to provide competent medical services. The court affirmed the order requiring the employer to pay for the medical expenses incurred by the claimant's chosen physician, holding that an employer's failure to provide proper care allows an employee to seek their own treatment at the employer's expense.

## Loehr v. Missouri Department of Transportation

645 S.W.3d 609 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court reversed the Commission, holding that the activity fell within the scope of employment. It concluded that the employer's direct benefit and the employee's attendance established a compensable injury.

Second stored summary The employee filed a claim for workers' compensation benefits following an injury sustained during a work-related training session. The Department of Transportation contested the claim, arguing that the activity was voluntary and did not arise out of and in the course of employment. The Administrative Law Judge initially found in favor of the employee, but the Labor and Industrial Relations Commission reversed this decision, concluding that the activity did not meet the criteria of being a mandatory work requirement that would trigger liability under the workers' compensation statutes. On appeal, the court examined whether the Commission erred in its interpretation of the 'course of employment' requirement. The court analyzed whether the employer derived a direct benefit from the activity and if the employee was acting within the scope of his duties at the time of the injury. The decision hinged on the interpretation of statutory language concerning activities occurring during work hours.

## Logan v. Zimmerman Brush Co.

455 U.S. 422 · Supreme Court of the United States · 1982 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that a legal cause of action is a protected property interest. The state cannot extinguish that interest through its own procedural errors without violating the Due Process Clause. Logan filed a charge of employment discrimination with the Illinois Fair Employment Practices Commission. Due to a scheduling error by the commission itself, the required fact-finding conference was not held within the mandatory 120-day period required by state law. Consequently, the commission dismissed Logan's claim. Logan challenged this, arguing that the deprivation of his right to pursue his employment discrimination claim violated the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment. The Supreme Court agreed with Logan. The Court held that a cause of action is a species of property protected by the Due Process Clause. The state had created a system to adjudicate claims, and it could not destroy that right through its own administrative failure without providing the claimant an opportunity to be heard. The Court emphasized that the state must provide a meaningful opportunity for the claimant to pursue his claim once the state has established a legal mechanism for redress. The commission's dismissal, based on its own procedural error rather than the merits of the case, effectively denied the claimant his property interest without adequate due process.

## Lollar v. A.O. Smith Corp.

795 S.W.2d 51 · Missouri Supreme Court · 1990 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that jury instructions in product liability cases must clearly articulate the risk-utility test. Instructions that fail to guide the jury on how to balance these factors constitute reversible error. The plaintiffs sought damages for injuries resulting from a malfunctioning water heater, alleging both manufacturing and design defects. A primary issue was the jury instruction regarding the 'unreasonably dangerous' nature of the product. The defendant argued that the instructions given to the jury were confusing and did not properly capture the legal nuances of the risk-utility balancing test. The Missouri Supreme Court reviewed the jury instructions for error, emphasizing the need for clarity in guiding the jury's decision-making process in product liability cases. The Court found that the instructions incorrectly allowed the jury to find the product defective without properly considering the balance between the product's design risks and its utility. The judgment was reversed and remanded because the jury instructions failed to provide a clear standard for the 'unreasonably dangerous' element, which is the cornerstone of Missouri strict liability law. This case serves as a key precedent for the drafting of jury instructions in complex products litigation to ensure they align with established risk-utility principles.

## Lollar v. State Farm Mutual Automobile Ins. Co.

169 S.W.3d 591 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2005 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the requirement for filing an affidavit of merit is mandatory and failure to comply leads to dismissal. The court confirmed that there are no exceptions to the statutory deadline provided in Section 538.225. This case involved a medical malpractice claim where the plaintiff sought damages against a physician and related entities. The core issue concerned the procedural requirements of Section 538.225 RSMo, which requires plaintiffs in medical malpractice actions to file an affidavit of merit stating that they have obtained the written opinion of a legally qualified health care provider who believes the defendant failed to use such care as a reasonably prudent and careful health care provider would have under similar circumstances. The defendant moved to dismiss the action for failure to timely file the required affidavit. The plaintiff argued that the statutory deadline should be tolled due to exceptional circumstances. The trial court dismissed the action, and the appellate court reviewed whether the trial court acted within its authority. The court examined the strict compliance required by the statute and whether any equitable exceptions could apply when a plaintiff fails to provide the health care provider affidavit within the specified timeframes allowed by Missouri law.

## Lomax v. DaimlerChrysler Corp.

243 S.W.3d 474 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2007 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the jury's verdict, holding that there was sufficient evidence for a reasonable jury to find a causal connection between the workers' compensation claim and the termination. The court found no reversible error in the instructions given to the jury. Lomax filed a wrongful termination suit against DaimlerChrysler, claiming he was fired for exercising his rights under the Missouri Workers' Compensation Act. After being injured on the job, Lomax claimed the company retaliated against him by creating a hostile work environment and eventually terminating him. The company asserted that the termination was for legitimate, non-discriminatory reasons. The jury returned a verdict in favor of Lomax, which the defendant appealed. The appellate court reviewed the sufficiency of the evidence, particularly whether the temporal proximity between the injury and the termination was sufficient to establish a retaliatory motive. The court analyzed the jury instructions provided by the trial court, ensuring that they correctly reflected the legal standard for workers' compensation retaliation in Missouri. The decision is notable for its analysis of what constitutes 'causal link' evidence in retaliation claims and how appellate courts review damages awarded for lost wages and emotional distress in such employment litigation. The court's ruling underscores the importance of a clear connection between the protected act and the subsequent adverse employment action.

## Lomax v. Sewell

50 S.W.3d 804 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2001 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the board violated the Sunshine Law by failing to follow the mandatory procedural requirements for entering a closed session. Strict adherence to the formal vote and documentation procedures is necessary for any closed meeting to be legal. This case originated from a dispute involving a member of a public board who claimed he was excluded from deliberations regarding a personnel matter. The board had held a closed session to discuss the performance and potential termination of an employee. The plaintiff alleged that the board violated the Sunshine Law by improperly closing the meeting and by failing to provide proper public notice. The central issue was whether the board's reliance on the closed meeting exception for personnel records and hiring/firing was legally sufficient or if it functioned as a pretext to exclude board members and the public from transparent decision-making. The court examined the notice requirements and the specific statutory exceptions under Section 610.021, RSMo. The appellate court analyzed whether the board strictly followed the procedural requirements for closing a meeting, specifically the requirement for a formal vote to close the session and the documentation of that vote in the public record. The court emphasized that the Sunshine Law must be liberally construed to promote public access to government proceedings and that the burden of proving that a closed session was authorized rests on the governmental body.

## Lombard v. Archdiocese of St. Louis

221 S.W.3d 433 (Mo. App. E.D. 2006) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2006 · Missouri

Holding: The Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's dismissal and remanded the case. The court held that the plaintiff's claims were not barred by the statute of limitations under the discovery rule, as the plaintiff did not discover or reasonably could not have discovered the connection between the abuse and his resulting psychological injuries until later in life. The court also discussed the Archdiocese's duty of care in supervising its clergy. This case involved a lawsuit filed by a plaintiff alleging sexual abuse by a priest during his childhood. The plaintiff sued the Archdiocese of St. Louis, claiming negligence in its hiring, supervision, and retention of the priest. The plaintiff argued that the Archdiocese knew or should have known of the priest's propensity for abuse and failed to take reasonable steps to protect children under his care. The Archdiocese asserted defenses including statutes of limitations and charitable immunity (though later largely abrogated for negligence claims). The trial court dismissed the case, ruling that the plaintiff's claims were time-barred. The plaintiff appealed.

## Lombard v. J.J.L. & C.O.

890 S.W.2d 741 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1995 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that in a commercial net lease, clear language shifting repair responsibilities to the tenant is enforceable. Unless the lease specifically excludes structural repairs, the tenant remains liable for the maintenance of the entire premises. This case originated from a dispute between a commercial landlord and a tenant regarding the interpretation of a repair and maintenance clause in a long-term lease. The tenant, who operated a business on the premises, sought damages for costs incurred while repairing major structural defects that the tenant claimed were the landlord's responsibility under the lease. The landlord counterclaimed, arguing that the lease explicitly placed the burden of all repairs, including structural, on the tenant. The trial court found in favor of the landlord, interpreting the 'net lease' language to shift all maintenance obligations to the tenant regardless of the nature of the repairs. The tenant appealed, contending that the court's interpretation led to an unconscionable result and ignored the structural nature of the defects. The appellate court examined the principles of contract construction applicable to commercial leases, emphasizing the intent of the parties at the time of execution. The court analyzed whether the language in the lease was ambiguous and whether extrinsic evidence should have been admitted to clarify the parties' understanding of structural versus routine maintenance. The case required a deep dive into the commercial leasing laws of Missouri and the duty of the landlord to maintain premises in a condition suitable for the intended use as specified in the agreement.

## Lombardo v. City of St. Louis

377 S.W.3d 574 · Missouri Supreme Court · 2012 · Missouri

Holding: The public duty doctrine does not bar recovery for negligence involving the failure to perform ministerial duties. Municipalities may be held liable for systemic failures in training that lead to foreseeable injuries to individuals in their custody. This civil rights and negligence case involved the death of a man while in police custody. The plaintiffs alleged that the officers used excessive force and that the city was negligent in its training and supervision of the officers. While primarily a civil rights case under 42 U.S.C. 1983, it contained substantial discussion of the state-law negligence claims against the municipal entity. The trial court dismissed the negligence claims, citing sovereign immunity and public duty doctrines. On appeal, the Missouri Supreme Court clarified the limits of the public duty doctrine in Missouri, noting that it should not be used as a shield to block claims for intentional torts or gross negligence where an official duty is clearly defined. The court held that while the city enjoys qualified immunity for discretionary acts, this protection does not extend to ministerial acts where officers failed to follow established safety protocols regarding the welfare of detainees in their care.

## Lombardo v. City of St. Louis

594 U.S. 464 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2021 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that in assessing whether the use of force against a detainee is excessive, courts must analyze the specific facts and circumstances, including whether the force was applied after the suspect was fully restrained and whether the officers used techniques that carry a known, heightened risk of injury. Nicholas Gilbert was a detainee in a St. Louis police facility who refused to leave his cell. Officers entered, placed him in handcuffs and leg shackles, and eventually transitioned him to a prone position. During this process, multiple officers applied pressure to his back for several minutes. Gilbert died as a result. His estate sued under Section 1983, alleging excessive force. The lower courts ruled in favor of the officers, concluding that the use of force was not objectively unreasonable. The Supreme Court vacated the judgment, instructing the lower courts to reconsider the evidence under the appropriate legal standards. The Court noted that in evaluating whether the use of force was excessive, courts must consider factors such as the relationship between the need for force and the amount used, the extent of the injury, and whether the force was applied in a way that was known to be dangerous, such as the 'prone restraint' technique.

## Lombardo v. Lombardo

630 S.W.3d 918 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2021 · Missouri

Holding: A social guest is classified as a licensee, and the landowner's duty is limited to warning of non-obvious, known dangers. Summary judgment is appropriate when there is no evidence that the landowner had superior knowledge of the specific hazard compared to the visitor. The case involved a premises liability claim brought by a social guest against a homeowner following a slip and fall incident on an icy driveway. The plaintiff argued that the homeowner was negligent in failing to warn of the dangerous condition or clear the ice. The trial court granted summary judgment in favor of the defendant, applying the traditional Missouri rule regarding invitees versus licensees. On appeal, the court analyzed whether the owner had actual or constructive notice of the specific hazard. The evidence indicated that the temperature had dropped rapidly, and the homeowner had not been aware that a patch of black ice had formed in the specific location

Second stored summary where the fall occurred. The appellate court emphasized that under Missouri law, a landowner is not an insurer of safety for social guests and must only exercise reasonable care to warn of known, non-obvious dangers. Because the plaintiff could not prove the defendant had superior knowledge of the condition, the summary judgment was affirmed.

## Lombardo v. Lombardo

120 S.W.3d 232 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2003 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a property owner owes a duty to a licensee to warn of or make safe a dangerous condition of which the owner has actual knowledge. The jury verdict was affirmed as the evidence supported a finding that the defendant was aware of the dangerous condition. This personal injury litigation involved a dispute between family members over an accident occurring on private residential property. The plaintiff alleged negligence after sustaining injuries from a deck collapse. The defense argued that the plaintiff, as a social guest, was a licensee rather than an invitee, which significantly lowered the duty of care owed by the property owner. The central issue was whether the owner had knowledge of the structural defect and failed to warn the guest. The case required a detailed analysis of the status of guests under Missouri common law. Expert testimony regarding the structural integrity of the deck and the visibility of the rot that caused the collapse was central to the case. The court reviewed the trial court's instructions to the jury regarding the duty owed by a property owner to a licensee regarding known, non-obvious dangers.

## Lombardo v. SSM Health Care St. Louis

544 S.W.3d 211 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The Court held that the claim was one for medical malpractice rather than general negligence because the patient's safety was a fundamental component of the medical care provided. Consequently, the claims were subject to the procedural requirements governing medical malpractice actions. This high-profile case involved claims against a hospital for injuries sustained by a patient while in the hospital's care. The legal issue revolved around whether the claim sounded in general negligence or medical malpractice. The distinction was critical because medical malpractice claims are subject to the specific procedural requirements of Chapter 538 RSMo, including the affidavit of merit and caps on damages, whereas general negligence claims are not. The plaintiff argued that the hospital staff failed to prevent the patient's fall, which the plaintiff characterized as a routine safety issue, not a clinical treatment error. The hospital countered that the patient's care, including supervision, was intrinsically tied to the medical care provided by physicians and nurses. The Supreme Court examined the definition of 'health care services' and whether the oversight of a patient's physical safety during a hospital stay falls under the umbrella of medical malpractice.

## Lombardo v. SSM Health St. Louis University Hospital

648 S.W.3d 727 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that official immunity did not bar the claims because the staff's actions involved the violation of mandatory, ministerial safety protocols rather than discretionary medical judgment. The case was remanded for further proceedings. This high-profile case involved a medical malpractice claim stemming from the death of a patient who allegedly suffered from improper restraint techniques while under psychiatric care. The plaintiff, the decedent's estate, sued the hospital and individual medical staff for wrongful death based on negligence. The defendants argued that their actions were protected under the doctrine of sovereign immunity or official immunity, given the hospital's status and the nature of the emergency medical care provided. The trial court had to determine if the medical staff's actions constituted a discretionary act entitled to immunity or a ministerial duty where negligence could be actionable. The legal proceedings extensively analyzed the nature of medical judgment versus adherence to hospital safety protocols. The case was significant for its examination of the limits of official immunity in the context of private health care providers operating within a state-associated hospital system, setting a precedent for how staff conduct is evaluated under Missouri negligence law.

## Long v. Dillard

939 S.W.2d 568 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1997 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while a landlord has a duty to maintain premises, a landlord is not liable for injuries caused by defects of which they had no notice. Negligence per se requires a clear violation of a statute specifically intended to protect the class of persons to which the tenant belongs. This matter involved a tenant who sued their landlord for damages related to injuries sustained during a fire in the residential rental unit. The tenant alleged that the landlord was negligent in maintaining the electrical wiring and smoke detectors, which violated local housing

Second stored summary codes. The landlord argued that they had no notice of any electrical defect and that the tenant's storage of flammable materials contributed to the incident. The trial court granted summary judgment in favor of the landlord, finding no evidence of negligence. The tenant appealed, arguing that the landlord had a non-delegable duty to maintain the premises in a safe condition and that the violation of a housing ordinance constituted negligence per se. The appellate court reviewed the duty of care owed by landlords to tenants regarding premises safety. The court focused on the requirements for establishing landlord liability for injuries occurring on the leased premises, particularly regarding the landlord's knowledge of potential hazards. The analysis addressed the distinction between statutory duties and the general common law standard of care, evaluating whether the landlord had breached a duty that proximately caused the injuries sustained.

## Long v. Ford Motor Co.

43 S.W.3d 773 (Mo. App. W.D. 2001) · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2001 · Missouri

Holding: The Court of Appeals reversed the trial court's judgment, holding that the plaintiff presented sufficient evidence for a jury to find that the vehicle's design was unreasonably dangerous. The court found that the plaintiff met the burden of proof under the risk-utility test, demonstrating that the foreseeable risks of harm from the design outweighed its utility. The case was remanded for a new trial. This product liability suit stemmed from injuries sustained in a vehicle fire. The plaintiff alleged that a design defect in the vehicle's electrical system caused the fire, which resulted in severe burns. The defendant manufacturer argued that the plaintiff had not proven a design defect or that such a defect was the cause of the fire. The court applied the risk-utility test, requiring the plaintiff to demonstrate that the risks of the design outweighed its benefits. Evidence regarding the feasibility of alternative designs was also considered.

## Lopez v. J.M. Smucker Co.

522 S.W.3d 315 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the award, holding that the repetitive nature of the job was the prevailing factor. The evidence sufficiently linked the work motions to the physical injury. The employee sought benefits for a repetitive stress injury to her wrists caused by high-speed assembly line work. The employer challenged the claim, citing the lack of a specific, traumatic accident and arguing that the condition was an aging process, not a work-related injury. The Commission originally granted benefits, finding that the constant, repetitive motions were the 'prevailing factor' in the onset of the injury. The employer appealed, questioning the sufficiency of the medical evidence connecting the repetitive motions to the carpal tunnel diagnosis. The appellate court examined the statutory requirement that an injury be 'clearly and directly' traceable to the employment. The court concluded that the Commission's decision was based on competent medical testimony that sufficiently isolated the workplace motions from the employee's personal health factors, thus meeting the evidentiary threshold for a compensable work-related injury.

## Lopez v. Three Rivers Elec. Co-op

26 S.W.3d 151 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2000 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that while compliance with safety codes is evidence of due care, it is not dispositive. It remanded the case for trial, finding a genuine issue of material fact existed regarding the utility's knowledge of the work. The plaintiff, a construction worker, was injured when a crane he was operating came into contact with an uninsulated power line. He sued the electric cooperative, alleging they were negligent in the design, placement, and maintenance of the power line. The defendant contended that the risk was obvious and that they complied with all relevant industry safety codes. The case presented complex questions regarding the non-delegable duty of utility companies and the standard of care in high-voltage environments. The court examined whether the defendant had actual knowledge of the construction activity taking place in the vicinity of the lines and failed to take action to de-energize or relocate them. This case provides a detailed analysis of professional negligence standards in the utility industry and the impact of OSHA compliance on tort liability in Missouri.

## Lorenzo v. SEC

587 U.S. ___ · Supreme Court of the United States · 2019 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that individuals who disseminate false statements with the intent to defraud can be held liable under subsections (a) and (c) of Rule 10b-5, even if they did not 'make' the statements under the meaning of subsection (b). Disseminating false information constitutes participating in a fraudulent scheme. Francis Lorenzo, an investment banker, sent two emails to potential investors containing statements he knew were false, at the direction of his boss. The SEC charged him with violating both the anti-fraud provisions of the Exchange Act and Rule 10b-5. Lorenzo argued that under Janus, he could not be the 'maker' of the statements because he was merely relaying his boss's content, and therefore could not be liable for the misstatements. The Supreme Court looked at whether someone who does not 'make' a false statement can still be liable under the broad 'scheme' provisions of Rule 10b-5 if they knowingly send those statements to investors. The Court found that even if a defendant does not qualify as the 'maker' of a statement under the specific provisions of Rule 10b-5(b), they can still face liability under subsections (a) and (c) for employing a device, scheme, or artifice to defraud if they disseminate false information to the investing public.

## Lorenzo v. SEC

139 S. Ct. 1094 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2019 · Federal

Also captioned Lorenzo v. Securities and Exchange Commission

Holding: The Supreme Court held that individuals who disseminate false statements with the intent to defraud can be held liable under subsections (a) and (c) of Rule 10b-5, even if they did not 'make' the statements under the narrower interpretation of subsection (b). Francis Lorenzo, a director of investment banking, sent emails to prospective investors regarding a bond offering. He knew the information in the emails was false, but he sent them at the direction of his boss. The SEC found Lorenzo liable for securities fraud. Lorenzo appealed, citing the Janus decision, arguing that he did not 'make' the statement because he lacked the ultimate authority over the content of the emails. The D.C. Circuit affirmed the SEC's findings, holding that even if Lorenzo did not 'make' the statement under the narrow reading of Rule 10b-5(b), he still violated subsections (a) and (c) of Rule 10b-5, which prohibit 'employing a device, scheme, or artifice to defraud' and 'engaging in a transaction, practice, or course of business which operates as a fraud.' The case reached the Supreme Court to clarify whether someone who is not a 'maker' of a false statement can still be liable for securities fraud under the other prongs of Rule 10b-5.

Second stored summary Holding: The Supreme Court held that individuals who disseminate false statements with the intent to defraud can be held liable under subsections (a) and (c) of Rule 10b-5 and Section 17(a)(1) of the Securities Act, even if they did not 'make' the statement within the meaning of subsection (b). Francis Lorenzo, an investment banker, knowingly sent emails containing false statements to investors on behalf of his employer, which he knew were inaccurate. The SEC charged Lorenzo with violating Rule 10b-5. Lorenzo argued that he could not be a primary violator under Rule 10b-5(b) because he did not 'make' the statements, as he was merely transmitting them. He relied on the Janus Capital Group, Inc. v. First Derivative Traders decision, which held that only the party with 'ultimate authority' over a statement can 'make' it. The Supreme Court addressed whether someone who does not 'make' a statement under subsection (b) can still be held liable for violating the other subsections of Rule 10b-5 if they disseminate false information with the intent to defraud. The Court held that even if Lorenzo did not 'make' the statement, his dissemination of it with intent to deceive constituted a 'device,' 'scheme,' or 'artifice' to defraud under subsection (a) and a 'practice' that operated as a fraud under subsection (c). This decision expanded the scope of liability for participants in fraudulent schemes who do not have final authority over the written misstatements themselves.

## Lowdermilk v. Vescovo Building Co.

91 S.W.3d 617 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2002 · Missouri

Holding: Residential builders are subject to a duty to construct homes in a workmanlike manner. Adherence to building codes does not necessarily preclude a finding of negligence if the builder failed to act reasonably in their professional capacity. This case involved a negligence and misrepresentation claim regarding the construction of a new home. The plaintiffs alleged that the builder failed to properly inspect and stabilize the soil before construction, resulting in significant foundation damage. The defendant contended that the damage was due to natural environmental factors and that the builder complied with all local building codes. The trial court found for the plaintiffs, and the builder appealed, challenging the sufficiency of the evidence. The appellate court focused on the standard of care required of residential builders. The court held that builders owe a duty to subsequent purchasers to construct homes in a workmanlike manner and to adhere to industry standards, regardless of strict code compliance. The evidence presented during the trial regarding the builder's failure to perform adequate site investigation was sufficient to support a finding of negligence. The appellate court affirmed the verdict, emphasizing that code compliance is not a complete defense against a claim of professional negligence in construction.

## Lowe v. Hill

658 S.W.2d 512 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1983 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that continuous maintenance of land up to a visible barrier like a hedge for the statutory period is sufficient to establish adverse possession. The court affirmed the trial court's finding of ownership based on consistent, long-term possession. This lawsuit centered on a claim of adverse possession of a strip of land that had been separated by a hedge for over 40 years. The plaintiffs sought to quiet title to the area, arguing that their continuous maintenance of the hedge and the soil on the defendants' side of the survey line constituted adverse possession. The defendants, who had recently purchased the property, relied on their survey to claim the area. The trial court found in favor of the plaintiffs, citing the long-term, visible, and exclusive maintenance of the area. The

Second stored summary defendants appealed, arguing that the trial court ignored their expert testimony regarding the survey and misapplied the legal standards for 'exclusivity.' The appellate court reviewed the evidence, noting that the plaintiffs' maintenance was not interrupted or questioned by previous owners. The court reaffirmed that such consistent, visible maintenance is sufficient to show ownership in an adverse possession context, even if the parties were initially mistaken about the true survey line.

## Lowe v. Hill

658 S.W.3d 141 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2022 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that misrepresenting professional qualifications and failing to follow mandatory safety regulations can constitute a deceptive practice under the MPA. It found that such conduct transcends a mere breach of contract. Lowe, a homeowner, entered into a contract with a contractor for home improvements. After the project was completed, Lowe discovered significant defects and alleged that the contractor violated the MPA by misrepresenting his qualifications and failing to obtain the necessary permits. The contractor argued that the issues were merely breach of contract matters and did not involve the 'unfair and deceptive' elements required for an MPA violation. The court analyzed whether a contractor's failure to adhere to local building codes or misrepresentation of professional licensing status constitutes a per se violation of the MPA. The court examined the evidence of the contractor's promises at the inception of the contract compared to the actual work provided to the homeowner.

## Lowe v. Hill

430 S.W.2d 318 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Kansas City · 1968 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that boundary by acquiescence is a valid theory to determine property lines regardless of contradictory survey data. The mutual treatment of a physical barrier as a boundary line over a significant period is legally binding. The parties were neighbors who became embroiled in a dispute over a fence line. The plaintiffs asserted that the fence, which was set back from the deeded property line, constituted a boundary by acquiescence. The defendants, however, had performed a professional survey showing the true deed line was several feet beyond the fence. The plaintiffs argued that the long-standing existence of the fence and the parties' mutual failure to challenge its location during their ownership constituted an agreed boundary. The trial court entered judgment for the defendants, strictly adhering to the recorded plat survey. On appeal, the court held that the trial court erred by ignoring the doctrine of boundary by acquiescence. The appellate court explained that the boundary line can indeed be determined by the conduct of the parties over many years, regardless of what a survey might show. If neighbors have historically treated a fence as the division of their lands, that fence becomes the legal boundary by operation of law. The case was remanded for the trial court to consider the evidence of mutual acquiescence and the length of time the fence had existed as a marker for both properties.

## Lowe v. Hill

304 S.W.3d 269 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2010 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the protection period in the listing agreement was valid and that the agent had substantially complied with the requirements to notify the sellers of the potential buyers. The agent was therefore entitled to the commission. A real estate agent sued for a commission following the sale of property. The sellers argued that the listing agreement had expired and that the sale occurred after the expiration date without a renewal. The agent contended that the 'extension clause' or 'protection period' in the listing agreement entitled them to a commission because the purchaser had been introduced to the property while the agreement was active. The court examined the language of the listing contract to determine if the protection period was valid and if the conditions for claiming the commission after the expiration were met. The case raised questions about whether the agent had strictly followed the notification procedures for the protection period as mandated by the written contract. The dispute highlights the importance of precise drafting in real estate listing agreements to ensure agents receive compensation for leads generated during the term of the contract, even if the closing occurs after the listing terminates.

## Lowe v. Hill

603 S.W.3d 315 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2020 · Missouri

Holding: A general contractor may be liable for injuries to a subcontractor's employee if the general contractor retains the right to control the means and methods of the work. Control, whether contractual or actual, determines the duty of care in construction accident cases. The plaintiff, an employee of a subcontractor, sued the general contractor for injuries sustained on a construction site. The plaintiff alleged the general contractor failed to provide a safe workplace. The general contractor argued that they had no duty of care because the subcontractor was an independent contractor responsible for site safety. The court applied the 'retained control' doctrine, which holds that a general contractor may be liable if they retain a sufficient degree of control over the specific activity that caused the injury. The trial court found no such retained control and granted summary judgment. The appellate court reviewed the contractual and operational control exerted by the general contractor. Finding that the general contractor directed the timing and method of the work performed by the plaintiff, the court held there was sufficient evidence to establish a duty of care. The summary judgment was reversed as the issue of control remained for the jury.

## Lowe v. Hillmark Homes, Inc.

843 S.W.2d 391 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1992 · Missouri

Holding: The protections of the MPA cannot be waived by contractual provisions such as 'as-is' clauses. A merchant cannot contract away liability for deceptive practices used to induce a sale. A purchaser of a new home brought an action against a builder for violations of the Merchandising Practices Act (MPA), alleging that the builder used inferior materials in the construction despite promises of 'top-quality' craftsmanship. The plaintiff claimed that these misrepresentations led to structural failures shortly after moving in. The builder argued that the sales contract contained an 'as-is' clause

Second stored summary and a limited warranty, which should preclude any claims under the MPA. The trial court entered judgment for the builder, citing the contract terms. On appeal, the appellate court reversed, holding that a merchant cannot use a contract clause, such as an 'as-is' provision, to waive the protections of the MPA. The court reasoned that public policy prohibits the waiver of rights provided under consumer protection statutes. If the builder induced the purchase through deceptive statements, they cannot hide behind contractual disclaimers to avoid liability. This case is a landmark ruling in Missouri consumer law, establishing that the protections of the MPA are non-waivable and that consumers can challenge deceptive practices even when they sign agreements containing disclaimers.

## Lowe v. Hillshire Brands Co.

505 S.W.3d 814 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the employer failed to pay final wages in accordance with the strict statutory timeline. It confirmed that the employer's administrative error did not excuse the violation of the wage payment law. The court affirmed the award of damages to the plaintiff. In this matter, an employee brought an action against his employer for failure to provide timely payment of final wages upon termination. The employee alleged that the employer delayed the final paycheck beyond the period mandated by Missouri's statutes governing wages at the cessation of employment. The employer argued that the delay was administrative in nature and that the statute provided for certain exceptions. The trial court determined that the employer had violated the wage payment statute and awarded damages to the employee. The employer appealed, questioning the calculation of statutory penalties and the interpretation of the 'willful' requirement for additional damages. The appellate court analyzed the state statute which mandates the immediate payment of wages upon discharge. The court found that while the employer claimed the delay was due to payroll processing errors, the law imposes strict liability for the failure to pay within the specified timeframe. The appellate court affirmed the trial court's finding of liability, clarifying that the employer's intent is less relevant than the fact that the payment was not made within the legally required time window following the separation of employment. The decision reinforces the strict statutory obligations of employers regarding final wage payments.

## Lowe v. Nationwide Ins. Co.

521 S.W.3d 658 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the contractual one-year suit limitation clause was valid and enforceable. The insurer's denial of the late-filed claim was sustained. Lowe sued Nationwide for breach of contract after the insurer denied a claim for damage to his house caused by a severe hailstorm. Nationwide asserted that the claim was barred by the policy's suit limitation clause, which required any legal action to be commenced within one year after the date of the loss. The trial court granted summary judgment to Nationwide, finding that the suit was filed more than a year after the loss occurred. Lowe appealed, arguing that the insurer waived the limitation period by its ongoing negotiations and that the clause was unreasonable. The appellate court examined the validity of contractual suit limitation clauses in Missouri. The court noted that such clauses are generally enforceable if they provide a reasonable amount of time for the insured to bring suit. The court found that a one-year period was reasonable as a matter of law and that there was no evidence that the insurer misled the insured to induce a delay. Consequently, the court affirmed the summary judgment, ruling that the suit was time-barred.

## Lowe v. Sporicidin Int'l

47 F.3d 124 · U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit (applying Missouri law) · 1995 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the plaintiff's state law failure-to-warn claim was preempted by FIFRA. Compliance with federal labeling requirements precludes claims that a product label was inadequate under state law. In this case, a nurse alleged that she suffered respiratory injuries as a result of exposure to a disinfectant chemical produced by the defendant. The central issue was whether the federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempted her state law claim for failure to warn. The defendant contended that because the label had been approved by the EPA under FIFRA, any state law requirement for a different warning was expressly preempted. The trial court had dismissed the claims based on this preemption theory. The plaintiff appealed, arguing that state tort law provided a necessary remedy for unsafe products that the regulatory regime failed to address. The court had to analyze the intersection of federal regulatory law and state products liability law. The decision explores the extent to which federal label approval acts as a 'floor' or 'ceiling' for safety warnings and whether the plaintiff's damages claim is equivalent to an impermissible state-mandated label change.
