## Lozano v. BNSF Railway Co.

421 S.W.3d 448 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The Court held that the plaintiff provided sufficient evidence to submit the claims to a jury, emphasizing that expert testimony must clearly establish the causal link between the medical oversight and the resulting injury. The judgment for the plaintiff was largely upheld. While primarily a FELA case, the case involved significant discussion regarding medical testimony and the standard of care for diagnosing latent occupational health issues. The plaintiff, a railway worker, alleged that the defendant's medical department failed to properly monitor his health, leading to aggravated medical conditions. The central legal question involved the duty of care owed by medical staff employed by a corporation to its employees. The defense argued that the duty was limited and that the injuries were not foreseeable. The trial court's handling of medical expert testimony regarding the connection between the working conditions and the health deterioration was subject to scrutiny. The Supreme Court of Missouri addressed the sufficiency of the evidence required to hold a corporate entity liable for the medical negligence of its staff. The decision provides insight into how courts differentiate between general corporate negligence and professional medical malpractice in a workplace context, emphasizing the necessity of precise expert opinions to bridge the gap between workplace environment and subsequent medical injury.

## Lozano v. Estate of Meyer

251 S.W.3d 344 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2008 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a claimant seeking unpaid wages from an estate based on an oral agreement must provide clear and convincing evidence of the contract. Without a written agreement, evidence of the nature and duration of services is necessary but may not be sufficient to establish a binding wage claim. This case dealt with a claim against an estate for unpaid wages for services provided to the deceased during his lifetime. The plaintiff, a caregiver, asserted that she had an agreement with the deceased to be paid for her labor upon his death. The issue was whether the claim was barred by the statute of frauds, given the lack of a written contract. The court analyzed the evidence of an 'implied in fact' contract for services, examining the nature of the relationship and the expectation of compensation. The court addressed the standard for proving an oral wage agreement in cases involving decedents' estates, noting the high evidentiary burden required to establish such a claim when there is no written proof of wages owed. This decision serves as a key precedent for caregivers and domestic workers attempting to recover unpaid wages from estates, outlining the documentation required to overcome potential claims that the services provided were purely voluntary or familial in nature.

## Lozano v. Estate of Muegler

485 S.W.3d 832 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a right of first refusal in a lease is a valid and enforceable contract right. Such rights do not automatically expire unless the agreement clearly provides for their termination. The plaintiffs filed an action to enforce a right of first refusal contained in a lease agreement. The landlord had sold the property to a third party without offering it to the tenants. The landlord's estate argued that the right of first refusal was personal to the original tenant and had expired upon the termination of the original lease. The trial court disagreed, finding that the right was intended to run with the leasehold interest. The estate appealed. The appellate court examined the language of the lease and concluded that the right of first refusal was indeed a covenant that was intended to survive the initial term, provided the tenants remained in possession. The court held that such rights are valid and enforceable when clearly expressed in the contract. Since the landlord failed to provide the required notice of the sale, the court found the sale to be subject to the plaintiffs' right to purchase. The ruling reinforces the sanctity of contract rights in commercial and residential leases and ensures that landlords cannot easily bypass leasehold options without facing legal consequences. This case serves as a vital reference for the interpretation of option-to-buy clauses in lease agreements.

## Lozano v. Estate of O'Brien

566 S.W.3d 652 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a restrictive covenant is not abandoned unless violations are so pervasive that they destroy the essential character of the subdivision. Minor instances of non-enforcement do not constitute a legal waiver. The issue in this case was the interpretation of a restrictive covenant contained in a subdivision declaration of trust. The property owners sought to modify their property to build an accessory structure that other residents claimed violated the covenants prohibiting non-residential structures. The primary legal issue was whether the restrictive covenant had been abandoned or waived due to the existence of several other similar structures within the subdivision, which the homeowners association had previously permitted. The trial court granted a summary judgment in favor of the association, enforcing the covenant. The plaintiffs appealed, arguing that the selective enforcement by the association amounted to a waiver of the restriction. The appellate court examined the standard for waiver of restrictive covenants in Missouri, which requires evidence that the violations are so substantial and widespread that the original purpose of the restriction has been undermined. The court concluded that the presence of a few minor violations did not constitute a total abandonment of the neighborhood's residential character or the underlying covenant. Thus, the court upheld the association's authority to prevent the construction of the non-conforming structure, emphasizing that selective enforcement does not automatically result in the forfeiture of the covenant's protections.

## Lozano v. Montoya Alvarez

572 U.S. 1 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2014 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that the one-year period in the Hague Convention is not an inflexible statute of limitations and is subject to the doctrine of equitable tolling. Courts may extend the filing period if necessary in the interest of justice. This decision affects international child custody cases involving noncitizens and cross-border families.

Second stored summary A mother abducted her child from the United Kingdom and brought the child to the United States. The father sought the child's return under the Hague Convention on the Civil Aspects of International Child Abduction. The mother argued that the father's claim should be dismissed because he had waited over a year to file the petition, invoking the 'well-settled' defense. The issue was whether the one-year period in the Convention is a statute of limitations that bars claims or merely a period after which a child might be considered settled in a new environment, allowing for equitable tolling.

## Ltr. from Att'y Gen. to Public School Dist. Boards

Opinions of the Attorney General No. 71-99 · Missouri Attorney General / Judicial Review · 1999 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the student records exception only applies to specific, identifiable student data. General discussions regarding board policies on discipline must remain open to the public. This opinion addresses the application of the Sunshine Law to school board closed sessions involving student disciplinary matters. It clarifies the scope of the 'student records' exception. The law provides that records identifiable to a specific student are exempt, but the school board's deliberations on general disciplinary policy are not. The courts, in citing this guidance, have consistently held that school boards cannot close a meeting to discuss broad policy changes under the guise of student confidentiality. The distinction between a student-specific disciplinary hearing and a debate about expulsion policy is critical. The decision requires school boards to delineate between matters that affect only one individual and those that affect the community. It protects the student's privacy while ensuring that parents and taxpayers can observe the development of school disciplinary policy, maintaining the balance between individual rights and public transparency in the educational system.

## Ltr. from Att'y Gen. to State Reps regarding Sunshine Law Violations

Opinions of the Attorney General No. 59-92 · Missouri Attorney General / Judicial Review · 1992 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that meeting notices must be reasonably calculated to inform the public. Failure to provide sufficient notice or placing notice in a restricted area constitutes a violation of the Sunshine Law. While technically an advisory opinion frequently upheld by appellate review, this document and the subsequent cases stemming from it define the standards for 'public notice' of meetings. The issue was whether a notice posted in a private or restricted area constitutes 'public notice' under the Sunshine Law. The courts have consistently held that notice must be reasonably calculated to reach the public, including the news media. This specific series of decisions established that electronic notice, if used, must be accompanied by traditional methods if the electronic method is not accessible to the general public. It emphasizes that a public body cannot claim a meeting was properly noticed if the notice was intentionally placed in an area that the public would not reasonably see. This has become a standard requirement for all school boards, city councils, and other public bodies in Missouri to ensure that their meeting schedules are transparent and accessible, preventing the practice of burying meeting notices in obscure locations to discourage attendance.

## Ltr. of the Attorney General v. City of Washington

936 S.W.2d 124 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1996 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the contract negotiation exemption is limited to actual negotiations and cannot be used to close meetings for general strategic planning. Public bodies must demonstrate a genuine necessity to protect a bargaining position. In this case, the city of Washington faced allegations that its council held private sessions to discuss economic development proposals. The city argued that the discussions involved contract negotiations and that keeping these discussions public would have placed the city at a competitive disadvantage. The Sunshine Law allows for the closing of meetings to discuss the leasing, purchase, or sale of real estate, or the negotiation of contracts. The plaintiffs challenged the breadth of this exemption, arguing that the city was using it to hide general economic development strategies rather than specific, ongoing contract negotiations. The court reviewed the evidence to determine if a genuine 'negotiation' was occurring or if the city was simply brainstorming. It established that the exemption for contract negotiation requires the existence of an actual, ongoing negotiation process with an identifiable party, rather than abstract policy discussions. The ruling emphasized that exemptions are meant to protect the government's bargaining position, not to allow the government to deliberate on its general business without public observation.

## Luebbers v. Missouri State Board of Chiropractic Examiners

426 S.W.3d 657 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2014 · Missouri

Holding: The Court held that the employer failed to meet its burden of proving that the termination would have occurred regardless of the employee's whistleblowing. The Court reversed the trial court's decision in favor of the state board. This case involved a state employee who alleged wrongful discharge after he was terminated following a report he made regarding the board's misuse of funds. The employee claimed his discharge violated the whistleblower protection statute. The Board maintained that the employee was fired because his position was eliminated for budgetary reasons. The trial court ruled in favor of the board, finding no evidence of retaliatory intent. The plaintiff appealed, asserting that the trial court failed to properly weigh the evidence of pretext. The appellate court analyzed the 'contributing factor' standard required under Missouri law. The court examined whether the board's budgetary justification was merely a cover for the retaliatory discharge. The appellate court found that the board failed to provide adequate evidence to support the claim that the position elimination was purely budgetary and disconnected from the plaintiff's report. The court held that when a report of illegal conduct is made, the burden shifts to the employer to provide clear and convincing evidence that the discharge would have occurred regardless of the report, a burden the board failed to meet in this instance.

## Luebbert v. Industrial Commission

402 S.W.3d 605 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The appellate court affirmed the award. It held that the parking lot injury was compensable under the premises exception and that the subsequent injury was causally linked to the primary work injury. The case involved an employee who suffered a work-related knee injury and later sought benefits for a secondary injury caused by a slip on a patch of ice in the company parking lot. The commission awarded benefits for both injuries, finding the second incident was a direct result of the weakened state caused by the first. The employer appealed, challenging the causal link between the initial injury and the later accident. The appellate court examined the 'coming and going' rule and whether the parking lot incident fell under the 'premises exception.' The court discussed whether the parking lot was considered part of the employer's premises and if the second injury arose out of the course of employment. The analysis focused on whether the initial injury created a 'special risk' that continued even when the employee was not strictly at his workstation. The decision reaffirmed that the premises exception covers parking lots controlled by the employer and that subsequent injuries stemming from a weakened physical state can be compensable.

## Lueck v. City of Saint Louis

505 S.W.3d 345 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the municipal ordinance allowing for the forfeiture of accrued vacation pay was inconsistent with the state's public policy regarding earned wages. It ruled that the employee was entitled to payment for his earned vacation time despite the city's policy. The decision established that accrued vacation is a form of earned compensation that cannot be arbitrarily withheld. The plaintiff, a former municipal employee, alleged that the city violated Missouri's wage laws by failing to pay for accrued vacation time upon his resignation. The city contended that its internal policies, supported by a municipal ordinance, allowed for the forfeiture of accrued vacation pay upon voluntary resignation. The dispute turned on the interpretation of the city's ordinances relative to the state's general wage and hour statutes. The appellate court examined whether the state's wage laws set a baseline that prohibits the forfeiture of earned compensation. The legal debate focused on whether accrued vacation time constitutes 'earned wages' that an employer cannot withhold regardless of the circumstances of termination. The court scrutinized the Missouri statutes regarding the payment of wages upon discharge and whether those statutes were intended to encompass vacation time. This case explores the boundary between municipal home rule authority and the state's interest in regulating fair labor practices across all jurisdictions in Missouri.

## Lueckenotte v. City of Farmington

486 S.W.3d 395 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the policy's definition of 'property damage' did not include inverse condemnation claims. The court emphasized that such claims arise from constitutional taking, not accidental property damage as defined by the policy. This case involved a municipal liability policy and whether the city was covered for a claim of inverse condemnation. The insurer argued that the policy only covered claims resulting from an 'occurrence' that caused 'bodily injury' or 'property damage' and that an inverse condemnation claim, being constitutional in nature, did not meet these definitions. The city contended that the loss of use of property constituted property damage under the policy definitions. The trial court sided with the insurer, granting summary judgment on the grounds that the policy language did not contemplate constitutional torts. The appellate court reviewed the policy definition of 'property damage' to determine if it could encompass the financial and physical losses associated with a taking of property. The analysis focused on the plain and ordinary meaning of policy terms as understood by an average policyholder. This case highlights the challenges of fitting constitutional claims into traditional commercial liability policy frameworks and the judicial reluctance to expand insurance coverage beyond the explicit scope of the policy contract.

## Lueckenotte v. Farm Bureau Town & Country Ins. Co.

395 S.W.3d 594 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2013 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that there was sufficient evidence to support a finding of bad faith. The insurer's consistent undervaluation and reliance on clearly inaccurate repair estimates constituted a vexatious refusal to pay the claim. The insureds brought suit against their homeowner's insurer, alleging that the insurer acted in bad faith during the handling and settlement of their claim following a storm that damaged their roof. The insureds claimed that the insurer intentionally undervalued the cost of repairs and used biased adjusters to minimize payouts. The trial court entered judgment for the plaintiffs on the bad faith claim, leading to an appeal by the insurer. The appellate court examined the elements required to prove 'first-party bad faith' in Missouri, which involves demonstrating that the insurer refused to pay a claim without reasonable cause. The case provided an analysis of the evidentiary requirements for a bad faith claim, specifically what constitutes 'reasonable cause' and whether the insurer's conduct rose to the level of vexatious refusal to pay. The court scrutinized the communication between the parties and the insurer's internal claim handling procedures to determine if the denial was a legitimate disagreement or a bad-faith effort to avoid obligations.

## Lueckenotte v. Kevil

893 S.W.2d 862 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 1995 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that exclusivity is a mandatory element of adverse possession. If the record owner continues to use or maintain the property in a way that is not subordinate to the claimant, the element of exclusivity is defeated. The plaintiffs brought an action to quiet title, claiming ownership of a narrow strip of land through adverse possession against their neighbor. The defendants asserted that the plaintiffs' use of the land was not exclusive because the defendants also used the area for utility maintenance and landscaping purposes. The trial court ruled that the plaintiffs had failed to prove the element of 'exclusivity,' which is necessary to divest the true owner of title. On appeal, the plaintiffs argued that their gardening and maintenance activities constituted exclusive use. The appellate court reviewed the evidence, affirming the trial court's finding that the defendants' continued maintenance and access for utility purposes prevented the plaintiffs' usage from being 'exclusive.' The court explained that adverse possession requires the claimant to demonstrate total control over the property to the exclusion of the record owner. Because the evidence showed shared or permissive-like use, the court held that the requirements for a claim of adverse possession were not met, and title remained with the record owners.

## Lueckenotte v. Lueckenotte

488 S.W.3d 726 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court affirmed the trial court's order for a partition sale. It held that the lower court properly exercised its discretion in determining that physical partition would result in substantial prejudice to the property interests of the owners. This litigation involved a complex property partition action between family members. The parties owned several tracts of farmland as tenants in common. Following the breakdown of family relations, one group of owners sought a physical partition of the land, while the other group argued that the land could not be equitably divided and requested a sale in partition. The trial court determined that partition in kind was impractical given the terrain, agricultural improvements, and the requirement that the value of the shares remain proportional. The appellants challenged this, arguing that they had a right to retain their physical acreage. The appellate court reviewed the statutory requirements for partition actions under Missouri law, which favor partition in kind unless it would result in great prejudice to the owners. The court analyzed the appraisal reports and testimony from agricultural experts regarding the feasibility of dividing the tracts without diminishing their overall commercial value or utility. The opinion serves as a detailed exploration of the preference for in-kind partition versus partition by sale in agricultural property disputes.

## Lueckenotte v. Vandelicht

28 S.W.3d 880 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2000 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that underground utilities can be the basis for a prescriptive easement if there are visible surface manifestations that provide the servient landowner with notice of the existence and use of the facilities. The parties were involved in a dispute over a prescriptive easement for utility lines. The claimants had installed electrical and water lines across the neighbor's property to reach their home. The neighbor argued that the claimants had never received permission to bury these lines, and that the installation was a trespass. The claimants argued that the installation was open and notorious, and since it had existed for over twenty years, they had established a prescriptive easement. The trial court found in favor of the claimants. On appeal, the court looked at the 'open and notorious' element. It noted that while underground pipes are hidden, the visible electrical meter and

Second stored summary the existence of surface utility boxes put the landowner on constructive notice of the use. The court affirmed that if the evidence of the use is sufficiently visible to a reasonably observant landowner, the requirement for notoriety is satisfied. This case provided clarity on how prescriptive easements are applied to subterranean utility infrastructure in rural settings where surface manifestations exist.

## Lueker v. Missouri Department of Mental Health

490 S.W.3d 729 · Missouri Court of Appeals · 2016 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the psychiatrists were entitled to official immunity as their decisions regarding patient treatment and supervision were discretionary acts rather than ministerial ones. The judgment for the defendants was affirmed. This case involved a malpractice claim against state-employed psychiatrists for failing to adequately monitor a patient, resulting in the patient harming themselves. The core issue was sovereign immunity and the exceptions to it under Missouri law. The defendants argued that as state employees, they were protected by official immunity for discretionary acts. The plaintiffs contended that the medical treatment was a ministerial act rather than a discretionary one, thereby removing the shield of immunity. The court reviewed the nature of the psychiatric care provided, specifically focusing on the decision-making process involving medication and patient supervision. The decision explores the thin line between discretionary medical judgment and the ministerial duties required in patient care settings. This case is pivotal for understanding how sovereign and official immunity apply to medical providers working within public institutions, providing a comprehensive look at the legal protections afforded to government-employed physicians performing medical duties.

## Lueker v. Missouri Department of Transportation

563 S.W.3d 791 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2018 · Missouri

Holding: Sovereign immunity protects government entities for discretionary design decisions regarding public infrastructure. The dangerous condition exception only applies to ministerial maintenance failures, not to the underlying engineering design choices. This case addressed a negligence claim against the state department of transportation regarding the design and maintenance of a highway exit. The plaintiff alleged that the lack of proper warning signs and road markings caused a fatal accident. The defendant raised the defense of sovereign immunity, asserting that the design of the roadway fell under discretionary functions which are protected. The trial court denied the motion to dismiss, leading to an interlocutory appeal. The appellate court analyzed the sovereign immunity statutes, specifically the 'dangerous condition' exception. The court had to determine whether the alleged defect in the road design constituted a dangerous condition of public property. The court held that while maintenance of signs is a ministerial function, the overall design of the highway is a protected discretionary act. The appellate court reversed the trial court's denial of summary judgment, concluding that the state was immune from suit regarding the discretionary design choices of the highway.

## Luella LYNCH, Incompetent, by Perrin D. McElroy, Public Administrator, Her Guardian and Curator, Appellant, v. James LYNCH, Margaret E. Treadway, Executrix, Estate of Frank Farneman, Deceased, Respondents

## Luethans v. Washington University

894 S.W.2d 169 · Supreme Court of Missouri · 1995 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The Supreme Court held that internal reports regarding animal research do not automatically trigger the public policy exception. A plaintiff must identify a clear, specific Missouri public policy mandate that is violated by their termination. The plaintiff was a veterinarian who worked for the university and was fired after reporting perceived mistreatment of research animals. He alleged that his termination was a retaliatory act in violation of the Animal Welfare Act and public policy regarding animal care. The university argued that his position was at-will and that they had valid reasons for the termination. The Supreme Court of Missouri reviewed the case to determine if federal statutes like the Animal Welfare Act could serve as the basis for a state-law public policy exception to the at-will doctrine. The court held that while the Animal Welfare Act sets federal standards, it does not necessarily create a broad, enforceable public policy mandate that covers every internal employment dispute concerning animal research. The court scrutinized whether the plaintiff's reports were mandated by law or if they were merely disagreements with the university's research methodology. The court concluded that the plaintiff failed to identify a specific, clear mandate of Missouri public policy that was violated by his termination. As a result, the court affirmed that the at-will doctrine prevailed, and the claim for wrongful discharge could not be maintained in the absence of a clearly defined, applicable legal mandate.

## Lujan v. G&G Fire Sprinklers, Inc.

532 U.S. 189 · Supreme Court of the United States · 2001 · Federal

Holding: The Court held that due process is satisfied when a party has access to an adequate post-deprivation judicial remedy for a contractual dispute. A pre-deprivation hearing is not required when state-law remedies are available to recover funds. G&G Fire Sprinklers was a subcontractor on a state public works project. The state withheld payments to the general contractor, citing the subcontractor's alleged failure to pay prevailing wages, a practice authorized by the California Labor Code. The subcontractor challenged this withholding, arguing it was deprived of property without due process because it was not afforded a pre-deprivation hearing to contest the underlying claim of wage non-compliance. The Supreme Court held that the withholding of payment did not violate the Due Process Clause because the subcontractor had an adequate state-law remedy. Under the California Labor Code, the subcontractor could sue the general contractor for the withheld money, and the state's action simply triggered a contractual dispute that could be resolved in court. The Court concluded that where a person has a clear, accessible judicial remedy for the alleged deprivation of property, the requirements of due process are satisfied even without an administrative pre-deprivation hearing. The ruling emphasized that due process is not meant to replace the normal judicial channels for resolving contract disputes between private parties.

## Luttrell v. City of Pagedale

656 S.W.2d 860 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1983 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that budget deliberations by a quorum of a city's governing body are subject to the Sunshine Law. It ruled that there is no 'preliminary' exemption for policy-making sessions. The decision reaffirmed that the development of public expenditures must be transparent. A taxpayer filed a Sunshine Law action against the city, claiming that the board of aldermen met privately to discuss a city budget allocation. The city argued that since the budget was a complex administrative process, the discussions were too preliminary to be

Second stored summary considered a public meeting. The appellate court rejected this argument, focusing on the definition of a meeting as any gathering of a quorum to discuss public business. The court examined whether the legislative intent of the Sunshine Law permitted a 'preliminary' exemption for budget deliberations. The court found that no such exemption existed. The decision emphasized that the budget is a central policy instrument of a city, and its development should be as transparent as possible to allow for public discourse. The court held that the city's attempt to classify its budget deliberations as non-public work sessions violated the spirit and the letter of the law, as the budget directly affects the taxpayers.

## Luttrell v. Maupin

533 S.W.3d 733 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Western District · 2017 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the sellers breached the contract in bad faith. The court awarded the buyers specific performance and attorney fees, finding no legitimate basis for the cancellation of the contract. The plaintiffs sued for breach of a real estate purchase agreement after the sellers withdrew their property from the market hours before the closing. The sellers cited a 'buyer's remorse' as the primary motivation for canceling the deal, though they attempted to frame it as a failure of the buyer to satisfy a loan contingency. The buyers argued that they had secured financing and fulfilled all contractual conditions, making the withdrawal a breach of contract. The court examined the interpretation of contract contingencies and whether the sellers' actions were performed in good faith. The opinion discusses the requirement of 'good faith and fair dealing' in the context of residential real estate closings. The court looked at whether the sellers' purported reasons for cancellation were a pretext for avoiding the agreement. The case explores the remedies available to buyers when a seller refuses to perform, including specific performance and the recovery of damages incurred through the reliance on the pending sale, such as inspections and moving costs.

## Luttrell v. Stokes

77 S.W.3d 745 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Southern District · 2002 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that the boundary line had been established by acquiescence. The long-term recognition of the fence line as the property boundary outweighed the conflicting legal descriptions in the deeds. The plaintiffs filed a suit to quiet title against neighbors after discovering that a fence built by the defendants encroached upon their property. The dispute was complicated by a survey discrepancy where the plaintiffs' deed and the defendants' deed overlapped in their legal descriptions. The plaintiffs relied on a modern survey, while the defendants relied on a 1950s survey and their long-term usage of the disputed area. The case involved the doctrine of 'agreed boundary,' where neighbors had mutually recognized a boundary line for many years, even if that line did not strictly conform to the plat or legal description. The court analyzed the requirements for proving a boundary by acquiescence, which includes proof of a fixed line, a long-standing recognition of that line by the adjoining owners, and a lack of contest for a sufficient duration. The appellate court reviewed the trial court's finding, which had favored the defendants based on the historical treatment of the property, effectively overriding the more recent, technically accurate survey provided by the plaintiffs.

## Lynch v. Blanke Baer & Bowey Krimko, Inc.

901 S.W.2d 147 · Missouri Court of Appeals, Eastern District · 1995 · Missouri

2 copies of this record were merged in the library export.

Holding: The court held that for a wrongful termination claim to succeed under the public policy exception, the employee must point to a specific statute or regulation. General concerns about workplace safety, absent a clear legal mandate, do not override at-will employment. The plaintiff was fired following a disagreement with supervisors regarding compliance with safety protocols. He alleged that his termination was a direct result of his efforts to ensure the workplace met established environmental and health safety standards. The employer argued that the plaintiff's actions were insubordinate and interfered with the company's operational goals. The court reviewed the evidence to determine if the plaintiff's conduct was protected under the public policy exception to the at-will doctrine. The analysis

Second stored summary focused on whether the safety standards in question carried the weight of law or specific public policy mandates. The court held that while general workplace safety is important, not every internal complaint regarding safety constitutes a public policy exception unless it is tethered to a specific statute, constitutional provision, or administrative regulation. The court found that the plaintiff failed to identify a clear, specific legal mandate that his conduct was intended to uphold, noting that a general desire for safety does not satisfy the stringent requirements established in Missouri for such causes of action. Consequently, the employer's motion for summary judgment was upheld, as the evidence did not demonstrate that the plaintiff was discharged for fulfilling a legal duty or refusing to perform an illegal act.

## Lynch v. Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Missouri

175 F.3d 622 · United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit · 1999 · Missouri

Holding: The court held that a plaintiff in a retaliatory discharge case can defeat summary judgment by producing sufficient evidence to create a genuine issue of material fact as to whether the employer's stated reason for the termination was pretextual. Proximity in time and evidence of disparate treatment are significant factors. The plaintiff brought an action for wrongful discharge under Missouri law, claiming she was fired in retaliation for complaining about discriminatory treatment in the workplace based on her race and gender. While the case reached federal court due to diversity jurisdiction, it primarily analyzed Missouri common law regarding wrongful discharge and retaliation. The employer argued that the discharge was based on legitimate, non-discriminatory performance issues. The district court granted summary judgment for the employer, concluding that the plaintiff failed to establish a causal connection between her protected activity and her termination. On appeal, the court looked at whether the timing of the discharge in relation to the internal complaints created a sufficient inference of retaliation. The court explored the evidentiary standards in Missouri for proving that a defendant's stated reason for firing an employee was a pretext. The appellate court reversed the summary judgment, finding that there were genuine issues of material fact regarding the employer's true motive. The court noted that the proximity between the complaints and the termination, combined with evidence of disparate treatment compared to similarly situated employees, was sufficient to allow a jury to determine if the discharge was retaliatory.

About This Guide & Data Quality
Notes
About this guide
This is an offline reference compiled on September 3, 2026 from the legal reference library inside the LawMind AI
application (Base44 app 6a53429210c1ce40398a53a8). It was produced read-only: nothing in the live library was
altered, merged, or deleted.
What is included
Legal dictionary terms: 39,681 entries. Latin terms: 219. Encyclopedia articles: 1,458. Statutes and regulations:
10,284. Case summaries: 15,021.
Records excluded for suspected OCR corruption
The dictionary source includes a bulk import of Black's Law Dictionary from scanned page images, and a meaningful
share of it is structurally corrupted. 7,107 dictionary records were excluded from the main body: 604 confirmed by an
earlier sampled audit, and the remainder flagged by the same conservative test applied across the whole set.
Records were flagged for scan artefacts such as letters split by spaces ("A DM I N I C ULAR EVI D ENCE"),
definitions that begin mid-sentence, and fragments with no vowels. Nothing was repaired or reconstructed guessing at a legal definition would be worse than omitting it. Every excluded record is listed with its Base44 record
ID in the companion file lawmind_excluded_ocr_records.csv, so each one can be checked by hand against the
source.
Duplicate entries merged for readability
The library contains substantial duplication. In the statute set, 12,011 records were duplicates of another record and
are shown once here: the Missouri statutes are the worst affected, with 9,422 stored records covering only 1,030
distinct citations, and some individual sections stored as many as 257 times. The UCC set holds 3,442 records for
433 distinct citations. In the dictionary, 1,658 duplicates were merged, and where the same authority was stored
under different citation formats the variants are shown together on one entry. Case summaries: 979 merged.
Encyclopedia articles: 699 merged. This merging affects this document only - the duplicates still exist in the live
library.
How complete the case summaries are
Two thirds of the case records are citation stubs rather than real summaries. Of 15,021 case entries, 9,665 (64 per
cent) carry no summary text at all - the stored summary is just a placeholder naming the reporter volume - and 9,922
have no holding. Those entries are kept because the citation, court and year are still worth having offline, but each
one is marked "Citation record only" so it is never mistaken for a real summary. The 5,356 entries that do carry a
genuine holding and summary are the substantive part of Volumes 9 and 10.
Known limits of this snapshot
Three limits are worth stating plainly. First, coverage: the dictionary, Latin terms and encyclopedia were read to
exhaustion, but the statute and case-summary sets are larger than the export interface can page through in one
pass, so those two are substantially but not provably complete - Missouri case summaries in particular hit the
interface's 10,000-record paging ceiling. Second, residual corruption: the exclusion test is deliberately conservative,
so some corrupted dictionary entries remain in the main body; treat an entry that reads oddly as suspect and check
the original. Third, currency: this is a snapshot of one moment and statutes and case law change. Verify anything
load-bearing against the official source before relying on it in a filing.
Recommended next step (not yet done)
A dedicated data-cleanup pass on the live library is recommended and has not been carried out. It should
de-duplicate the statute set - the Missouri import in particular appears to have run repeatedly - and quarantine the
OCR-corrupted dictionary records for re-import from a clean source. This guide is a faithful picture of the library as it
stands, including its defects.
